items.body: Grief is a universal experience that no one can truly be prepared for, and one that each of us inhabits differently, in ways we are unable to control or predict. Written for Paula Ďurinová’s film Lapilli, Petra Hermanova‘s soundtrack follows an exploration of death through stones, caves and volcanic landscapes, asking how the physical world absorbs and preserves traces of loss. The title refers to the fragments of rock ejected during a volcanic eruption—small stones suspended between destruction and renewal—and Hermanová’s music inhabits that same uncertain territory, poised between fragility and endurance. The opening suite, “Five Stages”, moves at a measured pace, every gesture carrying its full weight without ever tipping into emotional excess. Rather than illustrating the five stages of grief to which the title presumably alludes, the music creates a contemplative space in which listeners are left to negotiate that process for themselves, offering emotional cues without ever prescribing a response. Pieces such as “Outcome (Massives)” and “Soft Void” shift the focus towards resonance, silence and the physical behaviour of sound itself. Broken autoharps, their cracked strings given one final voice, merge with the film’s environmental soundscape until it becomes difficult to distinguish music from water droplets, stone or air. Each sound seems pared back to its essence, as though carved from rock rather than composed. By degrees the textures thicken and subtle trajectories begin to emerge, most clearly in “The Cave”, before “Dusk, Breath” brings the work to a close, the organ lending the final moments a quiet, almost liturgical sense of resolution. If In Death’s Eyes confronted bereavement as an intimate human wound, Lapilli broadens that perspective, suggesting that grief belongs as much to landscapes and geological time as it does to ourselves. Rather than offering consolation, Hermanová creates a place where mourning is simply allowed to continue, carried by stone, air and the slow passage of time. In the following interview conducted via email Petra Hermanova elaborates on her production process. Both In Death’s Eyes, your previous album and Lapilli are deeply concerned with death, grief, and transformation, but they seem to approach those themes from different angles. In In Death’s Eyes, death often appears as an intimate, almost bodily presence, whereas Lapilli explores loss through rocks, caves, minerals, and geological time. Did working on Paula Ďurinová’s film change the way you think about death? Did it shift your focus from personal grief toward a broader relationship between mortality, landscape, and material transformation? The way I think about death was most significantly changed by experiencing the death of a loved one. Anything that came afterwards was more damage control. Paula and I went through a grieving process around the same time, and we also worked on our debuts in parallel. When I was in the Merseburg Cathedral recording organ for my album, Paula was descending deep inside of cave systems to film for her documentary, and we kept texting each other photographs of these incredible spaces. They were profound experiences and I remember quite clearly that life made sense again in those moments, the pain was transmuted. I tried to think about working on my album as a way of contributing to the canon of music dealing with human mortality, but it still ended up being a very personal work. I came to a different understanding with Lapilli. Having been invited to write music for someone else’s reckoning with death, I got to observe a separate grieving process. Suddenly there were different associations, metaphors and coping mechanisms in place, and this was a much stronger departure from the personal to the universal. The autoharp plays a central role in both works, yet its function feels different. On In Death’s Eyes, it often acts as the voice of the individual sufferer, standing in tension with the transcendence of the pipe organ. On Lapilli, the autoharp seems to become part of the landscape itself, with its detuned and deteriorating strings echoing caves, stone, and erosion. How did your relationship with the instrument evolve between these two projects, and what drew you to its increasingly fragile and material qualities? Autoharp is a matter close to my heart, maybe more of an obsession. I always feel a bit sad that I can only ever bring two with me while I’m performing because they are all so different. Writing music for film is more free in this aspect, and so my first thought was to use the broken autoharps in my collection, the ones that I don’t dare to restring and tune properly, because they’re too fragile, too cracked. There is an analogy somewhere in there about the possibilities of someone who feels fragile and broken but still would like to be useful. I thought a lot about instruments that are no longer played and just lay somewhere, completely mute. Even one of my main instruments hung on a wall somewhere in Spandau for decades, before I got it. So it was about seeing what kind of sounds can be still coaxed out of these “dead” autoharps, and this couldn’t be further away from how I usually write music. There is a peculiar sports event called the Autoharp Toss in which participants of a musical gathering compete in tossing an autoharp beyond repair as far as they can. Instead of that, I took these autoharps and recorded their swan songs. Lapilli is the soundtrack to “a soft film about hard matter” and the liner notes ask how rocks, pebbles, and mountains die. The music often feels suspended between human memory and geological time, as if grief is being measured against processes far older than ourselves. When composing the music, were you trying to sonify the landscape itself, or were the sounds primarily a way of reflecting the emotional journey of the film’s narrator through loss? Lapilli is now a music release, but in the film it exists alongside the sound design Paula worked on with the composer and musician Agnese Menguzzato. In places they are so intertwined, that it can be difficult to distinguish what is music and what is sound design—in the caves, the pluck of an autoharp string may as well be the sound of a water drop. We talked at great lengths about all these scenes and what they represent. I am a very visual person, so while it sometimes felt a little bit like looking for the sound of the landscape, or of all these various geological processes the landscapes undergo, most often we were working in more abstract terms, superimposing sonic parallels onto fragments of text or mental states that informed these scenes. As the film moves through its stages, the instrumentation develops a narrative also, and the broken autoharps are at first accompanied, and then slowly replaced with the steady breath of an organ. In In Death’s Eyes, lyrics played a crucial role in articulating grief, uncertainty, and the tension between spiritual and earthly forms of consolation. Lapilli, by contrast, communicates almost entirely through instrumental sound, texture, and space. Did working on a film allow you to express things that language couldn’t? How different was it to construct meaning through timbre, resonance, and silence rather than through words and song? By the time I started composing for Lapilli, I had been working with the theme of death for almost two years. I saw it as an opportunity to extend and inhabit the same space with similar means, but with a very different set of constraints and reasons for them. In my practice, the usual starting point is silence. I then fill the silence with as little as I can, or as much as I want to. This time, the starting point was an already emotionally saturated image with an equally charged narration, so I had to construct different poetic principles for this work. How much can I add without overloading this moment? How sparse can I go—and will it still be music then? Previously I hadn’t considered making purely instrumental music, so this was pivotal, it opened a new channel for me. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: This Daily Discovery isn’t the usual kind… These features normally just point you towards something worth hearing and watching; this one also asks you to help. Alice in WonderBand are Ana Vrbaški and Marko Dinjaški, a Serbian duo who have been together on stage and off it for 28 years. They live out near the Fruška Gora National Park in the north of the country and make all their music from the body: hands clapping and snapping, feet stamping the floor, chests and thighs slapped for the low end, tongues and mouth clicks filling the gaps, Ana at the piano, Marko on didgeridoo and darbuka, and the tunes carried in their voices. Most of what they sing began as Balkan folk song, which they take apart and rebuild in the odd, uneven rhythms of the region. On 11 July, Ana was seriously injured as a passenger in a car accident, and she now faces a long period of treatment and rehabilitation. The couple had a full summer of concerts ahead of them, and all of it has fallen through, their income with it. Friends have set up a fundraiser to help meet the cost of her care and steady the months to come. You can donate HERE, or give directly through PayPal at THIS LINK. If a donation isn’t possible, sharing it helps just as much. The song in the video is one of theirs. “Dokonanje”, which roughly means being idle, is a track from their new album, The Courage to be Afraid. They recorded it in May with their daughter, Alisa Dinjaški, alongside “Vrbice, Vrbo Zeljena”, a Gorani song from Kosovo. It is an old piece, written almost twenty years ago, and the words still read like a motto. “Dokonanje” means being idle, but the song argues the opposite: the refrain insists “We’re not being idle”, then lists the digging, mowing and carrying of water that fills the day. The video was filmed at Slovenia’s Kavč festival, a travelling event that for ten years has staged concerts in living rooms, bookshops and town squares under Matija Solce. Alice in WonderBand played the Fragmenti bookshop in Kranj. This year Ana and Marko, together with Julia Lewandowska and Łukasz Malok from CISI, also brought Slavyk to life, a quartet that sets Silesian and Serbian folk traditions to English lyrics. Their debut, 11 Songs of Love and Suffering, was released this June on CPL Music. If you can, stand with Ana and Marko by giving or sharing THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Alive in Wonderband – Dokonanje (Live @ Kavč Festival, Fragmenti Bookstore) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Rising Appalachia‘s “Chance at Wholesome” is a folk song about a specific type of man: the one who performs devotion and withholds it, who lights a fire and vanishes before it catches, who offers the shape of love without the substance. Leah Song and Chloe Smith sing him down in close harmony. The sisters were born in Atlanta and have long been based in Asheville, in the North Carolina mountains, where they took up clawhammer banjo and fiddle in their twenties after a childhood of classical piano and weekends at fiddle conventions across the Southeast. Twenty years of Rising Appalachia has carried them from busking in New Orleans to Red Rocks and NPR’s Tiny Desk, all of it self-managed and independently financed. The group runs on sibling harmony, banjo and fiddle over world percussion, with David Brown on upright bass and baritone guitar, Duncan Wickel on fiddle and cello and Biko Casini on drums. The same lineup plays “Chance at Wholesome”, the sisters’ harmony carrying the verses. “Chance at Wholesome” is the second single from Trade My Troubles, a sixteen-track album due on 2 October, bookended by a traditional Irish traveller song and an Appalachian fiddle tune. The US autumn tour opens with two nights at Pisgah Brewing in Black Mountain, the band’s annual Hurricane Helene commemoration shows, then runs through the Southeast to Moab Folk Festival before finishing in New York. Stream “Chance at Wholesome” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Rising Appalachia – Chance at Wholesome appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Archisorcerus — I discovered this obscure gem in the autumnal times of the year 2024, and got immediately hooked by the music here. This project has offered only this jewel as of yet, however its mastermind "Lord Vrajitor" (and more aliases with the word vrajitor) still seems busy with some other projects, most of which, methinks, are within the black metal domains. Don't get outright frightened, this album of him/theirs (theirs, because he is not the sole musician in the album) is pure prog rock. Or not so pure... At least, it has nothing to do with metal, let alone the notorious black metal. Or is there a sinister connection?.. Haha. Vrajitor means wizard/sorcerer in the Romanian language. Too romantic, isn't it. Ha-ha! - As you can guess from my username, I'm quite interested in such "names", and I already had learned what vrajitor means before even hearing about this band.Well... This is really a solid album, I think. Not too avant-garde, though, unlike its label suggests. Vrajitor seems like a young guy, and perhaps in time he can sharpen his blade and cut through the vines which can block the path to achieve some real authentic originality. This really requires some maturity in general. I didn't want to say that this album is not original, I just cannot hear anything that makes me say "Wow, I've never heard anything like this before!" - Yet, this is a really atmospheric output that has a great soul, besides its musical solidity; which is an invaluable asset. It can sound nostalgic, magickal, occultic (and so forth), and the record is really of high quality in general.Though there are some problems in it, if not major. Firstly, the "fade-out trick" was used thrice, two of which are not okay for me by any means. Secondly, in the 4th track's 0:28 second, I really hear a timing error in drums. No matter how many times I listen to the album (which as of yet should be 20-30 times), that timing inaccuracy still disturbs me, though slightly. Normally I could have overlooked it, but in the rest of the album we hear some flawless musicianship, so that little timing thing really disturbs me a bit. The crash hitting is a bit late there. Dunno if it is a deliberate artistic twist, which can be seen in prog rock, but I frankly get displeased by it. These 2 are all. I mean I have no other "complaints" concerning this truly impressive work.If Lord/Magus Vrajitor releases some other works with this band of his, I'd definitely get excited enough to check them out. His black metal stuff?.. I don't envision myself doing so. Mind you, I like me some black metal stuff, but they are really too scarce... Maybe this album of Vrajitor's Tenebrarium has no direct relation with black metal musically, but it seems to have an indirect one... This album is labeled as "dungeon funk" as well. I had never heard of such a genre before discovering this band/album. Presumably, it is kinda like the genre entitled dungeon synth, albeit not that dismal, conversely uplifting perhaps. Lord Vrajitor also has a dungeon synth past, as I read/know... Yeah, kinda the medievalesque "air" of dungeon synth is here, but without the toxic depressivity. Let the oceans of good spirits seep in! The connection here is that, dungeon synth has some ancient and very strong ties with black metal. In the genesis of the dungeon synth, there already was the nefarious black metal residing in the nightside of Eden, whispering some ominous incantations in dungeon synth's ears...4/5 stars. So, definitely recommended.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Recorded in four consecutive days at the end of August, 1973, at Dieter Dierks studio in Stommeln, it was then released by Bacillus Records in November. 1. "Kabisrain" (7:59) Eddy Marron plays solo baglama to open things up. Bowed bass, Super String synth, gongs, cymbals, and shakers come next. Retaining a Middle Eastern sound and feel as more instruments are exchanged/introduced (steel string acoustic guitar, drum kit cymbals and timpani), the band continues to extend that which feels more like an introduction well into the sixth minute--the song never really congealing into something substantial. Interesting but not even in the same ball park as the wonderful music that POPOL VUH had been doing for three years. (12.5/15)2. "Magika" (8:45) jumping straight into something like you might hear on a TONY WILLIAMS album, the trio of electric guitar and electric bass and rock drums revolves around Peter Giger's dynamic drum exhibition over the course of the first minute, then they pick up on a John McLaughlin riff, bend it and tweak it before flat-lining it into a percussive romp. The ensuing motif is almost minimalist in its subtle-yet-constantly changing polyrhythmic weave. The at the three-minute mark some guitar chords signal a change: one that is spacious, without forward motion, and very bluesy and free--with not a few moments reminding me of Jaco Pastorius-era Weather Report. In the second half of the fifth minute Reinhard starts up a bass riff that remains rather fixed and forward moving over which Peter continues his rhythmic show and Eddy shreds on his distorted Hendrix/Albrighton/Coryell way. Here I'm finding myself thinking more of Jack DeJohnette's early albums as band leader--his collaborations with John Abercrombie. Wonderful musicianship expressing a lot of wildly free-form energy. (17.75/20)3. "Light Shining Out Of Darkness" (3:13) a very satisfying Jazz-Rock Fusion tune with multiple guitar parts, acoustic and electric, and both bass and double bass playing over Peter Giger's laid back power drumming. The opening 12-string guitar work is awesome. (Is it the "Super String synth" making the accordion sound?) (9.125/10)4. "Time machine" (17:47) a STEVE TIBBETTS-like Mahavishnu barrage of guitar and sophisticated syncopated Jazz drumming open this for the opening minute before an interlude of Mellotron-like synth (the "Super String synth"?) and delicate and chromatically-melodic electric guitar note play takes over for about a minute. Then the Tibbetts/Mahavishnu motif returns to start things back up, now moving at the four minute mark into a smoother, forward moving bass, drums, and rhythm guitar groove over which Eddy continues to shred with his Mahavishnu-styled and -sounding lead guitar. Sad that they felt it necessary to use an ad nauseum repeating four-chord rock motif to lay beneath Eddy's guitar shredding over the course of the entire second half of the song! (30/35)Total Time: 37:44Yes, I can hear/feel the Mahavishnu Orchestra inspiration in Dzyan's sound and approach but they have none of the polish and structure of the MO.C/three stars; an album that definitely has Jazz-Rock Fusion energy but seems to be often quite lacking in terms of goals, form, or structure; it feels like a band of extraordinary musicians who only want to show how extraordinary they are, thereby eschewing the creation of memorable music.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Carmine Capasso is a young and ultra-talented guitarist, making quite a name for himself not only in the Italian prog community with The Trip and solo work but also globally. He teams up with the legendary early bassist of PFM. This is a live recording of a pan-Italian 2-year tour and features tracks from the above-mentioned bands as well as other pieces from Lucio Battisti, Ivan Graziani, Ennio Morricone, The Shadows, I Quelli, ELP and King Crimson. Piero Chifa handles bass and rhythm guitar, the drums handled by Jacopo Casadio and Guiseppe Sarno on keyboards. As a counterbalance to AI as well as over-produced sterile manufacture, the band chooses a raw, organic and no overdub presentation, capturing the true essence of live, and verifiable expression. The sugar is in the material and not in the coating. The set-list has three distinctive sections, the more personal material first, a slew of Italian oldies and then a stunning series of legendary covers that features a few tracks we all know and adore. The mood is set right from the onset with a couple of pieces from his solo album, Carmine getting to shine on the terrific "Neve Nera" (Black Snow), a mid-tempo romantic shuffle, with glittering e-piano and subdued rhythm guitar strokes, carving a mini-solo to install the sizzle. A feelgood tune is next , the highly personal "Una Valigia di Perche", (a suitcase of why) dealing with trials and tribulations of a travelling musician, not always an easy task when one has a family as well. "Enigma" is a track from the Trip catalog and its a more expansive adventure, a harsher climate where the keys and guitar settle into more progressive realm. The bass and drum configuration is on it like a car bonnet, an extended instrumental foundation painstakingly elaborated, shining some deserved light on Capasso considerable capabilities. The keyboard contributions are also most worthy of applause. The Ivan Graziani-penned "Monnalisa" is the proverbial epic here, clocking in at 8 and a half minutes, an arch-typical Italian language progressive rock canzone, with plenty of theatrical vocals, wrapped up in a semi boogie-woogie soundscape, an ideal moment with a live concert sequence. The grungy guitar is all brawn and muscle, almost a ZZ Top feel to the solo, the just oozes a wide variety of emotions, including oodles of perspiration. It also fulfills the ritual of introducing the band members with mini-spotlights, so as to show off their considerable talents. Its hot stuff! Keeping those traditions is crucial and a little Morricone reminder will never hurt, especially when its instantly recognizable as vintage cowboy pasta. When The Shadows classic "Apache" follows suite, images of dusty tumbleweeds and towering mesas take the journey not just to the other side of the Atlantic but also back in time. Now, I am not familiar with the I Quelli piece (the band that spawned PFM), yet "Una Bambolina che fa no no no" is a commemoration of the very early days of prog, especially in Italy, with unconcealed pop tendencies, muddied with some gritty guitar shavings, with a discernable the Kinks feel, in my opinion. The Lucio Battisti -composed "Il Tempo di Morire" (A Time to Die) keeps the good times rolling, another rock-blues exercise in restraint and homage to the influences. Carmine' fretboard chugging like a train on twisted tracks, smoky audience sing-along to boot and a sense of emotional synchronicity with concert-goers to shed the inhibitions and rock out. The saloon-like atmosphere is led by the rambling Sarno piano work , and the screeching lead guitar solo that had all the whiskey bottles rattling. In essence, this is what a true and blue live experience recording should transmit and this one shines ever so brightly. Remembering when music was fun. Five monster tracks to slay whatever hesitations one may have held in advance, blown to bits within the very first notes on "21st Century Schizoid Man", a mainstay of sonic brutalism in its infancy at the time (still the heaviest track ever composed, when taken into analytical context), and these seasoned musicians pull it off without any hint of weakness. "Lucky Man" is initially unrecognizable from the ELP original, a clever twist that comes to fruition only when Carmine starts singing the famous lyrics, and the magical chorus elicits smiles of recognition. The guitar-centric sections in such a live setting give this piece a much admirable kick in the back side, the delicate piano and rolling bass in full gear. The mythical Moog synthesizer solo is reproduced toa tee, as it would be a crime to even dare to alter such a bejewelled moment. The three PFM tracks are outright classics, the always impressive and elaborate "La Carrozza di Hans", a demanding labour of technical prowess, concentration and emotive expression, very obviously inspired by the previous KC track. The Sarno/Capasso tandem weave quite the web of sonic capture, the vocals intimately alluring, while the rhythm engine alternate expertly between cruise control and maximum acceleration. What really stirs the imagination is how the audience is fooled thrice into precocious applause. "Impressioni di Settembre" and "E'Festa" are monuments to eternity, the kind of musical rekindling that never caters to ennui, always a wonderful experience, after thousands of spins over half a century, much like "Firth of Fifth", incrusted with timeless melodies that continuously provide goosebumps for both the body and the mind. And that my friends, is what music is all about, and this recording is the second-best thing to having been in the audience. I was there. 4.5 dreamy stories

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. "It Takes a Woman's Love (To Make a Man)" kicks things off with thunderous keyboards and vocals?dating back to the days when Robby and Steve traded licks; an explosive, short track that sets the tone for their signature rock style, blending heavy and folk elements.2. "Two Cents Worth" offers a similar vibe?short and energetic?though it lacks any real progressive flair.3. "Icarus - Borne on Wings of Steel" raises the bar?thank goodness, because anyone listening only to the first two tracks (as is common today) would miss out on this gem. A hard-rocking riff and vintage keyboards (featuring revolutionary Moog synths) combine to create a sort of proto-prog-metal sound. In 1975, there weren't many other bands doing this. The track relies on vocal harmonies, instrumental jamming, and?above all?a folk-prog-metal hybrid that was ahead of its time; the finale is ecstatic and defies description.4. "All the World" keeps the momentum going; it features backing vocals and orchestration, followed by a keyboard workout over a gritty riff?dynamic yet fierce. That riff reminds me of punk rock thanks to its latent aggression, while the sublime violin interlude adds a special touch unique to this band. The finale features staccato violin backing vocals reminiscent of Queen?back when both bands were experimenting with prog in their own distinct ways.5. "Child of Innocence" offers a breather after the side flip; it's a transitional track?starting with the energy of a potential radio edit (hard folk-rock) before shifting into a frenetic instrumental section that enters the realm of prog, with a hint of Thin Lizzy.6. "It's You" features violin and piano alongside a frantic folk rhythm?almost like a *bourr�e*?making it an electric and innovative track for its time. It feels like dancing in a Scottish pub on a stormy night while waiting to set sail again.7. "Mysteries and Mayhem" follows the "Child" formula: long enough to develop a prog atmosphere, yet short enough to keep the listener engaged. For me, this is the weakest track?whereas their long songs were always excellent, the shorter ones sometimes struggle to hold a prog fan's attention.8. "The Pinnacle" kicks off with a symphonic intro?grandiloquent, folk-infused prog metal at its peak! The tone, the vocals, the surrounding keyboards, and that majestic quality that made Kansas a spearhead of the genre. Personally, I'd classify them more as prog metal than symphonic rock?or perhaps right on the border between the two. The bridge?featuring a melody that Dream Theater would revisit much later?arrives while I'm talking; it just goes to show what a rock-solid track this is. Kerry and Steve show off their inventive keyboard skills; the symphonic element is front and center. A lingering, atmospheric feel, and plenty of emotion?though the guitar solo feels a bit too isolated for my taste, given the prominent role of Robby's violin. Then again, that's Kansas for you! (3.5)

items.body: Review by FrancescoProg — The birth of this new album was marked by difficult personal events and major changes within the band. In 2019, longtime co-founder Scott Kelly permanently left the group after serious domestic issues. This led Neurosis into a long period of pause and reflection. For this new phase, core members Steve Von Till, Jason Roeder, Dave Edwardson and Noah Landis enthusiastically welcomed Aaron Turner, a leading figure in post-metal, already frontman of Isis and Sumac, as the new guitarist and vocalist. Turner fit in perfectly, actively contributing to the songwriting with his creativity and talent. The album was recorded by producer Scott Evans in a fast process that resulted in an extremely raw sound.The album, speaks of spiritual and emotional survival in a difficult time, both globally and personally. The title itself sets, on one side, the image of a world on fire, a symbol of the environmental and geopolitical crises around us; on the other, the strength of love, which endures despite everything. This "burning world" also represents the hardships the band faced after Scott Kelly's departure, a time of great change and pain. The "undying love," instead, is the choice not to give up, to keep believing in empathy, love and the beauty of art, even when everything seems to fall apart. The album doesn't stick to pure violence, but also plays with tension and silence. Noah Landis has a key role, adding spectral synthesizers, industrial noises and samples that recall the darker Pink Floyd. Many tracks unfold through long, ritual crescendos, like the closing suite "Last Light" (17 minutes), which gradually turns into an industrial escalation.Aaron Turner, with his deep, cavernous and abstract growl, pairs perfectly with Steve Von Till's desperate screams. Alternating with these two voices are bassist Dave Edwardson's deep choruses and ghostly spoken word, creating a true tragic chorus that perfectly tells the story of the world's collapse."An Undying Love for a Burning World" is an album that grabs you right away, with its emotional charge and bold sonic choices. There are moments that struck me in particular.The album's opening is truly unforgettable for the intense emotional weight it conveys, a goosebump-inducing start. The instrumental introduction "We Are Torn Wide Open" builds an almost cinematic tension. The industrial drones and tribal tolls give a sense of emptiness and looming danger.In "Mirror Deep," halfway through the track, the music slows down, almost stops, creating a suspended atmosphere, then explodes into a section of incredible heaviness. It's right at this moment that Aaron Turner screams the line "True wealth between our fingers slip, as we count the dead". A passage that fuses the melancholic force of post-metal with a shattering impact. Noah Landis's synths take the track to near-spatial levels.Then there's "Blind": the central instrumental section opens into stretched, hypnotic dynamics, recalling the more psychedelic Pink Floyd and krautrock, slowing the pace and leaving room for the music. The following contrast, between clean vocals and powerful growls over an imposing wall of guitars, is one of the album's most intense and surprising passages."Seething and Scattered" has direct, syncopated riffs full of tension, spilling into an unexpected rhythmic turn. Jason Roeder's drumming creates an almost tribal atmosphere before the track heads into spectacular progressions.Finally, the ending of "Last Light" (a 17-minute suite), a colossal suite that closes with the desperate, anguished cry "What have we done?", which fades into a loop of industrial noise, drones and feedback.This album is undoubtedly a masterpiece. Turner didn't just replace Scott Kelly; he became a true creative engine, bringing his deep growl and his unique approach. It's not a nostalgia move, but a work that shows how Neurosis are still the kings of post-metal, able to reinvent themselves and rise even from major personal hardships.

items.body: Review by FrancescoProg — "Let's THRAK Again" is a tribute to the 1995 album THRAK by King Crimson, with the approval and blessing of founder Robert Fripp. This album is Stick Men's first studio record in over ten years, a project that brings together two longtime members of King Crimson's rhythm section from that era, bassist Tony Levin and drummer Pat Mastelotto, along with Touch Guitar virtuoso Markus Reuter.The trio wanted to recreate the same controlled chaos and the energy of the original album, describing it as "instrumental chamber music". They composed and arranged the twelve tracks to be performed live as a lean trio, with minimal use of sampling or electronics.To offer a truly unique experience, the band decided not to release just one mix, but two completely different versions of the same recorded material. The first, Reel One, mixed by Stefano Castagna, follows a track sequence devised by Tony Levin, focusing on a very specific sonic vision and philosophy. The second, Reel Two (yet to be released), mixed by Fabio Trentini, will feature a different sequence, curated by Mastelotto and Reuter, and uses (they say) entirely new sound choices and audio approaches. All tracks are previously unreleased compositions, recorded specifically for this project. The trio described the whole work as a series of pieces created from scratch to develop an "original sonic vocabulary".Stick Men themselves described the album's musical style as "heavy prog with nothing short of explosive kinetic energy", and I agree with that definition. A sound that blends the typical elements of darker, more mathematical progressive rock with industrial, art rock and avant-garde metal influences. The songs have intricate structures and odd time signatures, driven by powerful, massive riffs. Even though they're only three, the simultaneous combination of melodic lines and a rocky bass creates a dense, intense orchestral sound.The album alternates moments of pure instrumental acceleration with softer, more rarefied ambient passages, keeping a tense and always experimental atmosphere. The rhythm section blends the power of acoustic sounds with industrial samples, loops and electronic pads.My favorite tracks are: "Swimming in Tea", which is without a doubt the track that surprised me the most, chosen as the lead single, with an immediate structure and the special feature of having Markus Reuter on vocals, before giving way to a memorable Tony Levin Chapman Stick solo.The opening track, "Let's THRAK Again", for its ability to reproduce the complex rhythms and the "heavy prog" impact that distinguished the original 1995 King Crimson album."Haggin Triptych", an instrumental suite divided into three parts (Renoir, Carriage Parade and Yosemite Sunset), which is a masterful example of rhythmic interlocking. A triumphant and thrilling return, a true masterpiece of composition and musical performance, a must-buy for both King Crimson devotees and lovers of heavier avant-prog. Essential album.

They played excerpts/two-person versions of three of the songs from the new record which was totally composed on Sibelius using classical composers like Stravinsky, Reich, Bjork, Berg, Ravel, Autechre, Debussy, and many others as influences to their Fusion. And there are vocals--and full orchestras! But at the core/base of it all are still the maximalist fusion of the amazing virtuosi JD and DOMi. For any aged music lover I think DOMi and JD are offering something new, innovative, technically superior (like the "good ole days), and progressive. FULL REVIEW COMING as I get further into the music. Stay tuned!

items.body: Nolwenn Boyet and Ronni Gauderat make up the French duo Buzzkill. Active since 2024, Buzzkill previously released an EP on Ganache Records. For their debut album, “Wasteland”, they joined forces with Manic Depression Records, a move that will help expand their audience. “Wasteland” blends Cold-Wave and Minimal-Electro influences, with a raw, uncompromising sound driven by icy synth textures and deep, brooding basslines. Nolwenn Boyet’s cold, detached vocal delivery complements the music throughout. I spoke with both Buzzkill musicians about the making of “Wasteland”. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Buzzkill interview Q: Let’s start with the origins of Buzzkill. When and how did the band come together, and what are your individual musical backgrounds? How did those experiences inspire you to form Buzzkill? Nolwenn: We created a band shortly after meeting Ronni. At first, the project was very different from what it is today. We didn’t have the ambition to make something professional out of it, we just wanted to make music and spend time together. At the time we were a trio, with Ronni on bass and vocals, Axelle on synths and me on drums. When Axelle left the band, we wanted to try something else. We started experimenting with a duo setup where I took over the vocals and synths, and the drums became electronic. We quickly felt that something was working. We compose together quite naturally and found a good balance as a duo. At the end of 2024, we wrote our first EP, which was a starting point for us. It really captured the beginning of Buzzkill and helped define our identity. Ronni: I started playing music at 15, as a drummer in a Grunge band, which later became a Rock’n’roll band that I still play in today. At the same time, I taught myself guitar and started several other projects, including a Shoegaze band and a swamp Garage band with which I toured for eight years and released two albums. Today, I’m also working on a Synth-Punk duo alongside my other projects. My musical background is quite eclectic, maybe even a bit chaotic, but I’ve always liked moving from one style to another. The creative process is what motivates me the most. I just like writing music and exploring different directions. Nolwenn: My journey as a musician actually started with Buzzkill. I had never sung, played synths or composed music before. I had only played a bit of drums when I was a teenager. Meeting Ronni is what pushed me to get into music. I like this kind of unexpected path and I’m still learning as I go. Ronni and I come from very different musical backgrounds, but we share the same approach. Keeping things simple and raw. Q: Earlier this year, you released the debut album of Buzzkill, “Wasteland”. Looking back on the entire creative process, what stands out to you most? What was your vision for the album in terms of its sound and production? Ronni: What probably stood out the most to us were the conditions in which we recorded the album. We did it in a garden shed, during a heatwave. It was a strange feeling to create such cold music while being in 40 degree heat. Maybe that’s what naturally led us towards the atmosphere of “Wasteland”. Nolwenn: Like for our EP, we recorded everything ourselves. We used pretty much the same equipment, but we had improved a lot in the way we used it and knew more clearly where we wanted to go. With “Wasteland”, we wanted to create something that felt more like a complete album, with a stronger overall atmosphere. We also wanted to lean further into the Electronic side of the project. We spent more time working on synth textures, drum sounds and the atmosphere of each track. I also discovered my voice more and found the way I wanted to use it. For the bass, we wanted to keep that raw and upfront feeling, with a sound that doesn’t feel overproduced. It was already part of the EP’s identity, and I think it defines a big part of what Buzzkill sounds like. We were also careful about which songs we wanted to include. That’s why the album only has seven tracks. It felt complete that way, and we liked the idea of keeping it short and intense. For the mastering, we worked again with Mathis Kolkoz (Blind Delon), who also mastered the EP. We really like his work and trusted him for this. Q: “Wasteland” is a bleak and evocative title. What does it represent to you, and which emotions shaped the music and inspired the lyrics? Nolwenn: “Wasteland” represents our vision of an apocalyptic future. It’s a deliberately exaggerated and pessimistic vision, but deep down it doesn’t feel that unrealistic today. We wanted a strong title that would immediately evoke an empty and hopeless landscape. We were quite inspired by the post-apocalyptic and desert aesthetics of movies like “Dune” and “Mad Max”, as well as games like “Fallout” and “Borderland”. The lyrics came from our anger and anxiety about the current ecological and social crises, but also from the feeling of injustice around the fact that the most vulnerable people are always the first to suffer the consequences. Through “Wasteland”, we imagine a future where no one can escape the collapse, not even the most privileged. It’s a sad thought that maybe the only moment when these inequalities could disappear is when we’re all facing the end of the world. Q: In a way, “Wasteland” feels like the soundtrack to a world in decline – a place where people are struggling with both themselves and the reality surrounding them. How personal is this album, and what is your perspective, both as artists and as individuals, on the state of the world today? Nolwenn: This album is very personal because it comes from the way we experience the world today and the anxiety it creates in us. But I think it speaks to a lot of people, especially younger generations who know they’ll grow old in this world, or at least in what will be left of it. As I’m answering this interview we’ve reached 42°C in our city. There are major forest fires happening in our country and people are dying because of the heat, while political responses still seem completely disconnected from the reality we’re facing. It’s become impossible not to think every day about what the world will be like in 10, 20 or 30 years, and under what conditions we’ll be living. “Wasteland” is our cathartic way of putting words and sounds to the distress we’re feeling lately. Q: I’ve always found it fascinating that some of the darkest, most nihilistic themes can inspire such compelling and even danceable music. There seems to be an intriguing contradiction between despair and movement. How important is that contrast to Buzzkill, and what role does music play for you as a means of expression? Ronni: This contradiction is very much part of the DNA of Post-Punk. We’ve always liked that contrast in bands like Joy Division. We like the idea that music can make you want to dance while talking about very dark subjects. We also felt that fast tempos and repetitive rhythms were the best way to express tension and urgency. If we have to live in a world that’s falling apart, we might as well dance through it. Q: Let’s talk about the live Buzzkill experience. What can audiences expect from a Buzzkill performance, and what atmosphere or emotions do you hope to create on stage? How do your songs evolve in a live setting compared to their studio versions? Ronni: Live we try to keep things intense and direct. We don’t talk much, sometimes not at all. We like to step back and let the music take the lead. We try to build a set where the atmosphere can evolve naturally. We like playing almost without breaks because we enjoy the feeling of a 45 min set that keeps moving, with very little time to come back down. It’s a way to convey that overwhelming feeling we have. The bass also brings something very organic and physical to the live experience. I play it through both a bass amp and a guitar amp. Q: Finally, what are your expectations and ambitions for Buzzkill following the release of “Wasteland”? What can listeners look forward to in the near future? Nolwenn: We didn’t really expect “Wasteland” to get much attention at the beginning. We just told ourselves: let’s do our thing and see what happens. We were lucky to meet our friend and manager Stephy just before its release, and she really helped us give the album more visibility. Our main goal now is to keep defending the album on stage, in France of course, but also to start playing in other European countries. We’d like to keep developing the project, see where this album can take us, and keep writing because it’s what drives us in life. We also want to keep surrounding ourselves with people we appreciate, discover new projects from the underground scene, and share the stage with artists we love. We’re already thinking about the next album and we’ve started writing again. We want to explore new directions, maybe something a bit more Electro-Punk, with more repetitive and hypnotic structures, while still keeping what defines Buzzkill. To finish, we just want to say to everyone reading this: keep supporting the underground scene and independent artists. Keep going to concerts in dark and humid caves, discovering local bands and getting lost on Bandcamp. This counterculture only survives because people choose to support it. Thanks for that. And thank you, Stéphane and Side-line for the interview 🙂 Nolwenn and Ronni – Buzzkill

items.body: Krieg-B will release a new album, “Concrete Dominion,” on October 24, 2026, the same date as the band’s performance at the 19th Elektrisch Festival at Club Seilerstraße in Zwickau, Germany. The album comes via Emmo.biz Records. The label describes “Concrete Dominion” as combining the raw energy of EBM, darkwave and industrial music with powerful rhythms, massive basslines and hypnotic sequences. The album is built on the tension between human impulse and the cold architecture of machines, aiming for a soundtrack of urban atmosphere, mechanical force and relentless movement, a dark and intense journey through concrete landscapes where rhythm becomes the driving force. Formats and festival tie-in “Concrete Dominion” will be available as a CD with twelve tracks and an LP with eight tracks across two sides. The CD track list runs “Bite,” “Machinehead,” “Kill The Light,” “Cold Fragments” (feat. Misty), “Perestroika,” “Locked,” “Blackout,” “Libera Nos A Malo,” “Par Dessus Les Cendres,” “Molotov,” “New Zone Of Terror” and “Signal Ahead.” The LP carries eight of those tracks: side one holds “Bite,” “Machinehead,” “Kill The Light” and “Cold Fragments” (feat. Misty), while side two holds “Locked,” “Libera Nos A Malo,” “Molotov” and “Signal Ahead.” Emmo.biz Records is also selling bundled sets tied to the Zwickau show. A “Supporter” set pairs the LP and CD with a 10″ festival sampler featuring an exclusive 12″ mix of “Kill The Light” plus a ticket to the 19th Elektrisch Festival, and a “Fan” set bundles the LP, CD and the 10″ sampler without the ticket. A standard “Combo” set with just the LP and CD is limited to 77 copies, with the vinyl pressed on red and black streaked wax. About Krieg-B Krieg-B is a French-Belgian duo formed in June 2023 by Dominique Lallement, also known for his work as Kriegbereit, Cobalt 60 and K Bereit, and Benoît Buyse, who records as Dreadfool, Anamorphosis and Nihiliste. Based in Reims, France, the pair build on decades of industrial, EBM and darkwave music. Krieg-B released its debut album, “War Drums’ Resonance,” in September 2024 through Emmo.biz Records, in a limited edition of 77 copies that paired the 11-track record with a bonus disc holding a cover of Cabaret Voltaire’s “Nag Nag Nag” and a T-shirt. The band was confirmed for the 19th Elektrisch Festival line-up in April 2026, alongside Portion Control, Escalator, Oszylator and Cyborg Projekt X. “Concrete Dominion” is the duo’s second full-length album.

items.body: Melbourne-based gothic/darkwave/industrial duo Velatine has released the Dead Radio EP on July 28, 2026, available digitally via Bandcamp and streaming platforms including Spotify. The four-track EP centers on new versions of “Playing with the Orbits”, a song the band first released as a single earlier in 2026. Playing with the Orbits – Dead Radio EP by Velatine Tracklist for Velatine’s ‘Dead Radio EP’ The tracklist comprises “Dead Radio Remix”, “Late Night Club Mix”, “Dead Radio Remix (Extended)” and “Absinthe Remix”. The closing “Absinthe Remix” combines acoustic guitar, violin and industrial electronic elements with the duo’s established gothic and darkwave sound. “Playing with the Orbits” was written by Velatine member Loki Lockwood about the 2019 murder of Bianca Devins, an American teenager killed by a man she had met online, and the subsequent circulation of images from the crime scene on social media. The song had previously been released with a different vocalist; the “Dead Radio Remix” on this EP is presented as a reworked version that better reflects the project’s current direction, shaped by the band’s recent live performances. About Velatine Velatine is a gothic/darkwave duo from Melbourne, Australia, formed by Loki Lockwood and Maggie Alley in late 2021. Lockwood had previously been active as a producer in the projects The Drones and Spencer P. Jones before starting Velatine. The duo released its first seven-inch single, “Comic” / “No God”, in March 2022, followed by the industrial-leaning track “Deadly Requiem” that August and a second seven-inch, “Whisper Park” / “One and Only”, in November 2022, accompanied by a video directed by Mathew T Ellery. A remix of “No God”, paired with footage from the 1973 film “Frankenstein”, followed shortly after. In February 2023, Velatine released its debut album, “I Won’t Be Civilised”, on Spooky Records, preceded by the singles “No God”, “Comic” and “Whisper Park”. The band has continued to perform live regularly since, a period the duo credits with shaping the more industrial-leaning direction heard on the “Dead Radio EP”.

items.body: Baltimore-based quintet Crying Laughing will release its debut album, Talking, on Tape, CD and digital formats on September 10, 2026, through Hausu Mountain. The band fuses saxophone-led minimalism in the Steve Reich, Terry Riley and Philip Glass tradition with post-punk energy and the rhythmic sensibility of Moondog’s street recordings. Talking by Crying Laughing “Talking” runs eight tracks: “Toppled Column,” “Bass Alarm,” “Tato,” “When They Come to Town You Must Exile,” “Ricemeat,” “Inner Life,” “Crocodopolis Theme” and “Geese Six.” Crying Laughing recorded the album in one day in a basement studio outside Baltimore, tracking each song as a live performance through a network of microphones and isolation booths set up by engineer Chris Freeland. Crying Laughing’s line-up and Baltimore connections Crying Laughing formed in 2024 around saxophonists Christian Best and Rose Hammer Burt, drummer Jen Kirby and bassist Marc Miller, joined by keyboardist Steve Strohmeier. Kirby and Best’s prior work together in the duo Smoke Bellow, which released albums on Trouble in Mind and Moon Glyph before ending in 2024, formed the group’s starting point. Miller founded the math-punk band OXES in 1998 and the experimental ensemble Microkingdom in 2006, while Strohmeier has recorded or toured with Beach House, Dan Deacon, Daniel Higgs and Lower Dens. Hammer Burt participates in Baltimore collectives connected to the venue The Red Room and its High Zero improvised-music festival. Hausu Mountain first became aware of the band through mutual friends in Horse Lords, whose line-up includes label artist Andrew Bernstein. Hausu Mountain describes “Talking” as a fusion of polymetric saxophone composition with the energy of post-punk and the rhythmic sensibilities of Moondog, calling it “head music as much as body music.” Saxophonist Christian Best described the band’s writing process: “Each song begins its life as a seed of an idea: a whole arrangement, specific rhythms, melodies, or sometimes just a theory of interaction. The band then collaboratively expands and later condenses those ideas down into their most concise form. Compositionally we aim to not encroach on each instrument’s space. All of us contribute to the overall rhythm and melody of each piece, trading roles and interweaving with each other.” Drummer Jen Kirby, who plays a modified kit with a small snare and tuned rototoms, described her own approach: “a response to the people I’m playing with and my natural technical limitations due to total hackery of technique.” About Crying Laughing Crying Laughing is a quintet based in Baltimore, Maryland, formed in 2024 by musicians who had already spent years in the city’s experimental music scene. Saxophonists Christian Best and Rose Hammer Burt lead the group’s dual-sax arrangements, with drummer Jen Kirby and bassist Marc Miller forming the rhythm section and Steve Strohmeier adding keyboards, harmonium, piano and marimba. Kirby and Best previously played together in Smoke Bellow, which released records on Trouble in Mind and Moon Glyph before the band ended in 2024. Miller’s other projects include the math-punk band OXES, formed in 1998, and the experimental ensemble Microkingdom, formed in 2006. Strohmeier has recorded or toured with Beach House, Dan Deacon, Daniel Higgs and Lower Dens, and Hammer Burt performs in Baltimore’s Red Room and High Zero improvised-music circles. Crying Laughing joins Hausu Mountain with “Talking,” its debut album, recorded live in a single day at a basement studio outside Baltimore with engineer Chris Freeland.

items.body: UK trio Holy Tongue will release their second album, Basilikum, on LP and digital through AD 93 on October 9, 2026, catalog number WHYT106. The record moves between dub, ritual percussion and cinematic psychedelia, and features vocalist Dali De Saint Paul on two tracks. Holy Tongue recorded “Basilikum” as a series of improvisations in the Swiss Alps and London, built on vintage drum machines and what the label describes as “instinctive interplay.” AD 93 describes the album as combining dub techniques with ritual percussion, hypnotic pulse and Popol Vuh-style landscapes, with the trio treating playing, recording, editing and transformation as part of the same creative act. ‘Basilikum’ tracklist and featured vocals “Basilikum” runs eight tracks: “I’ve Stood in This Room for a Long Time Before,” “Coca” (feat. Dali De Saint Paul), “Orange 28,” “Bloom in D Minor” (feat. Dali De Saint Paul), “Vuoto 25,” “ROSEROOT,” “Single~Eyed” and “Nature.” The lead track “Coca” carries De Saint Paul’s vocal alongside the band’s dub-rooted rhythm section. About Holy Tongue Holy Tongue formed in London in 2018 as a studio project between producer Al Wootton and percussionist Valentina Magaletti, also a member of Moin, before expanding into a full trio with the addition of Susumu Mukai of Vanishing Twin. The group’s music draws on dub reggae, free improvisation and post-punk, referencing labels and artists such as On-U-Sound and Muslimgauze alongside post-punk bands like Liquid Liquid and 23 Skidoo. Following a trilogy of EPs, Holy Tongue released their debut album, “Deliverance and Spiritual Warfare,” in 2023, and followed it in 2024 with a collaborative album, “The Tumbling Psychic Joy of Now,” made with dub producer Shackleton. “Basilikum” is the trio’s second album, due October 9, 2026, on AD 93, the London label formerly known as Whities.

The band shares the first single from the record, “Repetition,” alongside a video, out now. “Repetition Compulsion” completes Black Doldrums’ “State of Mind Trilogy,” a three-album exploration of the psychological forces that shape identity, memory and human connection that began with the band’s 2022 d
items.body: London post-punk trio Black Doldrums will release a new album, “Repetition Compulsion,” on November 13, 2026, through Fuzz Club Records. The band shares the first single from the record, “Repetition,” alongside a video, out now. “Repetition Compulsion” completes Black Doldrums’ “State of Mind Trilogy,” a three-album exploration of the psychological forces that shape identity, memory and human connection that began with the band’s 2022 debut, “Dead Awake,” and continued on 2024’s “In Limerence.” The title refers to the psychological concept first explored by Sigmund Freud, and the album, according to Fuzz Club, “examines the unconscious tendency to recreate familiar emotional patterns, destructive behaviours and inherited cycles from the past” across its eleven tracks. ‘Repetition’ explores an unconscious cycle At the core of “Repetition Compulsion” is the creative and personal partnership between founding members Kevin Gibbard and Sophie Landers. “The songs are either about Sophie, for Sophie, or inspired by her,” Gibbard says. On the new single, he explains: “The song came from an idea to challenge ourselves to write something around one riff and something dirge-like. It also fit the theme of the album and the topic of repetition by literally experimenting with repetition in the musical sense. The opening line – ‘is your mind split in two’ – is something taken from our conversations on our many long walks around London where Sophie was talking about the psychological term splitting. It seemed to fit the feel of the song and theme of the album so much so it now opens up both the album and our live shows. I consider it very much Sophie’s song because she was the source of inspiration and that’s why we have her backing vocals fairly prominent to create a dual vocal effect. I also had the after-thought to have Sophie mime the first line in the video which is actually her line anyway.” On the album as a whole, Gibbard adds that “the album invites listeners to confront the echoes of the past while questioning whether those patterns can ever truly be broken.” Black Doldrums draw on 80s gothic post-punk, synth-pop and darkwave, alongside the film scores of John Carpenter and Vangelis, building songs from layered analogue synths, chorus-soaked guitars and driving rhythms. Repetition Compulsion by Black Doldrums The eleven-track “Repetition Compulsion” runs “Repetition,” “The Uncanny,” “Waiting,” “Beat The Rain,” “Echoes,” “Compulsion,” “No One’s Talking To Me,” “Bat Bomb,” “No Words Can’t Lie,” “Die With Me” and “Eulogy.” About Black Doldrums Black Doldrums is a post-punk trio from London, UK, built around the creative and personal partnership of Kevin Gibbard and Sophie Landers. The band released its debut album, “Dead Awake,” in 2022, followed by “In Limerence” in 2024, both through Fuzz Club Records. “Repetition Compulsion,” out November 13, 2026, closes the “State of Mind Trilogy” that runs across all three albums, arriving after heavy UK and European touring.

items.body: The Noise Who Runs, the UK-France project of former Sneaker Pimps member Ian Pickering, shares a video for “The Summer Talking,” the third single taken from the “Re: GenX” album. The indie-pop track pairs shimmering hooks with lyrics about climate denial, political inaction and the stories people tell themselves to avoid uncomfortable truths. The accompanying video contrasts postcard-perfect holiday imagery with the growing environmental crisis. “This song is about love, memory and self-deception, but also about a culture that keeps choosing short-term comfort over uncomfortable truths. Whether it’s a relationship, a dream of somewhere better, or believing just one more summer holiday comes without consequence, we become very good at telling ourselves what we want to hear,” Pickering says. ‘The Summer Talking’ pairs romance with climate warning Built around the refrain “it’s just the summer talking,” the song follows dreams of escape and new beginnings as they reveal themselves to be fragile, seasonal illusions. On the video, Pickering explains: “The video isn’t against holidays or people wanting to escape. It’s about why governments still refuse to treat the climate crisis with the urgency it demands. Most people want meaningful action on climate change and inequality, yet the biggest polluters continue to behave as though different rules apply to them. If we’re serious about protecting the future, governments have to lead, and the super-rich can no longer be exempt from the sacrifices expected of everyone else.” The Summer Talking by The Noise Who Runs “The Summer Talking” opens the “Re: GenX” album, out now via TNWR Records, whose ten tracks also include “Bang Bang,” “Trust Me I’m A Psychopath,” “This Song Sucks (Mind The Gap),” “Just The English Way,” “The Bodies Are Under The Bus Again,” “Home Front Truths,” “We Are Breach,” “Commercial Road” and “All Assuming You.” The song was recorded, engineered and produced by The Noise Who Runs, with additional production, mixing and mastering by Colin Cameron at The Cell Studio. About The Noise Who Runs The Noise Who Runs is the songwriting project of Ian Pickering, previously known for co-writing songs including “Spin Spin Sugar,” “6 Underground” and “Tesko Suicide” with Sneaker Pimps, and for his work with Front Line Assembly. After relocating from Hartlepool in north-east England to Lille, France, Pickering released The Noise Who Runs’ “Preteretrospective” album in 2023, followed by the “Come and Join the Beautiful Army” EP in 2024. Side-Line has followed the project’s singles since 2023, including “Tune Out, Turn Off, Drop In,” “Bang Bang” and “Commercial Road.” “Re: GenX,” described by Pickering as addressing war, consumerism, inequality and the erosion of collective responsibility, is out now via TNWR Records, with “The Summer Talking” its third single.

items.body: New York darkwave duo R. Missing will get a limited clear-white transparent vinyl LP of its album “Like the Sound of Injured Love” on October 2, 2026, alongside a regular digiCD edition, through the Italian label Young & Cold. The album originally came out digitally in December 2025 and combines darkwave, coldwave, dream pop and electronic elements. The LP is limited to 444 copies, while the digiCD comes in a Digipak sleeve limited to 250 copies; both carry the same eleven tracks. Young & Cold describes the record as an atmospheric album that opens with a mysterious, captivating tone from its first track, driven by electronic sounds that give the music a modern, dreamy quality alongside calm, distinctive vocals. The label singles out “Dreamletting” and “Let in the Night Outside” as highlights of R. Missing’s style, and calls “Telepolartears” memorable for its “fascinating sound.” Tracklist for ‘Like the Sound of Injured Love’ The LP spreads its eleven songs across two sides: side one holds “Like the Sound of Injured Love,” “Telepolartears,” “Dreamletting,” “Let in the Night Outside,” “Dear Contests” and “Supermuted,” while side two holds “Ola Tremble,” “infinifalls,” “Pony Yeah,” “Shadowist” and “Cloud Without Tear.” The digiCD carries the same eleven tracks in a single sequence. A video for the title track, “Like the Sound of Injured Love,” is available online. About R. Missing R. Missing is a darkwave duo based in New York City. Side-Line previously covered the project in August 2023 for a cover of Siouxsie and the Banshees’ “Spellbound.” “Like the Sound of Injured Love” was released digitally in December 2025 and combines darkwave, coldwave, dream pop and electronic production. Young & Cold, the label behind this physical edition, now brings the album to a limited clear-white transparent vinyl LP and a digiCD, distributed through Audioglobe.

items.body: Industrial rock act Celldweller has released a new single, “Respawn,” out now on FiXT. The track is the second single from Celldweller’s sixth studio album, “GOD MODE,” following the single “Fakebreaker” featuring SWARM and REEBZ. “Respawn” combines guitars, vocals and Klayton’s industrial production through a metal lens. The lyrics run: “I’ve died a thousand times, but I’m still here. Access has been denied, but I’m still here.” Gaming culture shapes ‘GOD MODE’ Klayton built “GOD MODE” around gaming and game culture across different eras. “Spending my formative years in the 1980’s, gaming systems like the ATARI 2600 (I had the Sears knockoff) and ColecoVision were important and iconic to me,” he stated. “Those memories sparked the concept for my new album GOD MODE, an album revolving around gaming and game culture across different eras, which makes the concept of my next single ‘Respawn’ self-explanatory. I was inspired to throw elements of metal, industrial and punk-rock into a blender to see what would spawn. Lyrically it’s a reminder to myself that even when things seem dire, hopeless, or fatal, I will respawn.” “Respawn” is available now on all major streaming platforms from FiXT. A “GOD MODE” Season Pass with bonus tracks and early access to upcoming singles is available exclusively through EVEN. About Celldweller Celldweller is the primary recording project of Klayton, who also records as Scandroid and produces under Circle of Dust and FreqGen. Klayton founded FiXT as an independent, artist-owned label in 2006 together with James Rhodes. Celldweller’s discography includes the self-titled debut album (2003), “Wish Upon a Blackstar” (2012), “End of an Empire” (2015), “End of an Empire – Chapter 3: Dreams”, “Offworld” (2017) and “Satellites” (2022). Klayton returned with the single “My Disintegration” in 2019, and FiXT’s roster has since grown to include acts such as Scandroid, The Browning and THE DEFECT. “GOD MODE,” Celldweller’s sixth studio album, is now underway, with “Respawn” following the album’s opening single “Fakebreaker.”

items.body: German EBM project Endzustand will release its second studio album, “Macht Gesellschaft”, on September 11, 2026, through Echozone. The project began as a one-man project and has since evolved into a duo. Echozone describes “Macht Gesellschaft” as combining hard EBM with socially critical lyrics, in line with its predecessor, but harder and more cynical. The album follows the July 2026 single “Maschinenangst,” which aimed its lyrics at artificial intelligence, social networks and the growing weight of technology on daily life. Second album continues Endzustand’s social critique The band mixes classic EBM rhythms with lyrics addressing technology, control and society. The band’s 1980s reference points include acts such as Nitzer Ebb, Die Krupps and DAF. “Macht Gesellschaft” carries that approach further, with Echozone describing the album’s tone as more cynical than its predecessor while keeping its focus on social criticism. About Endzustand Endzustand is the EBM project of Ralf Rönckendorf, a former German soldier who lost his eyesight and three comrades during a 2010 mission in Afghanistan. Rönckendorf built the project around classic electronic body music, using it to process his experience through bold lyrics and straightforward EBM rhythms. Endzustand released the single “Hass” in September 2020, followed by its debut studio album, “Werk des Krieges,” in October 2020 via Echozone, and the “Roter Freitag” EP in 2021. The project now records as a duo, with Rönckendorf joined by Rudi on drums. Endzustand returned in July 2026 with the single “Maschinenangst,” the opening preview of “Macht Gesellschaft,” the duo’s second studio album, due September 11, 2026.

items.body: Synthwave act GUNSHIP have released an official music video for “Time After Time,” their cover of Cyndi Lauper’s song featured on the soundtrack of Corin Hardy’s 2026 supernatural horror film “Whistle.” Hardy directed the video himself, built around previously unseen footage from the film. The DVD and BluRay release of “Whistle” is set for August 28, 2026. The video revives the movie-and-music-video tie-in tradition of the MTV era, pairing the song with an extended sequence cut from the finished film. “Whistle” follows a group of high school students who discover a cursed Aztec death whistle, stars Dafne Keen, Sophie Nélisse, Sky Yang, Jhaleil Swaby, Ali Skovbye, Percy Hynes White and Nick Frost, and had reached the number one spot on Amazon Horror and on VOD charts in the US and UK following its February 2026 theatrical release. GUNSHIP and Hardy resurrect a lost sequence “Working with Corin is a total dream,” GUNSHIP stated. “He’s an old friend who we bonded with over our love for cinema and music, and we were honored to have our song featured in the film. After the Whistle premiere, we were chatting over a pint, and he told us about a beautiful pseudo ‘one shot’ sequence he was heartbroken to lose in the final film. We suggested resurrecting it and using it as a music video. Corin got it immediately and the result is perfect. It’s heartbreaking, haunting and pure 80s noir soaked.” Corin Hardy described the pairing in similar terms: “I wanted Whistle to feel like a horror movie I might have watched around the late 1980’s, alongside films like A Nightmare on Elm Street, The Lost Boys, and The Breakfast Club. Films steeped in teen-angst and heightened feelings. Music was such a huge part of creating the romance of those cinematic worlds. Gunship’s synth-drenched cover of Cyndi Lauper’s ‘Time After Time’ was always top of my list. Their unique heart-on-your-sleeve sound was the perfect choice for a key moment in the movie. To come together post-release and create this extended music video is simply the cherry on top. Dan, Al & Al (Gunship) have provided the film a real companion piece in the world of Whistle… it makes me want my MTV again!” The collaboration extends GUNSHIP’s history with Hardy, who previously contributed vocals to the band’s track “Cthulhu.” “Whistle” is produced by No Trace Camping and Wild Atlantic Pictures and distributed by IFC Films, Shudder and Black Bear. About GUNSHIP GUNSHIP is Dan Haigh, Alex Westaway and Alex Gingell. The band builds its sound with vintage analog synthesizers and retro electronic gear from the 1980s, combining sweeping synth lines with driving electric bass arpeggios. GUNSHIP released the album “Unicorn” across five formats in October 2023. The band’s track “Cthulhu” features guest vocals from Corin Hardy, a collaboration that grew out of the pair’s shared interest in horror and cinema. “Time After Time,” GUNSHIP’s cover of the 1984 Cyndi Lauper song, was placed on the soundtrack of Hardy’s film “Whistle,” and the new official video marks the latest chapter in the band and director’s ongoing work together.

About Silent Impulse Silent Impulse is the industrial electronic project of Joe Abrescia, formed in 2024 in the United States. The project mixes electro-industrial elements, pairing melodic synth work with harsh percussive frameworks and distorted textures. Silent Impulse released the “Invasive Forms” album in March 2026, and follows it with “The Shape of Consequence,” a three-track EP due July 31, 2026, exclusively through Bandcamp.

items.body: Cork, Ireland duo Crá Croí will release a new single, “Lord Of The Wild,” on August 7, 2026, via Soundcloud ahead of a wider streaming rollout. The track is the sixth standalone single from the band and follows five previous releases, arriving ahead of their debut album, “Tá Brón Orm” (Irish for “sadness is on me”), due October 30, 2026 with twelve new songs. Crá Croí’s sound fuses post-punk atmosphere with synth-driven beats and cinematic production. The duo, known as RG and CD, self-produce and self-release their music, extending the same DIY approach to their visuals. Cernunnos mythology drives the new single The song draws on the mythology of Cernunnos, “the hunter” or “the horned one,” a figure tied to the elemental forces said to guard sacred groves and ancient places. The band describes the “wandering king” being called home as a symbol of humanity reconnecting with something primal. An accompanying DIY video was also made for the release. About Crá Croí Crá Croí is a Cork-based duo whose music sits between beauty and breakdown, pairing post-punk atmosphere with synth-driven production and stark lyricism. Entirely self-produced by the pair, the project has released five standalone singles to date. “Lord Of The Wild” is their sixth single and a lead-in to their debut album, “Tá Brón Orm,” set for release on October 30, 2026 with twelve tracks.

items.body: Chicago industrial and EBM act The Ineffectuals released “INFX: EP01” on July 22, 2026. The four-track EP is digital-only via Bandcamp and marks the first release in a planned series under the band’s INFX alias. The tracklist runs “Disinformation,” “Blow My Top,” “Ultramagnetic Field” and “Cloning Technique.” The release is the “first in a series of EPs under the INFX moniker.” INFX: EP01 by The Ineffectuals The INFX moniker returns The Ineffectuals first used the INFX name in 2022, for the all-electronic six-track release “Tempered Expectations,” made in the Pilsen neighborhood of Chicago between 2020 and 2022. “INFX: EP01” revives that alias for the band’s purely electronic material, separate from the guitar-and-bass lineup used on their full-length albums. About The Ineffectuals The Ineffectuals is the Chicago project of Jeremiah Meece and Tim Nordberg, based in the city’s Pilsen neighborhood. The two began by making electronic music together before expanding the sound for live performance with vocals and bass guitar. Their debut release, “Tempered Expectations,” came out on April 1, 2022 under the INFX name, running six tracks: “Poppers,” “German Cars,” “Unplanned Euthanasia,” “Venereal Horrors,” “Sybaris” and “Decomission.” The band’s first self-released full-length as The Ineffectuals, “First Offering,” followed on February 29, 2024, with ten tracks including “Son of C.H.U.D.,” “Ducktator” and “Gimme a Hit.” Reviewing the album in July 2024, I Die: You Die described it as a mix of “post-punk, synthpunk, and EBM.” A second album, “The Serious One,” arrived on November 1, 2025, with eleven tracks including “The Mimic,” “Birth” and “Infanticide.” “INFX: EP01” continues the project’s pattern of alternating full-band albums under The Ineffectuals name with shorter, more electronic-focused releases under the INFX alias, and opens a new series of EPs in that vein.

items.body: About two years after the EP “Love Me Now (Not)”, American artist Azul Far returns with the debut album from her sonic alter ego, The True Union. Production duties were handled by Travis Bacon and Sebastian Komor, with additional contributions on selected tracks from Jamie Cronander (Combichrist), Hellhammer (Mayhem), and Tony Särkkä (Abruptum/Ophthalamia). If you were already familiar with the EP, this album will hit you with even greater intensity. A palpable sense of rage runs throughout the record, fueled by personal experiences and emotional turmoil. Call the result Metal, Industrial, or simply a fusion of both—occasionally enriched with symphonic arrangements. Dark, aggressive, EBM-infused basslines further reinforce the album’s power, while Azul Far’s vocal versatility proves equally impressive. She effortlessly shifts between ferocious outbursts and more melodic, almost Pop-oriented passages, even as the music charges forward like a runaway train. The songs are short, uncompromising, and explosively powerful, giving the album the impact of a sonic blitzkrieg—it is over almost before you realize it. The True Union is a relentless listening experience that leaves little room to catch your breath. It is a fierce and uncompromising debut that is sure to claim plenty of victims—or rather, devoted new fans. (Rating:8). Side-Line first reported on the album’s Alfa Matrix release in April 2026, when “Sleepwalk” arrived as an 11-track digital album produced by Sebastian Komor. Listen to “One By One feat. Komor Kommando”: One By One (feat. Komor Kommando) by The True UnioN About The True Union The True Union is the industrial metal and dark electro project of American singer and composer Azul Far, founded in 2009. A 2022 Side-Line report on the act joining Alfa Matrix listed The True UnioN as a Dallas-based act in its opening line, while the same article’s detail section placed the project in Denver, Colorado; Side-Line has not resolved which city applied at the time of founding. The project was originally conceived as a studio-only outlet, with Far beginning to recruit musicians for live performance from 2017 onward. The True UnioN joined the Belgian label Alfa Matrix in 2022, first appearing on the label’s “Sounds From The Matrix 023” compilation with the track “Purousthai”. The same year, the project released the EP “Love Me Now (Not)” on Alfa Matrix, produced by Sebastian Komor with additional work from Siggi Bemm, Travis Bacon and guitarist Jamie Cronander (Combichrist). The EP also featured Azul Far’s guest vocals on “One By One”, a track written for the Komor Kommando EP of the same name, after Komor worked on production and mixing for The True Union. In March 2023, Azul Far discussed the project in a Side-Line interview titled “An order amongst the chaos!” The True Union’s debut full-length, “Sleepwalk”, followed in April 2026 on Alfa Matrix as an 11-track digital and CD album, again produced by Sebastian Komor, with additional contributions from Travis Bacon, Jamie Cronander, Hellhammer of Mayhem, and the late Tony “IT” Särkkä of Abruptum and Ophthalamia, who died in 2017.

items.body: Finnish Gothic Rock act Hateful Chains will release a new single, “Entities,” on August 7, 2026. The song is the band’s first written fully collaboratively, combining a swing/shuffle beat with a 7/4 time signature. “Entities” grew out of an idea by guitarist Kimmo Laaksonen to pair the shuffle groove with the odd meter, with vocalist Flora Kok then contributing lyrics and a chorus. The band describes the track’s subject as things that always come back to haunt you: “the entities you thought you’d cast away have returned and they are waiting for an opportunity to take you back. In fact, they never left in the first place: they were lurking inside your walls all this time.” The imitating vocal lines and odd timing build a strange, eerie atmosphere, with elements of Southern Rock adding a threatening edge. First collaborative songwriting credit for the band “Entities” was written by Flora Kok and Kimmo Laaksonen together, with lyrics by Kok and arrangement credited to the full band. The single is released via Eight Floor Music (FI-KL5-26-00005). About Hateful Chains Hateful Chains was launched in Finland in 2018. The band combines the dark sounds and aesthetics of Goth with elements of Indie Rock and Metal. They signed with Danse Macabre Records in 2020 and released their debut album, “Invite,” in 2021, followed by a second album, “Lambs and Goats,” in 2025. In 2026 Hateful Chains made their first appearance at Wave Gotik Treffen. The band is Flora Kok on vocals, keyboards and acoustic guitars, Kimmo Laaksonen on guitars, Jani Ilander on bass and Jani Vilhunen on drums. “Entities” continues the band’s run of singles following “Lambs and Goats,” with the collaborative writing process marking a new step for the group.
