items.body:
Mazzy Star and Prin€ess fiends will be in their element with the bittersweet slowcore and swoon of Goldenstar’s debut, a fine new addition to the Montreal’s sound, fixed up with engineering/mix/master by Francis Latreille (Priori and Patrick Holland (Project Pablo).

"goldenstar is a band from Montreal. Chamber Music is their EP. It’s out on OST. It takes them to the altar of a relatively new but already widely resonant North American musical canon: it’s a self-avowed slowcore record, a term that conjures intimacy, slow-glowing guitars, and ride cymbals that bathe and shimmer. It’s a term fraught with the legacy of universally beloved forebears like Duster, Bedhead, Codeine, et al. A pantheon of sorts. Slowcore carries weight. But this is no retread. Chamber Music’s palette is recognisable, but reconstituted through the idiosyncrasies of its songwriting: the creeping unease on opener ‘Forget’ and the sleepwalking lamentation of ‘Spinning Out’, songs whose warmth are framed by an ever-present anxiety that ebbs and bobs like lantern light on ocean water.

‘Thread’ unspools a kind of shaky optimism, undercutting every swell of hope with a chord change that eases the realisation of its falseness. The downcast note it ends on is carried through to the EP’s second half, which brings the pace down to a hypnotic sway. ‘Belemen’ and ‘April 3’ are scenic views through tired, dark-circled eyes, twinges of memories felt but elusive, meaning that recedes further every time it’s recalled. Instrumental closer ‘I Blink and See Nothing’ concludes numbly, spiralling downwards like a stomach butterfly turned to a moth. These are songs that speak to stillness and solitude and slow-burning pangs of regret: words unheard and half-thoughts left unspoken, a creeping sense that taking your own advice will only ever reveal the meaning it lacks. It’s about hollowness, it’s music that constructs a chamber in the familiar surroundings of a well-worn void. Welcome down."

items.body:
aloisius's enigmatic life is beautiful label/collective/ fully establishes its lore on this colossal compilation: 39 tracks of whimsical pop, edgy improv, freewheeling poetry, noise, dusty psych, abstract hip-hop, folk and saccharine soul from artists you'll know and a fair few you won't. Featuring Bianca Scout, VOICE ACTOR, James Massiah, Kenichi Iwasa, THE NARRATOR, Isaiah Hull and many, many more.

If you've spent any amount of time orbiting Cafe Oto, streaming NTS or even browsing these pages, you'll surely have interfaced with life is beautiful, even by accident. The self-styled "gesamtkunstwerk" was established by the mysterious aloisius in 2022 initially as a radio show, before he decided to complicate things with a collective, a series of live performances and a record label a year later. And after booking artists like Klein, Lauren Duffus, YHWH Nailgun, John Glacier and DJ Spanish Fly, and releasing genuinely off-kilter records from James Massiah, Pretty V and THE NARRATOR, life is beautiful comes correct with its first compilation - and it's good. We shouldn't have expected less from a label who dump their demos and experiments ("resources and inspiration") on a file exchange portal on their own site, but the set is remarkably generous, scraping together ideas, performances and fully-fledged tracks from  a host of their core members, regular collaborators and close associates. 

Fittingly, the set opens with tracks from each of the founders, who establish the label's core sound. NWAKKE begins with 'i need you in a positive way', a cloudy hypnagogic R&B marvel that juxtaposes her cool-headed vocal runs with melancholy drones, spy movie strings, tape-fucked field recordings and piano punctuations. Then the mic's handed to Amber Joy, aka THE NARRATOR, who also works as the label's artistic director; on 'SUDDENLY', she follows spring's beguiling 'RADIOWEAVER' with another skittish post-everything collage that chops 'n pastes cheap synth vamps, molasses-slow breaks and choral vocals into a dreamy modern hymn. And aloisus' 'you are god' runs out of its stuck groove as if it's from the very same thought, blurring gospel moans across Prince-like drum machine loops and EZ-listening piano phrases. Bianca Scout hands us a taster of her collaborative project with London's Cajm on the hypnotic 'Welcome to Hello' , while poet Isaiah Hull teams up with y+Your for the wonked 'vampire money'.

Japser Maurice, aka jaso, turns in a short, guitar-led theme and cellist abi asisa shifts the set into a completely different direction on 'calling', complimenting her eerie dissonances with clipped, decelerated beats. Basically there's a whole record of music from the crew before 'veneration...' has begun in earnest, and it only gets better from here, running through aesthetic experiments from multi-instrumentalist Kenichi Iwasa, self-styled "beat wizard" psychedelic ensemble. (who's one half of Brum's Everything is Psychedelic with Tony Bontana) and Thom Dehli before we reach the compilation's crown jewel, a 21-minute live performance from okk70 ensemble. We can't tell you exactly who's playing, but it's worth the price of entry alone, a squirming slo-mo jazz side that gets to the roots of the life is beautiful sound.

Elsewhere there's a chewably eccentric solo moment from Bianca Scout ('superscribe 24'), a phenomenally moody collaboration between VOICE ACTOR and aloisius ('24'), a spirited, lo-fi transmission from London's josiane pozi and a deeper than deep jam from orchestra379, aloisius' "collective improvisation project" that's featured artists like Ben Vince, Kenichi Iwasa and abi asisa. Honestly there's so much more than we can even readily dive into - label comps are so often a slog but this one's stuffed to the gills with genuinely creative experimentation from some of the London scene's most beguiling outsiders.

items.body:
Smouldering and aching in all the right places, Dawuna's latest mixtape is a muted hypnagogic R&B tour de force, pieced together while recovering from a traumatic head injury and conveying all the fragile, dizzy and ineffable beauty imaginable. Trust, it’s next-level gear tipped FFO D’Angelo, Prince, Niecy Blues, Soulquarians, Rodney Jerkins.

‘African Family Laptop Musik’ is Ian Mugerwa’s 4th dispatch as Dawuna since 2020’s still unfathomable ‘Glass Lit Dream’, an album that we called the debut of the century thus far and which, still, somehow, seems to have evaded any kind of widespread crossover despite being a record that triggers total joy and bewilderment every single time we play it to the uninitiated. Since that album, and shortly after a relocation to Baltimore, Mugerwa was involved in a car accident that triggered a period of hospitalisation and amnesia. 'African Family Laptop Music' emerges from that difficult period; recorded and pieced together while still in recovery. He doesn't remember much about the project at this point, just small flashes, but it's easily the most personal, touching material he's shared to date. 

Mugerwa calls the compositions simple, but it’s the kind of simple many have spent a lifetime trying to engineer. On opener 'I am a woman too', daring lo-fi sound design lends texture to multi-tracked vocal harmonies and a beat rapped on a table with knuckles and finger clicks, before tuning in to a chat between elders on ‘Obulesi’, that he laments in the bloozy ache of the incredible ‘Family Trauma Drama’. Lashed to a celestial vocal performance, he fleshes out the arrangement with downsampled waltzing hats and a single snare hit with synths that sound like they've been lifted from a mid-'80s Sierra adventure game, before being filtered out to a low hum. There's a quiet virtuosity on show; it's lo-fi, with all the aesthetic hallmarks of some of the very best outsider gear, but Mugerwa builds on the foundations of 'Glass Lit Dream' and 'Naya' to provide an unmistakably Black ideation of hauntology. Approaching the very concept of memory from a unique vantage point, he muddles dreams and impressions, sorting through the canon (think 'Songs in the Key of Life', 'Sign O' the Times', 'Baduizm', 'Brown Sugar' and 'Full Moon' just for starters) as it vanishes from view. 

What makes the record hit even harder is that Mugerwa collages the more “proper” songs with skits and interludes that help map the narrative, taping conversations with his family and abstracting them with disorientating glitches, synths and FX. ‘Pressure’ pushes deep on a bittersweet bruise with lyrics about “the pain on your brain making fun of you”, set to the heaviest smudge of bass and organ recalling Angel Bat Dawid’s ‘The Oracle’, whilst the latter stages reveal precious gems in the harpsichord sway of ‘Bipolar Memory’,thru the lip-biting downswang and helium-voiced Camille vibes of ‘Grabba Boy Problem’ and a poignant sign-off addressed to his father - not sure if that’s his dad or him upstairs - in a delicate prayer ‘Undo This Damage,’ which once over, is bound to make you rake back over all Dawuna’s gear to date. 

"This is the last lil offering from a personal side of myself before I give y'all something big," he assures cryptically. "Enjoy."

Incredible, really.

items.body:
Mad one! Jahtari bossman Disrupt serves the ultimate 8-bit gamer dub mixtape; an hour of frazzled, natty melody and fizzing drums loaded with flashbacks from the label catalogue and classic video game scores...

Practically scented with nostalgic ‘80s mustiness and scent of singed circuits, the ‘Secret Level’ mixtape goes all-in on the chiptune tip with cuts from beloved game scores and loads of tunes they inspired, all liberally drenched in dub FX edging on outright noize. No doubt it’s bags of fun for anyone who grew up the ‘80s and early ‘90s, throwing back to a far simpler era when days could be whiled away putting pixelated avatars thru their paces on your TV or handheld. All very innocent and endearing daft but crafty tackle for late Gen Xers, xennials and chiptune fetishists, then.

items.body:
Death is Not the End catalogue "multi-media theater" pioneer Alwin Nikolais' foundational output, 21 energetic and prophetic early electronic experiments that redrew the synthesizer's boundaries, accompanying his inventive avant-garde dance productions.

The owner of the very first Moog synthesizer, Nikolais is one of electronic music's unsung heroes, a choreographer, dancer and composer who understood the revolutionary potential of electronic music long before most of his peers. Using his Moog and a notoriously complicated Synclavier system, he composed the majority of the music to his productions himself, having had an early training on the piano and organ, moonlighting as a silent film musician. His interest in dance had been triggered by an obsession with percussion and for his earliest dance pieces he imagined the dancers banging on car parts and children's toys, creating their own live score. But the more he learned about tape music, the more Nikolais became convinced that he could control his own unique sound. He assembled a library of abstract loops and hits, composing 11 scores between 1956 and 1962 in the musique concrète mode, but was drawn to electronic sounds when his assistant James Seawright provided him with an archive of synthesizer bleeps and drones recorded at the Columbia-Princeton Center for Electronic Music.

It was Seawright who told Nikolais about Robert Moog,and convinced him to confront the young engineer at an electronics expo in New York. And after trying Moog's prototype and sharing his ideas, Nikolais used his Guggenheim Fellowship money to purchase the first Moog - a legendary synth that's now displayed in Ann Arbor's Museum of Musical Instruments. It's that instrument we can hear in all its glory on the earliest pieces included on the anthology, most prominently on the 1966 composition 'Chimera: Dance I'. Extraordinarily, Nikolais doesn't appear to be motivated by the Moog's ability to shadow other instruments, instead intrigued by its rhythmic capabilities, generating dissonant tones, scraped distortions and whirring resonances that he assembles into loping movements. And a decade later, he's still coaxing genuinely befuddling sounds from the Moog, making it shriek Banshee-like on 'Tribe: Dance' and duck beneath the earth's mantle on 'Styx: Excerpt'.

In the late '70s however, Nikolais' attention turned towards the New England Digital Corporation's Synclavier, a digital synthesizer and (later at least) sampling workstation controlled by an early computer that foreshadowed the next couple of decades of electronic music. Ever the early adopter, Nikolais used this system to write his next slew of scores, harnessing the notoriously complex FM additive synth architecture and finding his predictably idiosyncratic sweet spot. On 1980's 'Mechanical Organ: Dance II', for example, Nikolais plays the Synclavier's uncanny tones off bone-rattling live percussion sounds and 'Pierrot: Dance II' uses the early sampler technology to shadow the drums with pitchy vocalizations. The most startling thing about the set is that we haven't heard it before - really, it's worth a look just for the almost 10-minute deployment of ring modulated tones, FM harps, analog wubs and corroded samples that concludes the set, an excerpt of Nikolais' batshit score for 1985's 'Crucible'.

items.body:
Their third album, ‘Treasure’ also debuts Simon Raymonde on bass and finds the band scaling new heights in the most emotionally raw way imaginable. Impossible to overstate just how influential and well loved this album is - from the quietly anthemic Pandora (For Cindy) - probably played in every bedroom by every teenager in 1984, to the sublime 'Beatrix' and 'Otterley' - tracks that were played on Autechre’s Disengage Kiss FM show in the early 90’s and which gave us our first introduction to one of the most magical and timeless albums ever made.

"The band returned to being a trio in 1984 with guitarist Simon Raymonde joining their ranks in time for third album, Treasure. Produced by Robin Guthrie and featuring tracks ‘Lorelei’, ‘Ivo’ and ‘Persephone’, Treasure is often celebrated as one of the band’s finest works. As Pitchfork put it when including the album in their Top 100 Albums of the 1980s, “Treasure was titled simply enough. An adjective for the endlessly inventive melodic lines you'd find buried in these songs, and a verb for what you'd do with them for years to come.”

items.body:
The most perfectly formed Cocteau Twins album, perhaps one of the most perfectly formed albums of all time - soaked in bittersweet sorrow and nostalgia, it’s almost painful listening to it 30 years later.

Numerous publications have declared it one of the best albums of the 90s, with Pitchfork calling it “a core of ungodly gorgeous songs that is every bit as moving and relevant today as it ever was.”. Famously - 4AD founder Ivo Watts-Russell has called it his favourite all-time 4AD album, “by a long shot”. 

Recorded in the midst of much upheaval - the birth of Fraser and Guthrie's daughter, the death of Simon Raymonde’s father Ivor Raymonde, the disintegration of the band’s relationship with 4AD (this was to be their last album for the label) - the result is lucid and enveloping, you can even decipher some of Fraser’s lyrics on this one.

Anyway, Heaven or Las Vegas is really one of life’s great pleasures for anyone acquainted with it. And if you aren’t - get to it.

items.body:
Longtime Lynch collaborator Chrystabell reconvenes with the director for a hypnagogic voyage into sensual surrealism, and it's as close as Lynch has come to his work with the late Julee Cruise in decades, with Chrysta's ethereal vocals contorted and reverberated around starlit synths and spine-tingling muted orchestrals - some of which were composed by Angelo Badalamenti, no less. So good.

Unsurprisingly, there's a an enigmatic story behind this one. Lynch was on a nighttime walk through a forest when he noticed a bright light - the light became Chystabell's voice, and disclosed a secret to him. It's hard not to think of Twin Peaks here - even the title seems to reference Laura Palmer's ugly demise - and with contributions from the late Badalamenti, the mood is eerily familiar, to say the least. Chrystabell's been working with Lynch since 2007, when he used some of her music in 'Inland Empire'; he wrote and produced her debut solo album 'The Train' just a few years later, and she also took a central role in 'Twin Peaks: The Return', playing Special Agent Tammy Preston. So who better to bottle the essence of Lynch's caliginous American dreamscape?

But 'Cellophane Memories' is far more than an attempt to recapture the dark cabaret oddness of Julee Cruise's 'Floating into the Night'. The vapors still hang around the album, formed around plasticky synth strings, but Chrystabell's voice is unique, sweeping around the album as if it's hovering between this world and the next. She's a confident performer, letting her words drift through clouds of reverb whie Lynch replies with bold, illusory arrangements, backmasking her phrases and stacking melodies like esoteric clues. His echo-ed out, Loren Connors-like riffs are particularly gripping, bedding Chrystabell's folk-y recitations on the elegiac 'You Know the Rest' and turning 'Two Lovers Kiss' into a haunted lullaby. 

On 'The Answers to the Questions', Lynch harnesses the tremolo-heavy jangle of Americana, fading his plucks into hums over a beat that's so powdery it's practically just a gravelly shuffle. Chrystabell's ability to work with this kind of mottled canvas is why the album exceeds expectations; her fragmentary songs embed themselves in Lynch's well-worn imagery without losing their distinctive tone. At times, she sounds almost like Beth Gibbons, hauling a hazy past into a terrifying present, and at others more like Liz Harris, turning her homespun digressions into uncompromising empyrean ambience. Just check the feathery 'With Small Animals', where she curls her voice into vague chorals, accompanied by subtle shortwave-garbled drones from Lynch, or the forbidding 'Reflections in a Blade', a diaphanous modern giallo theme we never knew we needed.

'Cellophane Memories' is Lynch's most crucial musical diversion in years, not a re-imagining of the Julee Cruise era but a vital remodeling of the formula. There are plenty of imitations, this one's the real deal.

items.body:
Remastered from the original tapes by Robin Guthrie and reissued on vinyl for the first time, 'The Moon and the Melodies' is one of the Cocteau Twins' most sublime sets, a blissful marriage of horizontal piano-laced ambience and glistening dream pop.

"It's not Cocteau Twins, and it's not me," Budd said in a 1986 interview, "it's an odd combination peculiar to the mixture." He'd never heard the band until bassist Simon Raymonde reached out to cover 'Not Yet Remembered' from his 'Ambient 2: Plateaux of Mirror' collaboration with Brian Eno. Although the cover never materialised, Budd was struck by the trio's music and after a meeting in Los Angeles, they began to consider a full collaboration. 'The Moon and the Melodies' appeared at a good time, Budd had recently released his syrupy masterpiece 'The Pearl', and Cocteau Twins had sailed further into abstraction with their beatless oddity 'Victorialand'. The album also marked the end of an era for Guthrie, Raymonde and Liz Fraser, catching them on the cusp of their later shift towards more identifiable pop, and integrating Budd's signature languid piano worked seamlessly. Just check 'Memory Gongs', still one of the most pristine entries in either act's repertoire - seven and a half minutes of rubbery, tremolo piano reverberations and muggy, billowing soundscapes. 

But the big draw will no doubt be opener 'Sea, Swallow Me', a more recognisable Cocteaus cut that's had a new lease of life since it became a viral hit on TikTok, of all places. It's now one of the band's most recognisable (and most streamed) songs, and Budd's serene arpeggios take on a slightly different form when they're balanced with Guthrie's shimmering riffs, Raymonde's driving basslines and Fraser's soaring voice. The four alternate between proper songs and ambient reflections, as if they're each paying attention to each other's strengths while attempting to experiment. "It turned out like four songs that sounded like us and four songs that sounded like him, which wasn't really the plan," remembers Guthrie. And it's interesting that when it was originally released, the album was credited to each musician, rather than being listed as a Cocteau Twins album; indeed, Raymonde recalls that the sessions were enjoyably un-premeditated. "It captured a moment in time between friends that are enjoying making music together," he explains. "Really, that's the essence of it."

Elsewhere, Dif Juz's Richard Thomas plays sax on two of the album's most crushing tracks: the jangly, anthemic 'She Will Destroy You' and the cloudy 'The Ghost Has No Home'. The latter is one of the Budd-forward tracks, and stretches into the abyss with his piano fainting into Thomas's echoing horns and Guthrie's tempered, chiming guitar phrases. It's hardly surprising that the album marked the beginning of a collaboration between Guthrie and Budd that would eventually give us the iconic 'Mysterious Skin' soundtrack in 2005.

'The Moon and the Melodies' has never sounded better; it's aged well, pulling away from the expectations that caused some critics to misunderstand it when it emerged almost four decades ago, gradually establishing itself as a stylistic milestone in the years since.

items.body:
Reissued with new liner notes and two bonus tracks, Jeff Parker's beat-focused 2016 solo album is a deeply personal reflection of his musical influences, from J Dilla to Thelonius Monk.

Even now, Parker is still best known for his work on the Chicago scene, playing in bands like Tortoise, Isotope 217 and the Chicago Underground. And despite being one of the scene's most prolific artists, his work as a soloist, or at least with his name listed as the lead, has traditionally been harder to find. 'The New Breed' offered a different perspective for listeners who only knew his work as a guitarist or keyboardist. Since he'd moved to Los Angeles in the mid 2010s, Parker had been working his way through his archives and had found himself drawn to a series of beat experiments he'd made while studying vinyl sampling. So he put the tracks together in a more refined form and signed up Paul Bryan to engineer and play bass, enlisting saxophonist Josh Johnson and drummer Jamire Williams to fill in the gaps. 

And although Parker's sketches evolved considerably as they were expanded by the quartet's improvisations, you can still hear the traces of his beatwork. Just peep the MPC lilt that makes 'Get Dressed' so inviting, and the stifled street noise that elevates Parker's wormy guitar lines, or the Slum Village-era Dilla-style clipped bassline and concertina-ing organs on the brief 'Para Ha Tay'. The icing on the cake is 'Cliche', though, a smoother-than-smooth collaboration with Parker's daughter Ruby, who sings heartbreakingly sweetly over Parker's dusty beats and lulling solo. It's the neo-library tribute you never knew you needed - RIYL Madlib, Dilla, Yesterday's New Quintet or Pete Rock.

items.body:
Returning after a decade-long break with none other than Isis/Sumac frontman Aaron Turner at the helm, Neurosis move into a new era with their sickest album since the iconic 'Through Silver in Blood'. Tipped!

It would have been easy to assume that Neurosis would have folded after guitarist and vocalist Scott Kelly, one of the band's founder members, was dismissed following domestic abuse allegations. Indeed, as late as in January last year, it looked like things were fizzling out when drummer Jason Roeder claimed he was ready to sell his music equipment and retire from touring. And it would have made sense, too; Neurosis have been active since the mid-1980s and defined a sound that would evolve into "post-metal", pulling influence from hardcore, prog, industrial music, ambient and sludge and inspiring a legion of followers. They never really lost their mojo, either - even their last album, 2016's Steve Albini-recorded 'Fires Within Fires' was pretty universally regarded as one of that year's best metal releases. But truth be told, they'd started to repeat themselves; locked into Kelly's grim, agonized lyrics, they were starting to sound like their own gloomy tribute act. If it was the end, they'd had a good run.

So 'An Undying Love...' is in many senses a total surprise Not only is the band back, re-energised, but they have a new vocalist and guitarist in tow: Turner, whose old band Isis were arguably the most important members of post-metal's second wave. You might consider the new Neurosis lineup as the ultimate post-metal supergroup, then, and 'An Undying Love...' is the record that proves the credentials of everyone involved. Unlike its tight, almost too brief predecessor, this album is a return to the epic, sprawling songwriting that both Neurosis and Isis perfected at their respective peaks. And it's incredibly expansive, too; anyone who's been following Turner in recent years will already know how open-minded he is, whether it's with his work with Moor Mother and Keiji Haino as Sumac or his various genre-bending collaborations. Here, there's an extra layer to the Neurosis sound that fills out their sludgy, lurching epics with the meticulously engineered haze of Isis's milestone 'Oceanic'.

Where Neurosis's last few albums had been shaped by their long-time collaboration with Albini, this one sounds like a clean break, mixed and recorded by Oakland's Scott Evans, who worked on Turner's Sumac records. It's still Neurosis, with those slow, almost symphonic atmospheres and the unmistakably tight rhythm section, but there's even more going on here, whether it's the unsettlingly effective breakdowns that often replace the band's usual instruments with synths and pounding drum machines, or the stacked feedback loops and scratches that fill their riffs with even more tension. Turner's lyrics, too, offer the band a new dimension to explore. "The separation that burns our hearts / is the root of all our disease," he bellows on the opener 'We Are Torn Wide Open' over radio interference. "We've forgotten how to live so we suffer." Self-referential in their own way at first, they move on as the band does, rolling through themes of environmental collapse, division and redemption. 

It's worth it just for the payoff delivered by the album's side-long finale 'Last Light', shifting from hi-BPM dark gabber into pure symphonic sludge, using its hefty runtime to properly display what this nu-Neurosis (NeurIsis?) is capable of. Really, it's not just the band's most vital record in years, it's one of the best metal albums we've heard in way, way too long.

items.body:
Will Long dons his dancing slippers for another deep house sojourn on his Long Trax Productions, blowing kisses in the direction of Larry Heard, Ron Trent, DJ Sprinkles.

One decade since minting the ‘Long Trax’ series on Terre Thaemlitz’s label, Comatonse, Will Long slow cooks six new additions on his personal folio, taking all the time needed to get right into the groove. Trust there’s no fireworks or over-produced trickery, just hypnotic deep house that unfurls with a real sense of space, patience and deferred gratification.

Long in his element, following his nose to pair the barest ingredients in classic style and pattern, as with with the likes of ‘About Where It's At (Now You Went N' Did It mix)’, which takes over 4 mins happily swinging away before introducing its lonesome flute motif, or a standout ‘Have to Have Something’ lost in the flow, where the bassline only thickens as it goes along. 

We’re also partial to the square bass budge of ‘Have To Have Something (S' a Lotta Shade mix)’, and the mesmerising meld of creamy bass and piquant cowbell pinging on ‘The Problems’, also found warped with trippier effect on its Metallic Dub reshape.

items.body:
Numero dust off the wiry, angular new wave of Mikel Rouse’s Tirez Tirez; one time Another Side label mates of Arthur Russell, Parade Ground and Tuxedomoon, and support act for Talking Heads, sharing all of their panache for sophisticated songwriting and pert grooves, at best in the bossa shimmy of ‘Living in This Dream (I’m So Proud)’ and a light-headed title tune...

“Tirez Tirez was founded by Missouri native Mikel Rouse, and gave its first performance as the opening act for the rock band Talking Heads at a 1978 concert in Kansas City, Missouri. The band's initial line-up was Rouse (vocals/guitar), Rob Shepperson (drums) and Jeff Burk (bass). Tirez Tirez issued two very rare self-released LPs in their earliest days: No Double Bagging Necessary (1978) and Rush & Dissonance (1979). All three members of the group subsequently moved to New York City in 1979, and self-released their debut single ("Scattered"/"Scenery") in November of that year. The band's third album (1980's Etudes) was recorded in New York City, but it did not initially see a US release, and was at first only picked up for distribution by the tiny British independent label Object Music. The LP went on to sell a very respectable 2,000 copies in the UK, and US indie Aura Records later issued in the album in the US in late 1981. Aura also issued "Razorblades", a single taken from the album.

Bassist Burk left Tirez Tirez in 1982, and was replaced by James Bergman. Philip Johnston (keyboards/woodwinds) was also added to the group at about the same time. This line-up (Rouse/Shepperson/Bergman/Johnston) recorded 1983's Story Of The Year, which was released only in Europe via Belgian label Les Disques Du Crépuscule. Although he had left Tirez Tirez, original band member Burk would continue to contribute finished artwork to future Tirez Tirez album and single releases after his 1982 departure; the same would be true of original drummer Shepperson after his departure in early 1984.”

items.body:
Porto’s rapidly evolving Perf label go hard on a hip hop-weighted jungle noir flex with local mainstay Spitbender’s debut volley of breakbeat chicanery and dread dub noise tipped FFO UVB-76 Music, Mick Harris, Healing Force Project...

"Always lurking amidst the underground Porto music scene is Spitbender, the most stable moniker of the ever-morphing Francisco Antão. Spin gathers a collection of tracks that demonstrate his experimentalism & coy sonic precision. Spitbender takes cues from Jungle & Hip Hop producers to create his own unique blend of Downtempo. What becomes clear throughout the album is the attention to detail: it is infused as much by Industrial's red-line spectra as it is by the dubplate logic of the Darkside Continuum, yet it does so at its own tripped out speed. 

Spin begins with the laid-back but constantly shifting 'Global Overgroove'. Its breakbeat science moves in & out of DSP glitch-work & dub reflections. When its slinky bassline melody arrives, a certain dread sets in.

'Weyward Fold' drops into a driving, hard-edged chug, threaded with snippets of Malcolm X's disobedient pedagogy. The momentum carries into 'Headnod Doctor', where the bass distortion thickens & the cymbal circuit is overloaded, landing somewhere between Hip‑Hop grit & metal weight.

Side A ends with the downtempo roller 'Dogs and Moles (Skylurk Mix)'. The familiar break drifts into new territory, pulled along & wrapped in a slap-back echo. A quirky melody cuts through the haze, giving the track a fresh tilt. The mulch of the track forms a steady, unhurried pulse.

Spitbender's spacious atmospherics & groove-focused approach comes further into focus on 'Nothing Here But the Recordings'. Creating his own chapter in the book of Trip Hop, his minimalist touch is laid out in full.

'Force the Hand Ov Chance' pulls Boom Bap gently into dub mechanics, letting space do the heavy lifting. Its simplicity hides a deep pocket. 

Returning to broken-up distortion, 'Mirrors of Flesh (Dub Mix)' finds Spitbender using the mixer as an instrument to push & pull the heavy drums of Benjamin Brejon [of Méchanosphere] alongside the voice of Rui intoning the title phrase.

Sitting between the album's two poles, 'Out Take Dub' fuses the clipped‑obsession timbres of Spin's heavier moments with its blissed out flow. Feedback & distortion are welcomed & drawn long.

In the end, Spin hits like a fully formed statement—lean, focused, & unmistakably Spitbender. Every track pushes its own angle, but together they land with a clarity that feels earned. It's a sharp marker in his trajectory, & it leaves a charge in the air."

items.body:
12th Isle push the boat out to Rosso Polare’s uchronic folklore, pulling from the Milanese artist’s Italian folk heritage and weaving in chops by Persian electro-acoustic artist Cinna Peyghamy, plus Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, for an adventurous session braiding folk and concrète timelines... 

“Cacciamali is an exploration of diegetic sound, folk chants and traditional rhythms and instrumentation building upon Milan based Rosso Polare’s last outing Campo Amaro and the subsequent departure of co-founder Anna Vezzosi from the group. Where the 2024 album incorporated a heavy use of folklore as a new tool, Cacciamali explores the influence further by bringing in a host of collaborative players including Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, sound artist and researcher HMOT (Stas Shärifulla) and Persian/Parisian electro-acoustic musician Cinna Peyghamy.

‘Scoff Back Sickness’, as the title loosely translates, utilises the same approach, one based on non-hierarchical authorship and leaning heavily on field recordings that both contrast and blend with the tonal material, focusing on biophony, landscape and environmental audio as compositional material. Shifting closer now to a shared network of voices and materials, the dual narrative unfolds as such:

Side A is connected to the concept of the medieval quintain games, specifically flag throwing, where certain drumming patterns from the tradition have been overworked, distorted and transformed. Side B is an underlying local legend from the north of Italy, where some sources speak of a presumed duel in 1744 between a father and his son, ultimately ending with the son’s death. These two layers are not illustrative but structural: ritual / repetition / tradition on one side, and rupture / conflict / loss on the other. A struggle to keep floating, a long shout in the distance, suspended between memory, ritual and disappearance. The result is dense, thick with impulse yet also measured, and often leaves us disoriented and questioning a sound's origin the moment we think we have a grip on the process. The gentle nostalgia of close-mic’ed ‘Falò’ summons the spirit of René Aubry & Jean Schwarz’s concréte masterpiece ‘Five Women’ on the Still Waters ballet soundtrack, and the stark contrast of looping rhythms on both ‘Xiv - Pavo’ and ‘Monte’ deploys a driving, intentful break from the moments of worldly human interactions served by the field recordings.”

items.body:
Unmissable reissue of Valya Hooi’s standout debut, an immaculately frayed conception of dubwise dream-pop from the same Aussie quarters that gave us HTRK/Jonnine, CS + Kreme, F Ingers...

Valya's first record ‘Untitled’ was originally issued by Altered States Tapes in 2019 (the same year as her song-writing credit on ‘I Don’t Seem Myself Tonight’ from Jonnine’s ’Super Natural’ EP), and has somehow managed to evade our radar until now, when she’s making a fairly big ping in our world.

Working economically with her own vocals, plus guitar, keyboards, and slivers of clarinet supplied by Tarquin Manek (F Ingers, LST), the results can’t help but remind us to aspects of Laila Sakini or Teresa Winter’s music that we hold dearly - namely the reverb-laden vocals and drowsily psychedelic, daydreaming appeal - but also tend toward a sort of sublime, grown-up bedroom chamber darkness understandably shared with her peer Jonnine, and the low-key grooving suss of CS + Kreme, or even Mica Levi at her most strung out. 

An incredible album.

items.body:
Smouldering chamber folk abstracts by a spar of Kronos Quartet, wreathing keys and cello with subtle electronic gilding in homage to Gunnar Smoliansky’s photos, touching a sweetspot between The Humble Bee’s synaesthetic, meta-media delicacies and Nathan Salsburg’s creaking Americana...

"Danny Clay is a composer who often utilizes classical instruments, open forms, found objects, analog media, and digital errata in his work. He has collaborated with musicians and ensembles throughout the US, including Kronos Quartet, Eighth Blackbird, Third Coast Percussion, Volti, the San Francisco Girls Chorus, Wu Man, Sarah Cahill, Phyllis Chen, the International Contemporary Ensemble (ICE), Ensemble Dal Niente, the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra, and others.

10 years after his last solo release on IIKKI ("Stills" IIKKI001), Danny Clay comes back with "A Moment Beyond". A new intimate and out-of-time piece evolving between ambient, chamber music and contemporary music."

items.body:
Breezy new age house by an Antipodean artist with illustrious credits beside Michal Hutchence, Bono, Jamiroquai since the ‘80s, evened out with Kuniyuki and 451 remixes...

"Originally emerging from Melbourne’s post-punk and new wave underground in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Gus Till has spent more than four decades navigating a remarkably diverse musical path. From early electronic experimentation with Third Eye alongside Ollie Olsen, through a pivotal role in the formative years of the global psy-trance movement and collaborations with artists including Michael Hutchence, System 7, Manu Dibango, Todd Terry and Bim Sherman, Till’s work has consistently resisted easy categorisation, moving fluidly between ambient music, downtempo, house, trance and psychedelic electronica.

First released on Japan’s Dakini Records in 2006, ‘Rainsong’ captures many of these threads in a single expansive composition. Built around a pulsating bassline, layered live percussion and soaring vocal elements, the track sits comfortably between the dancefloor and more immersive listening environments. Unfolding patiently across nearly thirteen minutes, it combines hypnotic rhythmic momentum with a rich sense of atmosphere and musicality.

For the B-side, Kuniyuki Takahashi offers a distinct reinterpretation of the original. His remix gradually unfolds from a patient introduction into a deep and richly textured exploration of the track’s core themes. Subtle spatial processing, nuanced arrangement shifts and his unmistakable sense of atmosphere transform the source material while preserving its emotional core."

items.body:
Wiry, tart, cold, minimal wave shrapnel from original early ‘80s upswell of DIY machine music...

“40 years after its creation, MOß GARTEN – Sekvensstyrd 1981–1986 arrives as a compelling double vinyl LP, diving deep into the early Swedish DIY electronic scene. Inspired by pioneers such as Kraftwerk, Cabaret Voltaire, John Foxx, and The Human League, Mikael Isaksson developed a distinct sound situated between minimal electronics, industrial, synth wave, and experimental sound art. At its core was the sequencer: pulsing, programmed structures forming the backbone of dense, often hypnotic compositions.

Working initially with his cousin Jan or friend Thomas and later evolving into a largely one-man project, recordings were made on cassette tapes and in improvised studios—often under time pressure, frequently recorded and mixed within just a few hours. These very limitations gave the tracks their raw and immediate character. Pieces like “Moderna Kvinnor,” “Soon Soon,” “Ensam,” and “Music From The Border” exemplify the uncompromising, sequence-driven (“sekvensstyrd”) approach that defined this era.

Using an arsenal of analog synthesizers, early sequencers, and drum machines, the project created music that feels at once cold, mechanical, and deeply emotional. Sekvenssytrd 1981–1986 is more than a collection of archival recordings—it is a vivid document of a time when electronic music was conceived as a radical and deeply personal form of expression.”

items.body:
Berlin/Bristol’s bass don piles on and refines the ‘nuum pressure in acres of noirish jazz space for Italy’s XCPT, generating some of his starkest and strongest material, advised to fans of Wax Doctor, Healing Force Project, Photek, Demdike Stare...

With the ‘Airdrop’ trilogy of fractious, ‘unum-surfing collages tucked away from Peak Oil, Low End Activist indulges formative passions for jazz-inflected late ’90s D&B and Y2K tension on ‘JH Versions’. He effectively joins the dots of his brittle, pointillist drum programming with spectral vestiges of ‘70s jazz fusion and neo-noir film music in a similar way to Photek or Wax Doctor, but with more grime (and dark garage) under the cuticles, nailing an ideal of rugged late night music that deftly swerves cliche, or at least tweaks the tropes to his own ends.

‘Midnight’ strikes with a martial percussive discipline veiled by goth jazz keys and whispers, beside the stoned/drunken-master warehouse swerve and haunted dancehall of ‘Sapphire’ going like Photek meets The Caretaker. The depth-charged subs and ricochet drums of ‘Ultramarine’ feel like shadowboxing underwater to a crowd of sirens, and ‘Celeste’ plumbs the deepest levels of dark garage skip and blunted jazz, somewhere between Healing Force Project and Burial, while ‘Indigo’ signs off with creaking echoes of Wax Doctor’s louche, syncopated flex and Pat Thomas’ jazz jungle throwback.

items.body:
Dutch A/V duo Wanderwelle plunge Davey Jones’ locker in a richly metaphoric expression of worries about climate change and marine devastation, blending hydrophonic acoustic and electronic sources to spell out a sonorous, subaquatic narrative FFO Mark Jenkin film scores, Thomas Köner, AFX’s SAW II...

“After All Hands Bury The Cliffs At Sea (2023) and Black Clouds Above The Bows (2022), Amsterdam-based collective Wanderwelle presents the final entry of their album trilogy for Important Records (IMPREC). Conceived as a sonic reflection on the climate crisis and its devastating impact on coastal ecosystems, Ghosts Beneath The Brine (2026) addresses the mass deaths of fish, seabirds, crustaceans and countless other creatures that call these seas home, now rapidly being overfished, warming and acidifying.

Where antique cavalry trumpets played a central role on Black Clouds Above The Bows and a dying church organ shaped All Hands Bury The Cliffs At Sea, cymbals form the core of Ghosts Beneath The Brine. The instruments were submerged in seawater for extended periods of time and played with a bow at various stages of corrosion. As the bronze alloy gradually reacted with the saltwater, their sound transformed, becoming darker, more fragile and unstable. Over time, the metal began to sing in ghostly overtones, as if haunted by the waters that shaped it. Much like large groups of fish shimmering beneath the surface, the cymbals slowly lost their shine, both sonically and physically, as salt and time took hold.

Alongside its environmental narrative, the album draws from maritime mythology. Echoes of the sea bishop, the kraken, devil whales and sea serpents emerge throughout its soundscape. Once feared and revered, these creatures now exist only in the liminal space between folklore and memory, haunting the collective imagination like omens from a forgotten age. Through immersive textures and submerged harmonies, Wanderwelle intertwines myth and mourning, inviting listeners to drift between the real and the spectral. If humanity continues on its current course, familiar species such as sharks, oysters and even gulls may soon share the same fate as their legendary predecessors, becoming ghosts beneath the brine.”

items.body:
Skewed dub specialist label Blundar host a mutant cumbia dub haunting by Bogotá’s ezmeralda, a leading figure of wayward ambient shook up from the Latin American bush of ghosts...

Preceded by an LP for Tra Tra Trax’s Ambie-Tón divison, and an EP with Éter Editions, ezmeralda continues to stake out a unique sort of tresillo metaphysics perhaps familiar to fans of Debit’s Modern Love albums or Elijah Minnelli fancies, or even The Caretaker’s slant on dusty ballroom standards, but applied to traditional cumbia. Everything inside is slowed and diffused to a vaporous crawl; bone-rubbed rhythms and basslines smudged into oblivion, and air hashed with spectral traces of flutes and accordions; ancient cries heard thru a modern lens.

For 16 minutes ezmeralda suspends perceptions of time and space with a sublime, deferred gratification, never quite fully revealing the forms, operating by suggestion in finely extracted and layered arrangements. The A-side feels as though we’re shored-up on some Mangrove-covered Caribbean coastline of Colombia at night, threats lurking below the briny surface and thick in the air, before the B-side brings the phantoms forward in what feels like Pole processing Elijah Minnelli’s anachronistic cumbia blooz...

Enter the Magnetic Heliosphere. 

 Mikkel Rev returns to A Strangely Isolated Place with Evocation , his third full-length album shaped deep within the forests of Norway. 

 Since Mikkel’s debut, The Art of Levitation first arrived in 2023, Mikkel has been quietly building his own corner of the ASIP catalogue. Last year's Journey Beyond expanded that vision further, revealing an artist increasingly comfortable balancing the emotional pull of early trance with a more reflective, ambient-leaning approach. While his work elsewhere naturally gravitates towards the dance floor through his own collective, Ute Recordings and other club-focused outlets, his ASIP releases have always evolved differently. Beginning with a larger body of material that’s gradually shaped together, each album seeks to find a narrative without a dancefloor in place; one that moves naturally between momentum and stillness, carrying something of the spirit found in those early-'90s records that drifted effortlessly between peak-time energy and the quiet hours in room two. 

 astrangelyisolatedplace · Mikkel Rev / Evocation (ASIPV057) [Previews] 

 Long-form compositions like "Step Inside" and "MRI" favor gradual development over immediate impact, while "Dream Sand" introduces shimmering rhythms that subtly shift the album's momentum and pace. The piano-led "The Infinite" offers a definitive nod to the enduring emotional pull of classic trance before "Sanitorium" closes the record with one of Mikkel's most restrained and affecting pieces to date.

 Evocation continues Mikkel Rev's remarkable run on ASIP, extending a catalog where echoes of trance's formative years find new expression through the communal energy and natural surroundings of the Nordic forest gatherings that have become an integral part of his world.

 Ventral Is Golden returns on artwork duties, with Lupo handling the mastering and cut. Released on August 28th as a gatefold double LP on dusty purple smoke and digital.

items.body: My daughter and I walked up Seventh Avenue on a balmy, post-thunderstorm July night to one of the most well-known, and most sacred, of all jazz venues on the planet, the storied Village Vanguard, to catch the opening night of a week-long residence by the trio Paradoxical Frog. Readers of the Free Jazz Blog might care to know this was a historical occasion and one that involved the reuniting of three musicians often discussed here at the FJC: pianist Kris Davis, saxophonist Ingrid Laubrock, and drummer Tyshawn Sorey. Behind the famous red doors that evening would perform an avant-garde trio that had not played together in over a decade. And the band’s unconventional leanings are perhaps less alien to the Vanguard than one might first guess. Davis and Sorey have performed at the Vanguard countless times, and Laubrock’s appearance is as rare and welcome as the recent celebrated stint of the James Brandon Lewis Quartet in the West Village club. This is to say nothing of the audience in the house that night: I spotted Sylvie Courvoisier a few seats behind me, and encountered William Parker outside the doors after the first set had concluded. Davis actually opened the show fact-checking the record. “I was corrected on social media,” she said. “It has not been fifteen years since the three of us played together; it has been eleven.” In any case, for listeners to either of the group’s two Cleanfeed recordings, 2010’s Paradoxical Frog , and 2012’s Union , it had been a long wait to hear these three masters perform in this distinct context. The opening night’s set consisted of four long compositions, all of which have appeared on record at some point. The first performance, a combination of Laubrock’s “Masterisk” and Davis’s “Union” spanned over twenty-nine minutes. Seeing the work live allowed me to confirm just how through-composed these Paradoxical Frog pieces are. Note the extensive paper scores in Davis’s and Sorey’s hands and the extensions on Laubrock’s music stand: a necessary tool to display the lengthy writings of each work without requiring the saxophonist to flip pages of these surprising compositions that challenge functional harmony and defy circular rhythm. The third work was “Whistlings” from 2020’s Blood Moon , the Intakt Records duo of Davis and Laubrock. The live performance, over twice the length of the original recording, featured Laubrock on soprano saxophone and Tyshawn Sorey on a sonic array of material, at times the room so quiet that Sorey’s percussion would consist of simply waving his brushes in the air, an effect that hauntingly filled the room with audible whisperings. The set concluded with Sorey’s “Slow Burn,” clocking in at over sixteen minutes and featuring the mysterious repetition of single notes on Davis’s piano keys. It was moving to see these three unite again, and I am certain I do not speak alone in voicing my hopes for more work in the future, maybe even a Live at the Village Vanguard recording to place among some of the mythical voices who have passed through that hallowed underground room. items.body:
BTS have announced that they will not submit their music for consideration at the 69th Grammy Awards, set to take place in February 2027.

The group shared the news via Instagram Stories across all seven members' accounts on 29 July, revealing that they had decided against entering this year's awards cycle.

"We have decided not to submit to the Grammys this year. We hope music can be heard and embraced for what it is, beyond region or language. Thank you to ARMY and everyone who continues to support us," the group wrote.

The decision comes just weeks after the Recording Academy introduced Best Asian Pop Music Performance, a new category that will debut at the 2027 Grammys. Created to recognise excellence in Asian pop music, the award covers works in one or more Asian languages, including K-pop, J-pop, and C-pop.

The addition of the category has sparked widespread discussion across the music industry. While some have welcomed it as long-overdue recognition of Asian pop's global influence, others have questioned whether it creates a separate lane for Asian artists rather than recognising them alongside other acts in the Grammys' General Field categories.

Although BTS did not explain the reason behind their decision beyond their statement, the timing has led many fans and industry observers to connect it to the newly introduced category.

The announcement is particularly notable given the group's long-standing history with the Recording Academy. Over the years, BTS have openly spoken about winning a Grammy as one of their career ambitions. They previously earned Grammy nominations for 'Dynamite', 'Butter', and 'My Universe', but have yet to take home a trophy.

Earlier this year, the septet made a record-breaking return with ARIRANG, their first full-length studio album in six years. The album debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, while lead single 'SWIM' topped the Billboard Hot 100, further cementing the group's global impact.

Whether or not BTS return to Grammy consideration in future years remains to be seen, but their latest decision has reignited conversations about how global music—and particularly Asian artists—are recognised on one of music's biggest stages.

items.body:
ZELO is keeping the summer vibes alive with the release of his latest single via VLACKSQUAD, 'ELA', marking the next step in the South Korean artist's evolving musical journey.

Following the release of 'Cola Comigo', the former B.A.P member continues to lean into Latin-pop influences, blending breezy rhythms with smooth R&B sensibilities and polished global pop production. The result is a track built for late-night drives, festival singalongs, and sun-soaked playlists.

Before its official release, ZELO gave fans a first taste of 'ELA' during his performance at WATERBOMB, one of South Korea's biggest summer festivals. The live debut introduced thousands of festivalgoers to the song's vibrant, carefree energy.

Anchored by a dreamy electric guitar and tropical-inspired production, 'ELA' pairs rhythmic percussion with an infectious melodic hook. ZELO's vocals effortlessly glide between melodic passages and rhythmic delivery, highlighting the versatility he has continued to develop as a solo artist.

While 'Cola Comigo' introduced his Latin-pop direction, 'ELA' expands on that foundation by weaving together Latin-inspired grooves, contemporary R&B, and ZELO's signature performance style. Rather than chasing trends, the single feels like a natural progression of his evolving sound.

'ELA' also taps into the nostalgia of 2010s global pop, recalling memories of festival nights, open-air parties, and unforgettable summer moments while giving that familiar feeling a fresh, modern update.

items.body:
For Réjizz, the future is no longer something waiting around the corner. On his five-track EP The Era, the Bangkok-born rapper, singer, and producer steps fully into the world he first imagined on its predecessor, The New Era. The project captures who he is now—more visible, more assured, and increasingly aware of the pressures that arrive alongside success.

Moving through jazz-infused hip-hop, darker cinematic production, and dance-driven rhythms, The Era places Réjizz’s Thai-Funk sound in several distinct emotional worlds. Across tracks such as 'I've Been Around', 'JRIZ', 'Uncomfortable Situations', 'Long Disco Relationship', and 'In My Position', he reflects on life away from home, modern dating, industry artificiality, long-distance love, and learning to trust his own direction.

In this interview with Bandwagon, Réjizz opens up about creating his most vulnerable project yet, choosing clarity over old vices, and the artistic freedom he hopes to reach in the next phase of his journey.

The Era follows The New Era, which represented the future you were working towards. When did you realise that future had become your present?

Since I started The New Era, I wanted to touch on different styles of music. It was always part of the long-term plan to introduce the audience to a new sound I was working on, and then I cemented the idea with The Era. Now that the EP has been released, it feels like the future has become the present.

You have described The Era as your most vulnerable and “realest” project yet. What were you ready to reveal here that you could not have expressed on your earlier releases?

I was stuck in a situation where my flow state and creativity were suppressed for a long time, and my quality of life suffered because of it. This EP gave me a space to finally express those feelings.

When I was younger, I usually dealt with this by giving in to my vices. This time, I decided to go straight-edge, which gave me clarity and made my writing more vivid than ever before. I wasn’t rushing to write. I carefully chose each word and used different rhyming techniques to express my truest feelings.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Marshall Records (@marshallrecords)

Each track occupies a different sonic and emotional world. What is the thread that connects all five songs and makes them part of the same era?

I’ve always touched on different sounds and universes throughout my projects, but the connecting part is who I am in that project. Réjizz is the connecting thread.

I’m no longer an underground artist trying to prove myself. It’s cool to win an award and be the first Thai artist to sign to Marshall Records, but success comes with new problems, and this project addresses that.

One thing that has been consistent throughout my projects is love. I always find a track or a verse to address that.

On 'I've Been Around', you explore the tension between pursuing the life you worked for and missing home. Has success changed what “home” means to you?

When I’m away, calling my mom or my lady gives me a sense of home for a little while. But it will always feel good to actually be back home.

Last year, I moved back to my childhood home, and that house really feels like home. So “home” to me still means going back and seeing my mom.

'JRIZ' is the EP’s only Thai-language track. Why did this story about modern dating feel most natural to tell in Thai?

A lot of Thai songs are about love anyway. I chose this track to be the most easy-listening one for a mass audience, so I wrote a love song with a slight twist.

'JRIZ' moves between male and female perspectives. How did you write from both sides while keeping each voice honest and nuanced?

At my age, my single friends are moving through the dating world fast. They rant about it to me all the time, so I wanted to use that as the premise of the song and write a verse from both the guy’s and the girl’s perspectives.

Each voice is honest because they are actual lines from friends around me.

'Uncomfortable Situations' transforms the guests at an industry party into aliens and monsters. Was that imagery inspired by a specific experience, or by feelings that built up over time?

The imagery was inspired by a real-life event where a lot of wealthy individuals came to this party to “network”, and a lot of talents were looking to be hired. Everyone connects on a surface level early in the night, but after a few drinks, their true colours start to show.

They say, “You can be famous if you just…” and by the time they finish their thought, it’s like they want you to change your whole identity, like you’re going to lose your soul. I believe a lot of talents change themselves to become famous.

So my analogy for these encounters is aliens and monsters that try to make you become one of them. I still encounter these situations to this day. Every time it happens, this song plays in my head.

In 'Long Disco Relationship', you compare long-distance love to two people trying to stay in step as the music shifts. In real life, what does it take to keep that connection alive?

Communication is the most important thing because it is the only thing you can do when you’re far away. Like on the dance floor, you must stick to the same rhythm to remain connected to each other.

'In My Position' addresses the different voices trying to influence your direction. How have you learned to distinguish meaningful advice from distraction?

Who the advice comes from is always crucial. If they share the same values as me and they’ve accomplished what I strive for, it makes the advice much more credible.

The ones who are a distraction are the ones who don’t align with my values. Usually, they’re trying to steer me into something I’m not.

At the end of the day, my instinct and gut feeling always tell me which one to trust. It’s like my Spidey-sense.

The Era documents who you are in the present. After completing it, what part of yourself are you most curious to explore next?

I am looking forward to the day when I reach my prime—when my working system is stable, I trust the people who work with me, and I have consistent tours. I want enough to make a living, but not so many that they drain my soul. I’ll constantly be in a flow state.

That’s when I’ll be carefree, and my music will be free to become whatever it wants.

I might want to make a trashy trap song one day, then an eloquent jazz-infused Mo Lam song the next. I’ll master English and Thai, seamlessly mixing them in my music. The ideas are unlimited.

That day is when I’ll truly take ownership of my own craft. I’ll probably name it Réjizz Mania or DOIN’ MY THANG. I don’t know—that stage is still to be explored.

items.body:
Tomorrowland Belgium 2026 has officially come to a close after two weekends at De Schorre in Boom, welcoming 400,000 festivalgoers from more than 200 countries while reaching a record-breaking 233 million livestream views across YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram.

Held 17–19 July and 24–26 July, this year's edition revolved around Consciencia, a new festival theme exploring six universal emotions — Wonder, Love, Anger, Joy, Desire, and Sadness. Rather than assigning stages solely by genre, Tomorrowland built each of its 16 stages around an emotional identity, with stage design, production, and programming reflecting one of the six themes.

The concept also came to life on the festival's largest Mainstage to date. Standing over 43 metres tall and 140 metres wide, the structure featured towering waterfalls, fountains, lasers, and six giant sculptures representing the emotions at the heart of Consciencia. The ambitious production marked a major return for Tomorrowland following last year's Mainstage fire, which forced organisers to rethink the festival's centrepiece shortly before opening.

Away from the Mainstage, more than 500 artists performed across the festival grounds. Among the standout moments was Calvin Harris' long-awaited Tomorrowland Belgium debut, closing the Mainstage on both Saturdays with a career-spanning set. During Weekend 1, John Newman joined Harris onstage for a live performance of 'Blame', while techno star Charlotte de Witte surprised fans with an unannounced Mainstage appearance after weeks of speculation.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Calvin Harris (@calvinharris)

The festival also had to adapt to unusually dry weather conditions. Belgian authorities imposed restrictions on fireworks and pyrotechnics during the opening weekend because of elevated wildfire risks. While limited close-range effects returned for Weekend 2, Tomorrowland replaced many of its signature fireworks with large-scale LED visuals across the Mainstage screens.

Beyond the music, organisers also teased what's next for the festival brand. A banner displayed near Dreamville hinted at a possible Tomorrowland expansion to Las Vegas in 2027 alongside events in France, Belgium, Brazil, Ibiza, and Thailand, though organisers have yet to officially reveal further details.

Not every headline was celebratory. During the opening weekend, two original paintings commissioned for the Consciencia theme were stolen from the Tomorrowland Restaurant. One artwork, Love, was later recovered and returned before Weekend 2, while Desire remains missing.

For fans watching from around the world, Tomorrowland's digital presence continued to grow. The festival's livestream attracted 233 million views—surpassing last year's 193 million and setting a new record for the event. The figures underline how Tomorrowland has evolved beyond an on-site festival into one of electronic music's largest global broadcast experiences.

The festival also drew a number of familiar faces from Singapore, with radio personality Sonia Chew, content creators Saffron Sharpe and Edo Lio among those spotted at Tomorrowland Belgium 2026.

The trio shared glimpses of their experience on social media, including a meet-up with headlining Dutch DJ Martin Garrix. Check out their posts below for a closer look at their Tomorrowland adventure.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SONIA CHEW (@soniachew)

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Saffron Sharpe มะนาว (@saffronsharpe)

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Edo Lio (@edo_lio)

Although organisers have yet to unveil the theme for 2027, they have suggested that the Consciencia storyline may continue in future editions, hinting that this year's exploration of human emotion may be only the beginning of a larger narrative.

You can now relive full sets and festival highlights on the festival's official YouTube channel, the Tomorrowland App, and Apple Music.

items.body:
Singapore's choral community is set to come together once again as the Voices of Singapore (VOS) Festival returns for its 11th edition, taking place 5–9 September across four venues in the city. The annual event remains Singapore's largest non-competitive choral festival, bringing together singers of all ages for five days of performances, workshops, masterclasses, and community-led musical experiences.

This year's edition will span CHIJMES Hall, Capitol Singapore Outdoor Plaza, VOS Capitol Studios, and, for the first time, the VOS Choral Hub at Enabling Village. The new venue expands the festival's inclusive programming, reflecting the organisation's ongoing efforts to make choral music more accessible to communities across Singapore.

Across the five-day festival, audiences can expect close to 50 programmes, including gala concerts, school choir performances, recitals, outdoor showcases, choir exchanges, workshops, and masterclasses. Rather than focusing on competition, the festival continues to champion collaboration and learning, creating opportunities for choirs to perform, connect, and grow together.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Voices of Singapore (@voicesofsingapore)

Leading this year's artistic programme are internationally acclaimed guest conductors Dr. Jeffery Redding (USA), Mak Chi Hoe (Malaysia), and Lieu Ryland-Jones (Estonia). They will conduct four specially formed Festival Choruses — Children's, Youth, Community, and Virtuosi — while also leading more than 10 masterclasses for Singapore school choirs and five public workshops for music educators and conductors.

Festival highlights also include four gala performances at CHIJMES Hall featuring VOS Choirs, the Filipino Voice Symphony, and the Festival Choruses, alongside six concerts showcasing school choirs from across Singapore. Audiences can also catch free outdoor performances at Capitol Singapore Outdoor Plaza, with programmes including the VOSF Open Mic, A Cappella Arena, The Voice Company, and the debut of Silver Sing, which spotlights members of VOS Silver Voices performing as soloists and in small ensembles.

Beyond performances, VOS Festival continues to place community and inclusion at its core. Silver Exchanges will bring together seniors from VOS Community Silver Voices programmes across Singapore, while Starlight Exchanges will unite SPED school choirs, mainstream schools, and VOS Starlight Voices in shared musical experiences celebrating neurodiversity and accessibility through song. Choirs will also have the option to participate in ABRSM Choral Exams hosted during the festival.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Voices of Singapore (@voicesofsingapore)

Speaking about this year's edition, VOS Festival Manager Gabriel Ching shared that one of the festival's greatest strengths lies in the connections formed between choirs. He added that introducing the VOS Choral Hub at Enabling Village opens the festival to even more singers and audiences through a space designed with inclusivity in mind.

For full programme details, visit: https://www.voicesofsingapore.com/vos-festival. Tickets and registration: https://www.eventbrite.sg/e/voices-of-singapore-festival-2026-tickets-1991671909295.

items.body:
After years of anticipation, BIGBANG are officially returning to the road. In celebration of the group's 20th anniversary, G-DRAGON, TAEYANG, and DAESUNG have unveiled the BIGBANG 2026–2027 WORLD TOUR < XX : COSMOS >, a 17-city, 33-show stadium trek that marks their first tour together in nine years.

The global tour kicks off in South Korea before making its way through North America and Europe, eventually arriving in Asia this October. Fans across the region can look forward to stadium performances in Taipei, Singapore, Hanoi, Bangkok, Hong Kong, Osaka, Nagoya, Tokyo, Fukuoka, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, Manila, and Kaohsiung as the group celebrates two decades since their debut.

Widely regarded as one of K-pop's most influential acts, the group helped lay the foundation for the genre's global rise with hits including 'Lie', 'Last Farewell', 'Haru Haru', 'FANTASTIC BABY', and 'BANG BANG BANG'. Fans can expect the group's signature stage production, dynamic performances, and plenty of sing-along moments throughout the tour.

Speaking about hosting the landmark performance, Quek Swee Kuan, Chief Executive Officer of The Kallang Group, said, “Fans in Singapore and across Asia are eagerly awaiting BIGBANG’s 20th Anniversary World Tour, and we are proud to bring this landmark event to The Kallang for V.I.Ps. items.body:
INTERNATIONAL（海外）
NEWS
ダウンビート誌「国際批評家投票 2026」（第74回）結果発表
2026年7月28日
編集部

74回目を迎えた2026年度の米ダウンビート誌「批評家投票」の結果が発表された。レジェンドへのリスペクトを残しつつ、確実に世代の移り変わりを反映した結果と言えるだろう。最大のトピックは10年連続「年間最優秀ギタリスト」の座を10年連続して押さえた女性ギタリストのメアリー・ハルヴァーソンが、併せて「年間最優秀アーティスト」と「年間最優秀グループ」に選出、３冠を達成したことだろう。メアリーは昨年の「トミーカ・リード・ユニット」のグループに続いて、今年８月には自己の「アマリリス」セクステットでのブルーノート東京公園が予定されている。
新人部門では、アダム・オファリルが、「最優秀アーティスト」「最優秀トランペット」「最優秀アレンジャー」の３冠を制している。
日本人アーティストでは、いまや常連の藤井郷子が、「ピアニスト」(16位)、「作曲家」(18位)、「編曲家」 (7位)、「ラージ・アンサンブル」 (13位) の４部門で、挟間美帆が「編曲家」部門で３位、田村夏樹が「トランペット」 (16位) 部門でそれぞれランクインを果たしている。

各部門の「最優秀」受賞は以下の通り；
Hall of Fame：Sheila Jordan
＊ヘンリー・スレッギルに次いでポール・ブレイが第３位。
Artist of the Year：Mary Halvorson
＊ベテランではチャールス・ロイドが11位。
Album of the Year：『Mary Halvorson/About Ghosts』(nonesuch)
＊ベテラン勢ではチャールス・ロイドとビル・フリゼールが５位と６位に。
Historical Album of the Year：『Keith Jarrett/At the Deer Head Inn Complete』(ECM)
Group of the Year：Mary Halvorson Amaryllis
＊ベテラン勢では、チャールス・ロイド・カルテット、ブランフォード・マルサリス・カルテットがそれぞれ７、８位に。
Large Ensemble of the Year：Maria Schneider Orchestra
＊べテランでは「サン・ラ・アーケストラ」が３位に。
Record Label of the Year：Blue Note
＊Pyroclasticに次いでECMが３位。
Producer of the Year：Zev Feldman
＊Manfred Eicher/ECMが２位に続く。
Piano：Kris Davis
Bass：Linda May Han Oh
Trombone：Michael Dease
Alto Saxophone：Immanuel Wilkins
Tenor Saxophone：James Brandon Lewis
Soprano Saxophone：Jane Ira Bloom
Clarinet：Anat Cohen
Organ：Larry Goldings
Keyboard：Craig Taborn
Violin：Jenny Scheinman
Percussion：Hamid Drake
Female Vocalist：Cécile McLorin Salvant
