items.body: After more than a decade releasing music as Arubu Avua, Victor Negri‘s Sem opens a new chapter by removing baggage and stripping away. The title translates as “without”, and the album emerges from a period marked by grief, relocation and uncertainty, assembling recordings made across years and continents into a fragile but deeply coherent whole. Built primarily from irregular guitar loops, field recordings, feedback and electronics, Sem is an album concerned not only with loss, but with what remains afterwards. Negri has spoken of listening almost exclusively to Loren Connors and Stars of the Lid while making the record, and their influence can be felt throughout. The music often moves at the edge of silence, allowing sounds to linger, decay and reveal their imperfections. Tracks such as “Voçoroca”, “Obrigado” and “Hinweg ists” embrace low-fi textures and ambient intrusion, transforming phone recordings, environmental noise and accidental details into emotional substance. Yet Sem is far from monochrome. “O crux ave, spes unica” introduces a surprising melodic warmth, while “Não” pushes towards abrasion, embedding experimentation within a dense drone. “Os cacos” carries faint traces of Brazilian musical modernism, its fractured lyricism hinting at Tropicália’s legacy without ever becoming nostalgic. Throughout the album, Negri treats memory as collage: unfinished sketches, decade-old recordings and fragments from abandoned futures are carefully reassembled into something new. For listeners familiar with the darker political landscapes of much contemporary experimental music, Sem occupies a different emotional register. It shares little with the extroverted energy of some of Negri’s earlier song-based work, yet neither does it descend into despair. Instead, it resembles an act of quiet reconstruction. The closing “Boa continuação” — literally “carry on” — ends in a haze of ambiguous sound, somewhere between electronics, water and static. It is a fitting conclusion to an album that understands grief not as an endpoint, but as a process of learning how to inhabit a changed world. In the following interview conducted over email, Victor Negri discusses the production process for the album. photo by Emanuele Porcinai After more than a decade releasing music as Arubu Avua, Sem is your first album under your own name. What prompted that shift? Did the deeply personal nature of the record require a different artistic frame, or did using your own name change the way you approached the music itself? Over the last couple of years, I’ve been thinking about how, when big changes and losses happen, it’s unclear how much of the shift is a pause for recollection, a stopgap, or actually a new, more permanent reality. Is this the next chapter already? And I think the name, in this case, reflects that uncertainty for me. This choice is a bit like stating: this is me now, or so it seems, without (“sem” means “without”) a life that used to exist, and I happen to have this name. That’s all I know, and everything else is a question mark: the “without” part is clear, the “with” not so much. But of course, if you use your own name in order to state it’s a more personal project, you may feel too exposed and then guard yourself, which may lead to less creative freedom. So the result could be a more personal project that’s somehow less honest or alive. In my case, I’m not sure I would release songs, with words and vocals, under my own name, for example. But this instrumental framework is more comfortable, at least for now. You’ve described Sem as emerging from a period of multiple losses, relocations, and a sense of speechlessness. The album contains no vocals at all, something new in your work. At what point did you realise that words were no longer necessary—or perhaps no longer possible—and that the record had to communicate through instrumental and textural means alone? In a way, it’s not a huge leap for me, as my song-based work does contain many instrumental tracks. This interplay or tension is something I ended up developing as a style: often, when I’m doing a longer instrumental passage, it may have developed from a song, or there may be a song coming up around the corner. So, stylistically, I think the change was about not relying on the voice and seeing how the other sounds can stand on their own, without that support. That being said, in this case specifically, I’d say it was more of a block. I wanted words to do justice to the situation in order to be preserved forever, which felt like an impossible task. I also wanted to avoid clichés, which turned out to be difficult when going through turmoil. Also, around that time, I was listening to more instrumental music and had recently done some improvised duo concerts with a friend in Portugal. So that also informed the decision and made it easier to follow this instrumental route. You mentioned that for months you could only listen to Stars of the Lid and Loren Connors, “the slowest possible music,” because “all words were excessive.” What was it about Loren Connors in particular that resonated with you during that period? Can traces of his approach to guitar, fragility, and silence be heard in pieces such as “Voçoroca,” “Obrigado,” or “Boa continuação”? Loren Connors’ music, in my opinion, allows for a feeling of surrender, in that it sounds devastating but it’s so restrained, you just have to stop and listen. It can be considered ambient, but it refuses to merge into the background, it demands that you pause and enter that world. Or your own world. To me Connors’ music would be the equivalent of a poem describing very small and minute details, in order to produce an overwhelming feeling of loss. And those details extend to the fragility you mentioned, in the playing, imperfect by traditional standards, scratchy, could fall apart any minute but never does. Plus the low fidelity recordings, the fade-ins and outs, which feel like accidentally tuning in to that world for a short while. All of that is really moving and inspiring to me. The three tracks you mentioned are examples of that inspiration, I think. They are based on acoustic guitar recordings I did with my phone, sitting outside the house in my hometown. Some of the ambience joins in, as well as the phone’s exaggerated compression and gating. Silence—or at least the possibility of silence—feels almost like another instrument on Sem. The loops often seem suspended in place, unsure whether to continue, dissolve, or collapse into feedback. How conscious were you of leaving space within the music, and did editing become a way of sculpting absence as much as sound? As for a conscious use of silence, there is a filtered hiss that opens and closes the album, which was originally a very low-volume recording of an empty room. When it’s amplified like that, you get the noise floor of the recorder, but at some point I thought I began to hear a voice in there. Probably there was some neighbor singing somewhere, but it was kind of eerie and made me think of EVP, trying to reach ghosts via electronics and white noise. This bit of silence made me wonder about the possibility of communicating with the dead, but at the same time I struggled to believe in that. So that’s what the silence bookending the project means to me, it’s a bit charged and ambiguous. Apart from that, I think there’s a general low fidelity and an openness to surrounding noise. I’m usually interested in that, so it may be less conscious. But when going through grief, the surrounding noise is slightly different: it’s the sound of being present in a new world, taking it in. I know at the time I was more easily overwhelmed than usual. So there’s often a need for a breath after a new bit of information: let’s try to digest that before we move on. A lot of it is very tentative, as you said, unsure where to go next, but it’s also a way to stay with each sound for a while and watch it go. The album is built from recordings made across many years and locations—Berlin, Porto, Lisbon, Campinas, and even phone recordings from more than a decade ago. In that sense, Sem feels both like a guitar album and a collage of memories. How did you navigate the balance between documenting the past and creating something new? Were there moments when assembling these fragments felt closer to mourning, archaeology, or reconstruction? I guess mourning tends to pull us into the past, into what was lost, and sometimes it leads to archaeology, especially if one feels there are missing or unresolved pieces. That was the case for me. It’s a look at what used to be, but also what could have been. These previous recordings are snapshots of potential music, futures that never came to be, in places I left. I somehow gravitated toward those pieces while looking in my computer for sketches and ideas to work with, and the demos seemed fitting. There was a slight detachment in approaching them as a listener, a listener who happened to be grieving, and they made a lot of sense. So I decided to work on those kinds of tracks, to start from there. Sometimes this archaeology can be impossible. I was dealing with the sudden death of a close family member, with whom I wish I could have been closer, and with whom I realized I have very few photographs together. So the dimension of this loss, or this presence even, is barely documented at all. There was, and still is, a sense of powerlessness, of having nothing to hold on to. In that sense, the collage feels like assembling things that never were, plans that never came to be. At the same time — and maybe that’s the reconstruction part –, I try to look at it as some kind of affirmative landscape, or proof that things did happen, that they were real. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Cinnamon Gum is the project of Gdańsk-based Maciej Milewski, a vocalist and multi-instrumentalist whose father spent years playing saxophone in a Caribbean cruise-ship big band, coming home each time with soul records and cinnamon-flavoured chewing gum that were near-impossible to find in Poland. Both ended up defining his career: Milewski’s 2024 album The Cinnamon Show, recorded entirely on analogue instruments and drawing from the falsetto soul of Marvin Gaye and Curtis Mayfield, broke him through at home and caught the ear of That’s Love Records co-founder Alejandro Garcia, who signed him to the New Jersey label. “Mary Liz” was cut in February at Studio Zoe in Princeton, to tape, with Max Shrager producing, mixing, and playing vibraphone. The ballad was written with Dorota Theisebach, a Polish vocalist who competed on The Voice of Poland in 2013, and the two voices carry it together through organ, a patient bassline, and live drums. The session was fully analogue from recording to mix, and the warmth that process gives the mid-range is where the track lives. It’s the lead single from Cinnamon Gum’s forthcoming third album. You can stream and get a copy of “Mary Liz” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Cinnamon Gum – Mary Liz appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There is something atypical about "Reverse in the Sand", from the interplay of keyboards and guitar to the composition and vocals, it features the intricate nuances characteristic of the Canterbury scene and those floating keyboards that drive the action; and that is just the beginning of the debut from the Italian band Instant Curtain.There is an atonal touch to the chorus of "Tell the Tales, May I," successfully executed by vocalist Massimo Gerini. It evokes the sound of National Health's Of Queues and Cures, specifically Phil Miller's guitar work, combined with the atonal vocal style characteristic of Wigwam, lending the track an otherworldly quality at times. And those are its finest moments.Giuseppe Petrucci plays the Rhodes, Mellotron, and Hammond on "All White," adding a variety of sounds that, along with the acoustic guitar, form the foundation for the electric guitar to deliver solos that cut right across the entire track.In "The Ship Battle Down," I detected something of the atmosphere of Genesis's Trespass, both vocally and instrumentally, combined with the aforementioned elements that gradually break the song down, much like a sunny day that slowly clouds over until turning gray. The guitar accompanies and illustrates this shift. For me, this is definitely the standout track on the album, what with the vocal shifts and those Anthony Phillips-esque guitar harmonies.Even songs with a more predictable progression... feature mid-sections that veer away from the expected and turn ethereal, like "And the Rest Divide Us", with an instrumental section featuring Hammond organ, bass, and guitar that feels quite apocalyptic which creates a very captivating atmosphere."Safe as the World" blends instrumental and vocal sections, interspersed with keyboard solos and guitar chords, until they merge into a single song, as if the band intended to embody the title within the music itself, making it explicit. "Stay" begins with a touch of fusion, leading into a new guitar riff that wouldn't sound out of place in the band Bill Bruford formed with Allan Holdsworth.There are traces of a "polar" guitar sound, cold and echoing, reminiscent of McLaughlin, and once again, the vocals intertwine seamlessly with the instruments, to the point where they almost become one. This is how "April," the final track, unfolds; with the high-pitched tones and echoes characteristic of the Norwegian band Needlepoint, it concludes a showcase of compositional complexity that is remarkable for a debut.

items.body: Review by blessed_of — When I first encountered the music of Roz Vitalis, I was introduced to their brilliance through the album TheHidden Man of the Heart. This initial experience turned out to be transformative, as the album left a profound and lasting impression on me. Each composition felt like a portal to an intricate world of emotions, thoughts, and atmospheres that only Roz Vitalis could create. From the very first listen, I knew that this album was something special. It resonated with me on a level that few works of art ever do. Every day since, I find myself returning to its tracks, allowing them to be both a soundtrack to my daily life and a source of solace and inspiration. Tracks like "Jungle Waltz," "Blurred," and "Someone Passed Over" have become indispensable to me, each carrying a distinct identity and emotional weight that draws me in time and time again. The complexity and depth of The Hidden Man of the Heart are nothing short of awe-inspiring. Roz Vitalis has mastered the art of blending a wide array of instruments and textures to create a sound that feels both expansive and intimate. The band's compositions on this album are a masterclass in progressive rock? thoughtful yet daring, meticulously crafted yet brimming with raw emotion. One of the standout qualities of this album is its ability to evoke vivid imagery and emotional landscapes. "Jungle Waltz" is a prime example. This track feels like a journey into an otherworldly forest, with its intricate rhythms and interplay of instruments painting a lush, almost cinematic scene. The dynamic shifts in the track keep me engaged every time I listen, as if I'm discovering something new with each playthrough. "Blurred" is another gem, exuding a contemplative melancholy that speaks to the complexities of human experience. The layers of melody intertwine seamlessly, creating a poignant tapestry of sound that feels both fragile and enduring. It's a track that invites introspection, and I often find myself lost in thought as it plays. "Someone Passed Over," on the other hand, carries a sense of solemnity and transcendence. The emotional depth of this piece is unparalleled, with each note and phrase resonating deeply. It's a track that feels almost sacred, and listening to it is nothing short of a cathartic experience. While the album itself is a masterpiece, the experience of hearing these tracks performed live is something else entirely. Roz Vitalis' ability to translate the intricate layers of their studio work to the stage is remarkable. In fact, I'd argue that the music from The Hidden Man of the Heart reaches its full potential in a live setting. The energy, spontaneity, and synergy between the musicians elevate the compositions to new heights. What truly sets Roz Vitalis apart in their live performances is their use of a wide array of instruments. The rich palette of sounds?from the ethereal keyboards to the soaring guitars and intricate percussions?creates a sonic tapestry that envelops the audience. Each instrument seems to have its own voice, yet they all come together in perfect harmony, creating an atmosphere that is both immersive and electrifying. The atmosphere at their concerts is unlike anything else. There's a sense of connection and communal experience, as if everyone in the room is collectively journeying through the landscapes painted by the music. The emotional intensity of tracks like "Jungle Waltz" and "Blurred" is amplified tenfold in a live setting, and "Someone Passed Over" becomes even more poignant, its solemnity filling the space with a profound stillness. My admiration for The Hidden Man of the Heart goes beyond its technical brilliance and emotional depth. This album has become a part of my life, a companion that I turn to in moments of joy, reflection, and even sorrow. Its ability to adapt to my mood and provide what I need in any given moment is a testament to its timeless quality. The fact that this was my first introduction to Roz Vitalis makes it all the more special. It's rare to encounter an album that feels like a perfect entry point into a band's world, but The Hidden Man of the Heart was exactly that for me. It's an album that not only showcases the band's immense talent but also invites listeners to explore their other works with eager anticipation. Roz Vitalis is a band that defies categorization. While their music is often labeled as progressive rock, it transcends genre boundaries, incorporating elements of classical music, jazz, and avant-garde experimentation. This eclectic approach is evident throughout The Hidden Man of the Heart, where each track feels like a unique exploration of sound and emotion. The band's ability to blend complexity with accessibility is one of their greatest strengths. Their compositions are rich and intricate, rewarding careful and repeated listening, yet they never feel alienating or overly academic. Instead, they invite listeners to immerse themselves in the music and discover its layers at their own pace. At its heart, TheHidden Man of the Heart is an album that speaks to the human experience. Its themes of introspection, longing, and transcendence are universal, and the music conveys them with a sincerity and authenticity that is deeply moving. There's a spiritual quality to the album, as if it's reaching for something beyond the material world and inviting listeners to do the same. This emotional core is what makes the album so enduring for me. No matter how many times I listen to it, it never feels old or stale. Instead, it continues to reveal new facets of itself, offering fresh insights and emotions with each playthrough. It's a work of art that grows with the listener, becoming more meaningful over time. Roz Vitalis' The Hidden Man of the Heart is more than just an album; it's a journey, an experience, and a source of inspiration. Its masterful compositions, emotional depth, and timeless quality have made it an integral part of my life, and I can't imagine a day without its music. Whether I'm listening to "Jungle Waltz," "Blurred," or "Someone Passed Over," I'm reminded of the incredible power of music to move, inspire, and connect us. To anyone who has yet to discover Roz Vitalis, I can think of no better starting point than The Hidden Man of the Heart. It's a testament to the band's artistry and a shining example of what progressive music can achieve. For me, it's a lifelong companion, a work of art that I will cherish forever.

items.body: Review by blessed_of — �Dedication to Bignick�: a triumph of musical depth and spiritual focus. Roz Vitalis is a Russian band working at the intersection of progressive rock, chamber academic music and post- avant-garde electronics. Their sound is a synthesis of intellectual rigor and emotional richness. It envelops like a prayer and disturbs like a piercing philosophical thought. This is not just music ? it is a form of spiritual work, where each note is a step towards meaning. The album �Dedication to Bignick� is a nine-part musical dedication, filled with sadness, respect and inner light at the same time. It opens with the composition �The Tragedy of the Ancient Spring�, which sets the tone for the entire work: majestic, tragic, restrained and honest. This track immediately immerses you in a special space ? a space of memory, reflection, inexpressible melancholy and quiet hope. The album closes with "Silence in Waiting" ? the culminating final point, dissolving the listener in silence, in anticipation, in a trembling pause between worlds. However, the true peak of the album, in my opinion, is "Loneliness - Bringing Power". This composition is like a concentrate of the entire essence of Roz Vitalis: melancholy here is not passive, but is transformed into a source of strength. The sound penetrates deeply into the consciousness, reveals internal resonances, leaving behind not devastation, but purification. Roz Vitalis performers demonstrate the highest level of skill and the finest sense of form. Their work is an example of honesty in art, devoid of vulgarity, ostentatious shock value and superficial emotionality. "Dedication to Bignick" is not just an album, but a gesture of extreme human and musical concentration. It is a gift made in silence and conveyed with deep love.

And no surprise, this persistent search for a new sound sometimes paysoff, and it is why a number of the band's melodies, those combining originality and inner harmony,render a rare sense of discovery of ever existing but just previously unknown treasuries in thePlatonic world of musical ideas. And their last album "The Hidden Man Of The Heart", may be thehigh-water mark of their creative development, perfectly represents the essence of their inventivequest. Of course, RV's works were never everyday easy music for pure distraction, yet it is very farfrom boring and monotonous, and the listener can enjoy a good diversity in the mood and sound in thealbum: from a bright, springy melody of Passing Over through a subtle and beautiful meditation ofSome Refugee Passed Over to an apassionata of Thou Shalt Tread Upon the Lion and Adder.Highly recommended for any lover of sophisticated, intelligent music.

Just three stars may sound a bit a harsh, but on the 17th LP, Vespero has used their listeners to much better music which I would rate four starts.

items.body: My Steve Reich odyssey has taken me to several cities so far this year, including Liverpool, Manchester, London, Cologne and New York, so it seemed fitting that at least one event marking the composer’s ninetieth anniversary year should happen closer to my doorstep, in Wales. In fact, it’s a two-hour drive from where I live to Aberystwyth, where Solem Quartet and singer Alice Zawadzki were performing as part of this year’s Musicfest Festival. Driving down the northwest coast of Wales towards Aberystwyth (through some astonishingly beautiful scenery, where the mountains tumble into the sea), it struck me that perhaps Reich’s music appeals to a more urban demographic. Wrong! Despite the venue’s small size, with Arad Goch Theatre’s stage (which means ‘Red Plow’ in Welsh) only just large enough to accommodate five performers and a couple of large floor monitor speakers, the auditorium was packed to the rafters. It made for an intimate and direct experience, especially given the nature of the programme. Which brings me to Reich’s Different Trains. That work, alongside the later WTC 9/11 (2010), ranks among the composer’s most powerfully resonant statements. Personal, political and historical elements converge in the thirty-minute piece written in 1988 for live string quartet and prerecorded tape. It marked a departure for Reich in its synthesis of speech phrases, Holocaust testimonies and personal biography. Divided into three uninterrupted movements, the first (‘America—before the war’) draws on two sets of recorded interviews: the first between the composer and his governess, Virginia Mitchell—who accompanied Reich as a young boy on his journeys from New York to Los Angeles during the late 1930s and early 40s after his parents separated—and the second featuring retired Pullman porter Laurence Davis, who worked on the train lines during that period. Violinists Amy Tress and William Newell’s imitation of locomotive rhythms, train whistles and clanging bells in the opening half reflected the excitement, anticipation and adventurousness of Reich’s childhood journeys. It captured Noel Perrin’s assertion in a New York Times article written around the time Reich composed Different Trains that ‘Trains and railroads haunt the American mind altogether.’ A sense of nostalgia clung to the air, supported by violist Stephen Upshaw and cellist Stephanie Tress’s imitation of Virginia and Laurence’s clipped speech phrases. Solem captured the shift in mood halfway through the first movement by adding intensity and urgency to Virginia and Laurence’s sequence of dates—’in 1939’, ‘1940’ and ‘1941’—directing the listener’s gaze away from the romantic journeys of Reich’s innocent youth towards the dark clouds of war hovering over central Europe. The horrors of identification (to use Naomi Cumming’s expression) were laid bare in the second movement (‘Europe—during the war’), with the optimistic train rhythms of the first now weighed down by Holocaust testimonies. Upshaw and Tress added a more mournful tone on viola and cello to Rachel and Rachella’s stark statements (‘The Germans walked in’, ‘No more school’), while violins and cello projected sharp piercing crescendos to the phrases ‘into those cattle wagons’ and ‘for four days and four nights.’ The sustained chord at the movement’s close possessed the sensory overload of a blank wall of white noise. The third movement (‘After the war’) offered hope with its return to America and some semblance of normality. Reich’s rhythmic patterns were exchanged between members of the quartet with the precision of a Swiss watch. One of the most striking aspects of Solem’s nuanced performance was the way they conveyed the idea that, although the world had returned to normal after the war, everything had changed. Memories could neither be erased nor forgotten. This came across most poignantly in the work’s conclusion, where a Jewish girl ‘who had a beautiful voice’ is told to sing to the German soldiers—a moment suffused with bittersweet pathos. Although dealing less with themes of loss and trauma, the songs by Zawadzki and Kate Bush heard after the interval were compelling in their own way. Of Zawadzki’s three songs, a bluesy, bacchanalian spirit animated ‘Ring of Fire’, while consonant and dissonant elements foregrounded the dual nature of a bipolar person in the folksy ‘My Boy of the Birds’. Astringent Bartók-like bitonalities surfaced in ‘Pragnienie’, the viola’s ruminative ostinato resonating with the Polish concepts of desire and longing. The evening ended with five picture-perfect arrangements of Kate Bush songs by Solem violinist William Newell, whose emotional range extended from the innocent expression of ‘The Man with the Child in his Eyes’ to the steely vulnerability of ‘This Woman’s Work’, the latter enhanced by Zawadzki’s subtle characterisation and impressive vocal control. Expressive exchanges were heard between Newell’s violin and Zawadzki’s voice in ‘Running Up That Hill’ and ‘Hounds of Love’. It reminded me of something Kronos Quartet violinist David Harrington said when I interviewed him about Different Trains, which could have been applied to the concert as a whole: ‘You know, when you think about the history of the string quartet, it’s a very personal medium for composers. They can really internalise their sound through it. That’s what has always attracted me to it.’ The post Solem Quartet feat. Alice Zawadzki: Steve Reich and Kate Bush (Musicfest Festival, Aberystwyth, 7/23/26) appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: HAAi, the London-based, Australian-born producer, songwriter and DJ also known as Teneil Throssell, shares “Ignition” featuring Echonomist. The track is the third song on her album “DIGITiSE,” out 9 October 2026 on Mute on vinyl, CD and digitally. ‘Ignition’: video and track details An official video accompanies the release: Watch on YouTube HAAi describes the collaboration: “‘Ignition’ is a collaboration with Echonomist, someone whose music has shaped many of my sets since I started touring. Sonically, it’s a driving broken beat track that maintains a lot of innocence. Lyrically, it is deeply personal: documenting my coming-of-age as a queer kid in a small town, desperate to leave. […] In the true spirit of DIGITiSE, ‘Ignition’ serves as a sequel to ‘Go!’, from my previous album HUMANiSE. Both tracks are so important to the storytelling of the albums, I’m glad to be able to take it to the place we feel the most free, the dance floor.” Echonomist adds: “From the moment HAAi and I started talking, we connected through music in a really genuine way. It didn’t take long to realize we shared a similar musical language, and that made this collaboration feel incredibly natural. She reminded me of how much I love breaks, and that inspiration became the starting point.” “DIGITiSE” carries the ten-track “RE-HUMANiSE,” “Printerlude,” “Ignition,” “Depth Perception,” “DIGITiSE,” “Technology,” “HUMANiSE Radio,” “THANK U,” “I Wanna Feel Like Someone” and “Talking Walls.” The album also features Skybreak, Cantoalegre (a children’s choir from Medellín, Colombia), Pat Alvarez, ILA, James Messiah and Kaiden Ford. DIGITiSE by HAAi About HAAi HAAi is the recording name of Teneil Throssell, a producer, songwriter and DJ born in Australia and based in London. She built her early profile through all-night DJ sets before moving into production, releasing her debut album “Baby, We’re Ascending” in 2022. HAAi announced her second studio album, “HUMANiSE”, out 10 October 2025 on Mute, alongside the single “Satellite.” She followed with the tracks “Hey!” and “Stitches” ahead of the album’s release, and later shared an EEG-driven video for “Can’t Stand To Lose (hard soft rework).” HAAi shared “DIGITiSE,” the title track and lead single from her third album, featuring Pat Alvarez, alongside the album announcement. “DIGITiSE” is described as a dancefloor-focused companion to “HUMANiSE,” bringing HAAi together with new collaborators Echonomist, Skybreak and Cantoalegre alongside returning collaborators Pat Alvarez, ILA, James Messiah and Kaiden Ford. “Ignition,” the second track shared from the album, pairs her with Echonomist and is due on Mute on 9 October 2026 as part of the full “DIGITiSE” release.

items.body: Cyclic Law has introduced Pansoph, a new independent French-language publishing house, opening pre-orders for its first two titles. The imprint is aimed at French-speaking readers who have had to seek out English-language editions of books on cinema, esotericism, counterculture and art, or who never received an edition of those books at all. The first two Pansoph titles are “L’Écran Satanique” by Nikolas Schreck, the French edition of the expanded 2022 version of his study “The Satanic Screen,” which examines the Devil in cinema, and “Le Tarot de Marseille” by Christophe Poncet, an investigation into the origins of the Tarot de Marseille. Both are open for pre-order through Pansoph’s website. Cyclic Law Pansoph publishing: the forthcoming lineup Forthcoming Pansoph titles include “Dario Argento : l’homme, les mythes et la magie” by Alan Jones, “Japan Art Revolution” by Amélie Ravalec, “L’Affaire Manson” by Nikolas Schreck, “Perdurabo” by Richard Kaczynski, “Je crache sur ta pellicule” by Heidi Honeycutt and “La Vie hallucinante de Terence McKenna” by Graham St John. Ravalec previously directed “Industrial Soundtrack for the Urban Decay,” a 2015 documentary tracing the origins of industrial music through Throbbing Gristle, Cabaret Voltaire, Test Dept and other early acts in the genre. Pansoph is based at Cyclic Law’s address in Saint-Antonin-Noble-Val, France, and readers can join its newsletter for pre-order openings and release announcements. About Cyclic Law Frédéric Arbour founded Cyclic Law in Canada in 2002, later relocating the label’s operations to Berlin. Cyclic Law specializes in dark ambient, ritual and industrial soundscapes, and has released albums by Raison d’être, Desiderii Marginis, This Morn’ Omina, Arcana and Visions, Arbour’s own recording project, among many others. The label marked two decades of activity with the compilation Cyclic Law’s 20th Anniversary Label Sampler in 2022 and has continued releasing new material since, including This Morn’ Omina’s “Insha” and Raison d’être’s first vinyl edition of “The Empty Hollow Unfolds”. Alongside the label, Cyclic Law already runs Cyclic Press, an existing imprint for English-language art books tied to the artists and themes in its catalog. Pansoph extends that publishing activity into French-language editions, giving Cyclic Law a second imprint dedicated to books on cinema, esotericism and counterculture for francophone readers in France, Belgium, Switzerland, Quebec and beyond.

items.body: South African electronic dark-pop artist Hunter As a Horse has released the debut album Paradise Lost through Metropolis Records on 24 July 2026. The record is out on LP, CD and digital formats and arrives with a video for the title track. Paradise Lost by Hunter As a Horse “Paradise Lost” is the project of South African musician and vocalist Mia van Wyk, who signed to Metropolis Records in early 2026. The twelve-track album includes five previously released singles – “Lighthouse,” “Here’s To All The Ones,” “Paradise Lost,” “Obey” and “Leviathan” – alongside seven new songs that move between rhythmically driven tracks such as “Dark Sky” and downtempo, atmospheric pieces such as “Masochist” and “Object.” The full tracklist runs “Here’s To All The Ones,” “Kiss Of Death,” “Object,” “Obey,” “Masochist,” “The Fortress,” “Paradise Lost,” “Go To Bed Now,” “Leviathan,” “Lighthouse,” “Dark Sky” and “Dead Things.” Van Wyk describes the album as an exploration of what she has kept hidden: “This album deals with my shadow, my transformation and my inner architecture. I have tried to show what is deep inside myself. I discovered that the things I was taught to bury were never my enemies, but are actually my power.” A video for the title track “Paradise Lost” has been released alongside the album. Van Wyk’s approach shifted with the 2025 EP “Anathema,” her first release built around a single connecting thread rather than a set of standalone songs. “It was the first time I really started thinking in terms of a connected body of work, so it felt natural to take that further with ‘Paradise Lost.’ It is designed to be heard as one piece, even though the songs are quite different individually.” She adds: “A lot changed for me during that time personally and I went through a kind of integration process where I started confronting things more. Writing the album felt like a natural expression of that.” Van Wyk traces the album’s themes to a longstanding pull toward the misunderstood: “I have always been drawn to the villains in stories, the ones who were feared and misunderstood, and I have often found beauty in places other people are afraid to look – the strange, the haunted, the macabre. This album is resurrection, obsession, desire, revenge, surrender, love and my shadow.” The Guardian described the project’s sound as “the mesmerising atmospherics of Lamb and Zero 7. Dark and very lovely indeed.” Songs by Hunter As a Horse have appeared in the television series “American Horror Story,” “Riverdale” and “Elite,” as well as the film “Wander Darkly.” About Hunter As a Horse Hunter As a Horse is the recording name of Mia van Wyk, a musician and vocalist based in the Western Cape, South Africa. Over roughly a decade, she self-released a series of EPs and singles combining electronic dark-pop production with personal, often cinematic songwriting. Hunter As a Horse signed to Metropolis Records in early 2026 and released the single “Lighthouse” on 30 January 2026, followed by “Here’s To All The Ones” on 6 March 2026. The 2025 EP “Anathema” marked her first attempt at a thematically unified body of work, a direction she carried into the singles “Paradise Lost,” “Obey” and “Leviathan,” each later folded into the debut album. Side-Line covered the announcement of the album ahead of its 24 July 2026 release on Metropolis Records.

items.body: Mesh have announced a second leg of their “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” tour, adding seven European dates this autumn and confirming their first live appearance of 2027. The new run begins on August 30 at Electric Summer in Taunton, UK, before continuing through Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic. The announcement also confirms MESH for EASTSIDE Festival in Halle (Saale), Germany, on July 2, 2027, marking the band’s first announced show of next year. Fronted by vocalist Mark Hockings and guitarist, keyboardist and programmer Richard Silverthorn, Mesh continue to tour in support of “The Truth Doesn’t Matter,” the band’s latest studio album, released on March 27, 2026, via Dependent Records. The album reached number 15 in Germany and number 23 on the UK Download Chart. Ticket information for the new dates has not been announced. Mesh tour dates for 2026 and 2027 August 30, 2026 – Taunton, UK – Electric Summer October 1, 2026 – Krefeld, Germany – Kulturfabrik October 2, 2026 – Braunschweig, Germany – Westand October 3, 2026 – Dresden, Germany – Strasse E November 5, 2026 – Łódź, Poland – Scenografia November 6, 2026 – Halle (Saale), Germany – Capitol November 7, 2026 – Liberec, Czech Republic – Sever Synth Festival July 2, 2027 – Halle (Saale), Germany – EASTSIDE Festival About Mesh Mesh formed in Bristol, England, in 1991, when vocalist Mark Hockings and keyboardist Richard Silverthorn met at a concert. The duo built a catalogue of electronic alternative albums built around sequenced electronics, synth bass, guitars and Hockings’ vocals, releasing records including “The Point at Which It Falls Apart,” reissued in a 25th-anniversary edition in 2024. Hockings also records as Blackcarburning, a solo project whose singles and albums Side-Line has covered previously. Mesh’s 2026 album “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” arrived on Dependent Records on March 27, preceded by the singles “Exile,” “Hey Stranger” and “This World.” The band opened the album’s first tour leg shortly after release, and the newly announced second leg carries the “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” tour into its second year, alongside the band’s first confirmed festival date of 2027.

items.body: German coldwave and darkwave duo Yakima Jera release Kalte Schauer, their second studio album, on vinyl LP on 28 August through the German label Young & Cold. The nine-track record is pressed on yellow vinyl with black splatters and follows the album’s digital release earlier in July as part of a two-disc “Album Collection” alongside the band’s 2024 debut, “Azrael Take My Hand.” Kalte Schauer by Yakima Jera “Kalte Schauer,” German for “cold shiver,” mixes cold wave, post-punk and dark synth textures across atmospheric guitars, driving basslines and understated electronic elements. The tracklist runs “The Call,” “Soul Vampire,” “Dertlı Dolap,” “You Know,” “Two Hearts,” “Secrets Of ML,” “The Abyss,” “To Be Free” and “Gemini.” Lead track Dertlı Dolap first appeared as a single in May 2025 and carries a Turkish-language lyric drawn from the poetry of Sufi mystic Yunus Emre, with an official video showing the duo performing in front of a windmill. About Yakima Jera Simon and Kara formed Yakima Jera in Munich, Germany, in 2022. The duo released the single “You” that December, followed by the mini-album “Capture” and the singles “Kara” and “Fire” in 2023. Yakima Jera’s debut full-length, “Azrael Take My Hand,” followed on 30 March 2024 through Young & Cold; Out Of Line issued the album on limited green marbled vinyl. The duo returned in May 2025 with the single “Dertlı Dolap,” drawing on Turkish-language lyrics and the band’s Middle Eastern heritage alongside its usual Joy Division and post-punk reference points. In July 2026, Young & Cold released “Album Collection,” a two-disc digital and CD set pairing “Azrael Take My Hand” with the new nine-track album “Kalte Schauer.” The vinyl edition of “Kalte Schauer” follows on 28 August 2026.

items.body: Boy George has released an AI-assisted re-recording of Culture Club’s “Karma Chameleon” as the flagship single for Artist Included, a new music and technology company built around artist-owned alternatives to original master recordings. The track, credited “Karma Chameleon (Artist Included),” came out on 15 June 2026 through a partnership with BMG Rights Management, timed to the singer’s 65th birthday. Artist Included was founded by entrepreneur Paul “PK” Kemsley, Boy George’s longtime manager, and entertainment attorney and film producer Jeremy Rosen, with Planet Hollywood founder Robert Earl serving as chairman of the board. Boy George holds the role of creative director. The company’s technology partner, Syntiant, built its model from archival demos and vocal recordings that original “Karma Chameleon” producer Steve Levine had kept since the 1980s and agreed to share for training. Boy George recorded a new vocal take, which Syntiant’s tools then processed to draw the performance back toward the tone of his 1983 voice. “Karma Chameleon” was the second single from Culture Club’s 1983 album “Colour by Numbers,” spending three weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and six weeks atop the UK singles chart. The song has since passed 900 million streams on Spotify and continues to generate sync licensing income, none of which reaches Boy George directly under the terms of Culture Club’s original record deal. Boy George Karma Chameleon: inside the AI re-recording Kemsley says that imbalance was the direct catalyst for Artist Included. He points to a recent Virgin anniversary campaign that licensed “Karma Chameleon” for roughly four million dollars across multiple uses, with the payment going to the owners of the master recording and publishing rights. “Four million changed hands,” Kemsley says. “George didn’t get anything at all.” Boy George describes the finished re-recording as startlingly close to the original session in an interview with Rolling Stone. “When I heard it, I was absolutely gobsmacked,” he says. “It sounds like another take from that original session.” He adds that the process gave him back a level of creative control he had lost over the decades: “It has the sound of me at 22 years old with all the experience of everything that I’ve learned.” Robert Earl describes Artist Included as a response to the anxiety AI has caused elsewhere in entertainment. “Since AI arrived, the whole creative community has been up in arms and fearful, particularly in the movie world,” he says. “Unauthorized AI is not going to do well. I think it’s a seminal moment; it just might take a little time for people to realize.” The company positions its approach as distinct from unauthorized voice-cloning tools, describing the new “Karma Chameleon” as a new human performance by Boy George rather than a synthetic recreation of one. For George, the appeal extends past the ownership question. “It’s hard to get excited about something that you don’t control,” he says. “This gives me an opportunity, not just me, but other artists, to have a different relationship with those songs.” Kemsley says Artist Included intends to approach other heritage acts from the 1980s and 1990s whose most valuable recordings remain controlled by record companies, positioning the model as an AI-assisted evolution of the re-recording strategy Taylor Swift used to reclaim her own catalog with the “Taylor’s Version” series. Here is the original recording: And this is the 2026 version. About Boy George and Culture Club Boy George, born George Alan O’Dowd in Bexley, England, formed Culture Club in London in 1981 alongside bassist Mikey Craig, drummer Jon Moss and guitarist Roy Hay. The band’s 1982 debut album, “Kissing to Be Clever,” produced the international hit “Do You Really Want to Hurt Me.” Its 1983 follow-up, “Colour by Numbers,” included “Karma Chameleon,” written by Boy George and Jon Moss, which became the band’s best-selling single. Culture Club split in 1986 and has reunited several times since, including for the 2018 album “Life” and ongoing tour dates with its original lineup. Side-Line covered the band’s 2016 “Live At Wembley” reunion show when it was released on various formats. Boy George has continued to record and tour as a solo artist and DJ, and in 2024 and 2025 released the “Let The Flowers Grow” duet with Peter Murphy, later issued in remixes by Juno Reactor and Delerium. Artist Included, and the re-recorded “Karma Chameleon” that launched it, marks his first venture built specifically around reclaiming ownership of his catalog through new technology.

The original “Reincarnation (Wiedergeburt)” was released on Echozone on 22 May 2026, backed by an official video: Reincarnation (Wiedergeburt) by The Grab Society About The Grab Society The Grab Society is a German electro and synth-pop project formed by Manfred Thomaser and Ulf Müller. Thomaser’s other active projects include !distain, Arsine Tibé, DEMOKRATIE, and The Independent Season. Müller has worked with Projekt Ich, M.U.N.T Connection, VOUL, SMOTCH, U.M. Fiedel, Tränenwelten, Mission Zanzibar, and 2MBK. The project launched on 28 April 2023 with the debut single “Outsider (Außenseiter)” on Echozone. A second single, “Underrated (Unterschätzt)”, followed on 23 June 2023 and reached number 7 in the German Electronic Web Charts on 10 July 2023. The third single, “Room (Raum)”, was released on 26 January 2024 and charted at number 10 in the German Electronic Web Charts on 11 March 2024. “Free (Gratis)” appeared on 2 August 2024, and a fifth single, “Eternal,” featuring guest vocalist Annabelle, followed. On 30 May 2025, Echozone issued “Extended (Volume I)”, collecting extended versions of the first five singles. On 11 July 2025, the project released a cover of the Trio song “Da Da Da ich lieb dich nicht du liebst mich nicht aha aha aha”. The Grab Society released “Reincarnation (Wiedergeburt)” on 22 May 2026, its first single of the year. Earlier tracks in the catalog, including “Room (Raum),” “Outsider (Außenseiter)” and “Underrated (Unterschätzt),” have each received their own Echozone remix packages. “Reincarnation (Remixed)” follows that pattern, extending the May single into a 16-track remix collection due 31 July 2026.

items.body: Haunt Me‘s second album, Watch You Bleed, returns on a limited clear vinyl with red splatters through Young & Cold Records, out September 15. A digipak CD edition follows on August 7. The album originally arrived in February 2025. Watch You Bleed by Haunt Me “Watch You Bleed” contains 12 tracks, including “Bloodlust,” “Filthy,” “Their Hate Will Destroy Them,” “Red Room,” “Surrender To The Night,” the title track, “Bleed For Me,” “Inhale Exhale,” “Cemetery Rendezvous,” “Scream For Me,” “Devour” and “VHS Horror Night.” Haunt Me mixes darkwave, post-punk and electronic goth elements across the record, moving between late-night atmosphere and dancefloor-oriented tracks built around themes of desire, obsession and nocturnal escapism. Haunt Me will tour Europe this fall in support of the release. Confirmed dates so far: 13 November – Hamburg, Germany – Markthalle Hamburg (Cold Hearted Festival) 14 November – Dresden, Germany – Alter Schlachthof (Cold Hearted Festival) 15 November – Poznan, Poland – Klub muzyczny “Pod Minoga” 16 November – Warsaw, Poland – VooDoo Club 18 November – Prague, Czech Republic – Subzero 19 November – Vienna, Austria – Club Weberknecht 25 November – London, United Kingdom – The Grace 29 November – Haarlem, Netherlands – Patronaat 1 December – Paris, France – Supersonic More dates are expected to be announced. About Haunt Me Haunt Me is a darkwave and post-punk project blending goth-tinged electronic production with melodic songwriting. The band’s back catalog includes the album “This Sadness Never Ends” and the release “En Tu Cama (Come Now, Sleep),” alongside standalone tracks such as “Our Ghost,” “Lost Frequencies” and “Wish You Were Here.” “Watch You Bleed,” the project’s second album, arrived in February 2025 on Blood Moon Red vinyl before this new clear-with-red-splatters pressing and CD reissue through Young & Cold Records, which the band supports with a run of European tour dates in November and December.

items.body: Denver goth-rock and post-punk band Opium released its first official music video on July 25, 2026, for the single “Dirge”. The track is taken from the band’s forthcoming debut album, “Winter,” due in August 2026. “Dirge” opens with a rhythmic bassline and builds around a low-register guitar melody under anxious, mounting drums. The vocal carries an anarcho-punk edge alongside the macabre drama of early deathrock, with additional guitar distortion gathering around the rhythm section as the track progresses. The video was directed and filmed by David Sundine and shot in black and white. It centers on actress Sarah Talmadge inside a domestic setting, using mirrors, blurred movement and doubled exposures, and closes on a body stretched across a hallway as another pair of figures enters through the door. “Dirge” is streaming on Apple Music. No release date or format details for the “Winter” album beyond its August 2026 timing have been announced. Opium’s ‘Dirge’ follows debut EP ‘PHANTOMS’ “Dirge” is Opium’s first single since the band’s debut EP, “PHANTOMS,” recorded in 2022 and released in April 2023. “Winter” will be the band’s first full-length album. About Opium Opium formed in Denver, Colorado, at the beginning of 2021. The band began writing together almost immediately and played its first show within a few months at Denver’s Hard Rock, building a local following through appearances at unusual venues and distinctive bills. Opium entered the studio in 2022 to record its debut EP, “PHANTOMS,” released in April 2023, which carried the band’s music beyond Colorado. “Dirge,” released July 25, 2026 with the band’s first official music video, is drawn from Opium’s forthcoming debut album “Winter,” scheduled for August 2026.

items.body: Los Angeles dark alternative project And It Was Night released an official music video on July 27, 2026, for the single “What’s Beyond the Light?”. And It Was Night is the solo project of composer and sound designer Rani Sharone. What’s Beyond the Light? by And It Was Night Sharone wrote “What’s Beyond the Light?” after moonlit walks, drawing on The Cure, Echo and the Bunnymen, The Church, My Bloody Valentine and The Mission. The track moves with a steady club pulse while guitars dissolve at the edges and electronics cast a dim sheen across the mix. Sharone filmed and edited the accompanying video himself, moving through open terrain and blurred natural forms while glitches and repeated gestures disrupt the footage. She describes the approach to the visual: “Short form videos have always proved to be a fun and creative way to give my music a visual pairing, so jumping into a full length video was an amazing exercise and challenge. I set out to create a dreamy and sometimes disorienting video filled with movement, nature, and things that directly inspired my lyrics for the song, including sights from my own neighborhood.” “What’s Beyond the Light?” is available on Bandcamp. And It Was Night’s ‘What’s Beyond the Light?’ follows single ‘Lovers of Evil’ “What’s Beyond the Light?” was released as And It Was Night’s third single in March 2026, alongside an earlier single, “Lovers of Evil,” inspired by the television series “True Detective.” The July 27 release adds an official music video to the existing track. About And It Was Night And It Was Night is the dark alternative solo project of Los Angeles-based composer and sound designer Rani Sharone. Sharone has recorded and toured with Puscifer and with his own band, Stolen Babies, and had an original composition premiered at the Walt Disney Concert Hall by classical violinist Hilary Hahn. Side-Line previously covered another Sharone project, Thrillsville, and its single and video for “Creeps In The House” in 2021. And It Was Night released “Lovers of Evil” and “What’s Beyond the Light?” as singles in early 2026, and released an official music video for “What’s Beyond the Light?” on July 27, 2026, self-filmed and edited by Sharone.

items.body: Some may already be familiar with the Mexican solo project Ego Bliss through the debut album “What The Future Holds” and the subsequent EP “Future”. This follow-up took more than two years to complete, making the wait a fairly long one. Ego Bliss remains true to its influences, delivering a style best described as powerful Electro-Pop. EBM elements provide the necessary punch, while other tracks lean more towards Future-Pop. Throughout the album, the production is polished and meticulous, resulting in a collection of consistently strong songs. “Afterlife” also offers enough variety to keep things engaging from start to finish. While the album may not feature an obvious hit single, it more than makes up for that with a solid selection of powerful, well-crafted tracks. I particularly enjoyed the contrast between the dark, aggressive basslines and the bright, melodic Electro-Pop arrangements, a combination that gives the album much of its appeal. (Rating:8). Side-Line reported on the album’s Infacted Recordings release in June 2026. Listen to “Moments”: Moments by Ego Bliss About Ego Bliss Ego Bliss is an electronic project from Tijuana, Mexico, and a recent signing to Infacted Recordings, the German label founded in 2001 and run by Torben Schmidt, which focuses on electro, synth-pop and futurepop. Before joining Infacted, the project issued earlier work through the Mexican label Sector Industrial Producciones; Side-Line reviewed the EP “Future” and the album “What The Future Holds”. According to the label, “Afterlife” was shaped over about two and a half years and draws on themes of loss and change. The twelve-track “Afterlife” is Ego Bliss’s first release for Infacted Recordings, following its earlier work on Sector Industrial Producciones, and is reviewed here on Side-Line.

items.body: Hollywood Vampires released a live video for Motorhead‘s “Ace Of Spades,” the second single from the band’s upcoming live album, “At Montreux Jazz Festival.” The performance was recorded during the band’s set at the Montreux Jazz Festival in Switzerland in 2018. The performance features Alice Cooper, Joe Perry, Johnny Depp and Tommy Henriksen, with bassist Chris Wyse taking over lead vocals for the Motorhead classic as a tribute to Lemmy Kilmister. Alice Cooper called Lemmy “one of a kind” and described “Ace Of Spades” as one of the defining songs in rock history. “At Montreux Jazz Festival” documents Hollywood Vampires’ full 2018 festival performance, combining original material with covers that reflect the band’s influences. The 19-track album includes performances of “Raise The Dead,” “Baba O’Riley,” “Heroes,” “Sweet Emotion” and “School’s Out / Another Brick In The Wall.” The album arrives digitally and on CD and vinyl in Europe and the UK on August 14, with the US physical edition following on October 16. About Hollywood Vampires Hollywood Vampires formed around Alice Cooper, Joe Perry of Aerosmith and actor-musician Johnny Depp, taking their name from the 1970s Los Angeles drinking club Cooper once belonged to alongside musicians including Keith Moon and Harry Nilsson. The band released its self-titled debut album in 2015, built around cover versions of songs by artists tied to that era, alongside original material. A second album, “Rise,” followed in 2019 with mostly original songs. Bassist Chris Wyse and guitarist Tommy Henriksen have been part of the band’s touring and recording line-up alongside the founding trio. The band’s live album “At Montreux Jazz Festival,” capturing its 2018 festival set, follows the “Ace Of Spades” tribute to Lemmy Kilmister as its second single.

items.body: “I’ve been wondering where your ache breathes, in mazes you design?” Metropolis Records has announced the signing of Swiss quartet Lone Assembly, whose debut album, Knots & Chains, was released in Europe in late February. Formed by vocalist Raphaël Bressler, guitarist Glenn Le Meur, bassist Jim Bodeman and drummer Romain Segu, Lone Assembly draw from new wave, synth-pop and post-punk, pairing forceful rhythms and expansive guitars with Bressler’s low, commanding vocal delivery. Knots & Chains is a stunning collection of poetry, exploring connection, struggle, resilience and the bonds that can offer support while also becoming sources of restriction. Its songs address personal relationships, internal pressure and the influence that physical environments exert over those who inhabit them. Although much of Knots & Chains deals with pain, alienation and emotional constraint, the album also leaves room for hope, courage and recovery. Its movement from enclosed spaces toward uncertain freedom gives the record the shape of a gradual release, even when that freedom remains fragile. “The album takes shape like a cycle, moving from suffocation to openness, from closed spaces to greater, albeit fragile, breathing space,” explains vocalist Raphaël Bressler. That transition is particularly clear on the single In The Open, where the search for air and space becomes a response to the album’s recurring sense of confinement. The song follows a person caught in a private cycle of pain, disorientation, and retreat, while longing for some open air beyond it. A remembered date bears the pressure of unresolved grief. At the brink of collapse, calling another person becomes a tentative route back toward freedom and relief. Watch the video, directed by Manon Stutz, below: Musically, the record carries the austere atmosphere associated with the Factory Records era, presented through modern production and a larger pop framework comparable to Editors, Pink Turns Blue and The Horrors – even a little INXS. Le Meur’s guitars stretch across the record’s dense foundations, while Bodeman and Segu provide a heavy, urgent rhythm section beneath Bressler’s baritone. Control forms one of the album’s central themes, appearing as something imposed by others, internalised by the self, or embedded within the spaces people occupy. You’re Pulling At The Same Strings examines the power one person can hold over another, with its lyrics searching for the hidden wound behind destructive behaviour and the emotional maze built around it. Other songs turn that scrutiny inward. The Pain Keeper and My Life’s Solid consider the private restrictions people place upon themselves, where endurance can harden into another form of confinement. “The City Works Like This,” meanwhile, presents the city as an active force capable of absorbing, rejecting, and reshaping its inhabitants, until the surrounding streets begin to exert a will of their own. Lone Assembly first attracted wider attention with their 2024 EP, That Never Happened, written in tribute to a lost loved one. During the making of the EP, the project developed beyond a group of friends playing together and became a shared space for grief, closeness and healing. Those foundations continue throughout Knots & Chains, expanding the band’s focus from personal loss toward the relationships, habits and surroundings that govern everyday life. Knots & Chains is out now. Further details regarding Lone Assembly’s first releases through Metropolis Records are expected to be announced. The LP and CD formats will be made available in North America on September 18th, 2026. Listen to it now below and order the album here. items.body: The Singularity: Ekleipsis is one of the most ambitious releases of 2026, from one of the most bustling men in the industry. Bear McCreary is an American soundtrack composer with six Emmy and four Grammy award nominations, plus a slew of musical and television-related merits. Over his 150+ releases, he's orchestrated soundtracks to beloved media series, including Battlestar Galactica, Metalocalypse, Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., God of War and many more. Aside from this work, he has also been working on a metal concept series: The Singularity. The first piece of this giant Ravensburger puzzle was released in 2024, and its successor, Ekleipsis has now arrived. There's really something for everyone in this record. Ya like Gojira? Coheed and Cambria? Meshuggah? Guns N' Roses? The fukin' Police? (Aside from GnR) I do, too! Which is great, because members of all these bands pitch in to assist McCreary in creating as big an album as his unparochial brain desires. The most prominent member is Bear's vocalist brother, Brendan, who appears eight times across the record's fifteen tracks. He's adequate on his own, when not rapping about politics, on "Kill Us Anyway". Powerhouses like Alissa White-Gluz (Dragonforce, ex-Arch Enemy), Stewart Copeland (The Police, Curved Air), Fall Out Boy's Patrick Stump and even McCreary's wife Raya Yarbrough, are miles better by comparison, however. Moreover, others like Slash, Steve Vai, Polyphia's Tim Henson, and The Red Hot Chili Peppers' Chad Smith, however, further dwarf Brendan with their glorious guitar additions. Even then though, a standard mid-tone is utilized amongst most patrons, which doesn't exemplify the amount of creativity we could see from the cast, with probably the best moment entirely coming from the only bout of gutturals on the record, courtesy of Meshuggah's Jens Kidman.You'd presume a collaboration between all these artists in a project like Ekleipsis would be outstanding, but the record is particularly disappointing. McCreary's symphonic, cinematic feel is apparent throughout the runtime, but a flat production, weak lyricism and uninteresting songs in isolation make it hard to enjoy—especially since it's over an hour long and not immediately reminiscent of a fluid concept piece. I was expecting Bear to concoct some extravagant sonic scenery. But, in essence, Ekleipsis is a compilation of middle-of-the-road alternative metal with a crew of artists better suited to other musical coalitions. Remember USA for Africa? This is like the metal-ish version of it, without the charity. Elsewhere, the thin mixing makes way for a struggle for any movie-like attributes to truly take hold of the release, and for me to appreciate it. It's not like the influences of the performers don't show: Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares darken the atmosphere on "Black Box", and when Tim Henson of Polyphia debuts on "Blueshift" the song gradually builds in gentle technicality. On "Cool Kids," the cringe-but-mainstay attitudes of Slash and Chad Smith also manipulate the track's attitude greatly, but eight-minute proggy epic "One Fine Day" doesn't benefit from Slash's soloing, which is really saying something. These virtuosos make themselves heard, but never collectively impress.

Kant)は1724年4月22日、東プロイセンの首都ケーニヒスベルク(現在はロシア領カリーニングラード)に生まれ、1804年2月12日に同じ地で没したドイツの哲学者。近代哲学の中心人物とされ、生涯のほとんどをケーニヒスベルクから一歩も出ずに過ごしたことでも知られる。合理論(理性を重視する立場)と経験論(経験・感覚を重視する立場)を統合し、19〜20世紀の哲学の枠組みを規定した人物と評価される。出典: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Immanuel Kant」https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant/■ Kant」https://www.britannica.com/biography/Immanuel-Kant■ 主要著作(年代順)・『生きた力の真の測定に関する考察』(1747年)― 最初の著作・『天界の一般自然史と理論』(1755年)― 自然科学分野の著作。後の星雲説につながる宇宙論を展開・『純粋理性批判』第1版(1781年)/第2版(1787年)― 最も有名な主著。人間の認識能力の限界と可能性を検討・『プロレゴメナ(学として現れうる将来の形而上学のための序論)』(1783年)・『人倫の形而上学の基礎づけ(道徳形而上学原論)』(1785年)― 定言命法を中心とした倫理学の基礎文献・『実践理性批判』(1788年)― 道徳・自由・意志に関する批判哲学の第2弾・『判断力批判』(1790年)― Philosophy「Immanuel Kant」https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant/出典2: Wikipedia「Opus Postumum」https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opus_Postumum出典3: Encyclopedia.com「Immanuel Kant」https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/philosophy-and-religion/philosophy-biographies/immanuel-kant■ 批判哲学の全体像カントの「批判哲学」の根本にあるのは人間の自律(オートノミー)という理念。人間の悟性(理解力)が自然を秩序づける一般法則の源泉であり、また人間の理性が自らに道徳法則を課すことこそが、神・自由・不死への信念の根拠になるとされる。この結果、科学的知識・道徳・宗教的信念はいずれも人間の自律という同じ土台の上に成り立つため、互いに矛盾しないというのがカントの構想である。出典: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Immanuel Kant」https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant/■ 認識論・形而上学:超越論的観念論『純粋理性批判』でカントは、空間と時間は物自体(私たちの外部に独立して存在する対象そのもの)の性質ではなく、私たちが対象をどう知覚するかという形式的な特徴に過ぎないと論じる。空間・時間の中にある対象は「現象」と呼ばれ、その背後にある「物自体」については実質的なことは何もわからないとされる。この立場は「超越論的観念論」と呼ばれ、『純粋理性批判』初版刊行(1781年)以来、その正確な意味をめぐって解釈が分かれ続けている。出典: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant's Transcendental Idealism」https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-transcendental-idealism/補足として、Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophyでは、超越論的観念論の採用こそが「批判期以前」と「批判期」を分ける決定的な転換点であると説明されている。経験の領域内でのみ認識(コグニション)が可能であり、経験的対象(現象)は心に依存するというのがこの立場の核心である。出典: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant: Transcendental Idealism」https://iep.utm.edu/kant-transcendental-idealism/■ 倫理学:定言命法カントは道徳的要請の根拠を「定言命法(Categorical Imperative)」と呼ばれる理性の基準に置いた。不道徳とはこの定言命法への違反であり、それゆえ非合理的な行為だとされる。定言命法は「命令」である点で命令文であり、何か特定の目的を条件とせず、理性的な意志を持つ存在であるというだけで無条件に適用される点で「定言的」である。出典: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant's Moral Philosophy」https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-moral/最も広く知られる定式は「あなたの意志の格率が、常に同時に普遍的立法の原理として妥当しうるように行為せよ」というもの。もう一つの有名な定式は「人間性を、単なる手段としてのみならず、常に同時に目的として扱え」というもので、他者への公平な尊重を要求する。この二つの定式が等価であるかどうかは哲学的に議論が続いている論点である。出典: Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kantian ethics」https://www.rep.routledge.com/articles/thematic/kantian-ethics/v-1/sections/kants-ethics道徳の価値を決めるのは行為の結果ではなく、行為の背後にある動機だとカントは考えた。義務(デューティ)に基づく倫理学(義務論・デオントロジー)の最も重要な提唱者とされ、行為に道徳的価値を与えうる唯一の動機は、理性が発見する普遍的原理から生じるものだけだとされる。出典: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant, Immanuel: Metaphysics」https://iep.utm.edu/kantmeta/道徳法則は経験によらず、実践理性そのものの構造(形式)からアプリオリに導かれる。すべての理性的存在者が同じ実践理性を共有する以上、道徳法則はすべての人を等しく拘束し義務づける。同時にカントは、この拘束性は自己に課されたものである、つまり人は自律的に自らに道徳法則を課しているのだと強調する。出典: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant, Immanuel」https://iep.utm.edu/kantview/■ 美学・目的論:『判断力批判』カントの美学と目的論に関する見解は、1790年刊行の『判断力批判』(原題 Kritik der Urteilskraft、近年は「力の判断力批判」とも訳される)にもっとも包括的に示されている。この著作は二部構成で、前半の「美感的判断力の批判」では美と崇高、そして芸術創造をめぐる美的経験と判断が論じられ、後半の「目的論的判断力の批判」では自然科学および自然理解全般における目的論(目的・意図への訴え)の役割が論じられる。出典: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant's Aesthetics and Teleology」https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-aesthetics/■ 政治哲学・社会哲学カントは、あらゆる理性的存在者には自由への生得的権利と、その自由を実現・保持するために社会契約によって統治される市民状態に入る義務の両方があると考えた。政治哲学に関する著作は、『人倫の形而上学』第一部「法論」を中心に、いくつかの短い論考からなる。代表的なものに、国家の基盤と役割を論じた「理論と実践」、国際関係を扱った「永遠平和のために」、そして「啓蒙とは何か」という問いに答えるエッセイがある。出典: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant's Social and Political Philosophy」https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-social-political/「永遠平和のために」の中でカントは統治形態を二つの軸で分類する。一つは「主権の形式」で、誰が統治するか(一人・少数・全員による支配)、もう一つは「統治の形式」で、どう統治するか(共和制か専制か)という軸である。世界の諸民族の相互交流が進むにつれ、「地球上のある一箇所での権利侵害はどこでも感じられる」ようになり、これが恒久平和にとって重要な「世界市民法(コスモポリタン・ライト)」の議論につながる。カントにとって永遠平和は「最高の政治的善」とされる。出典: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant's Social and Political Philosophy」https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-social-political/■ 影響・後世への遺産近代西洋哲学のあらゆる側面に、多かれ少なかれカントの影響が及んでいると言われる。ケーニヒスベルクの周辺からほぼ一歩も出なかったにもかかわらず、倫理学・道徳哲学・形而上学・美学の潮流を大きく変えた人物と評価されている。出典: The Great Thinkers「Biography of Immanuel Kant」https://thegreatthinkers.org/kant/biography/カントの体系的な認識論・倫理学・美学の仕事は、その後のあらゆる哲学、とりわけカント主義(カンティアニズム)や観念論の諸潮流に大きな影響を与えたとされる。出典: Britannica「Immanuel Kant」https://www.britannica.com/biography/Immanuel-Kant■ 主要な学習用リンク集(すべて活きたリンク)・Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Immanuel Kant」総論 https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant/・Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant's Moral Philosophy」(倫理学) https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-moral/・Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant's Transcendental Idealism」(認識論) https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-transcendental-idealism/・Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant's Aesthetics and Teleology」(美学) https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-aesthetics/・Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant's Social and Political Philosophy」(政治哲学) https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-social-political/・Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy「Kant, Immanuel」総論 items.album: マズロー ピーク体験論
items.excerpt: ■ ピーク体験とは何かピーク体験(peak experience)とは、マズローが自己実現を果たしつつある人々に特徴的に見られる体験を表すために作った言葉で、そうした人々は驚異・畏敬・恍惚感に満ちた体験を報告し、その中で個としての感覚が世界に溶け込んでいくと語った。その描写は明確にスピリチュアルな性質を帯びていたが、必ずしも宗教的なものとは限らなかった。マズロー(1908〜1970)は生涯をかけてこのピーク体験を研究した人物で、今日では「欲求階層説」の提唱者として最もよく知られているが、これは人間が生得的な欲求を優先順位に沿って満たしていき、「自己実現」、後年には「自己超越」と呼んだ段階へと向かう心理的健康の理論である。マズローは、自己実現できるメンタルヘルスの健全な人々——つまり自分の潜在能力を最大限発揮して最良の自分になれている人々——に研究の焦点を当てることでピーク体験という概念を広めた。研究の初期段階で、こうした人々の多くが人生観の形成に根本的な影響を与えた超越的な体験を報告していることに気づいた。ピーク体験を理解するため、マズローは人々に人生で最も感情的に強烈だった体験を語っ
items.body: ■ ピーク体験とは何かピーク体験(peak experience)とは、マズローが自己実現を果たしつつある人々に特徴的に見られる体験を表すために作った言葉で、そうした人々は驚異・畏敬・恍惚感に満ちた体験を報告し、その中で個としての感覚が世界に溶け込んでいくと語った。その描写は明確にスピリチュアルな性質を帯びていたが、必ずしも宗教的なものとは限らなかった。マズロー(1908〜1970)は生涯をかけてこのピーク体験を研究した人物で、今日では「欲求階層説」の提唱者として最もよく知られているが、これは人間が生得的な欲求を優先順位に沿って満たしていき、「自己実現」、後年には「自己超越」と呼んだ段階へと向かう心理的健康の理論である。マズローは、自己実現できるメンタルヘルスの健全な人々——つまり自分の潜在能力を最大限発揮して最良の自分になれている人々——に研究の焦点を当てることでピーク体験という概念を広めた。研究の初期段階で、こうした人々の多くが人生観の形成に根本的な影響を与えた超越的な体験を報告していることに気づいた。ピーク体験を理解するため、マズローは人々に人生で最も感情的に強烈だった体験を語ってもらった。その結果、人々はしばしばそれを神秘的・霊的な言葉で語り、強烈な幸福感と世界との一体感を報告した。マズロー自身の言葉として、以下のような描写がよく引用される。「限りない地平が視界に開けていく感覚、これまでにないほど力強く、同時にこれまでにないほど無力であるという感覚、恍惚と驚異と畏怖の感覚、時間と空間の中での自分の位置を見失う感覚。そして最後に、極めて重要で価値あることが起きたのだという確信が訪れ、その結果、当人は日常生活においてもある程度変容し、強められる」こうした体験は必ずしも激烈なものばかりではないが、多くの人がこの体験によって自分が変わったと感じ、それを繰り返そうと試み、以前より他者に対して思いやりを持ち、世界に対してより受容的で心地よく感じるようになったと報告した。■ 発見の経緯 ― 自己実現研究から生まれた概念マズローが開発した自己実現の概念は「自分の潜在能力を発展させ、本来なるべき自分になること」を意味する。自己実現した人々を研究する中で、マズローは多くの被験者が似通った独特の感情を報告していることに気づき、これがピーク体験の調査へとつながった。1959年の論文でピーク体験に見られる認知の特徴を19項目にまとめ、次のように結論づけている。「言い換えれば、ピーク体験の最中にある人は誰でも、一時的に自己実現している人々に見られる特徴の多くを帯びる。つまり、その瞬間だけ、その人自身が自己実現者になるのである」1943年の論文『人間の動機づけに関する理論』、そして1954年の著書『動機づけと人格』でこの考え方の土台を築いた後、マズローはピーク体験を主要テーマとした。■ ピーク体験の主な特徴(19の特性/16の側面)●簡潔な3特性モデル(Mathesら)1982年、E・W・メイシスによってピーク体験への傾向を測定する心理尺度「Peak Experiences Scale」が開発され、そこでは3つの核となる特徴が整理されている。1. 充足感(Fulfillment):強い肯定的感情を伴い、本質的に報われる深い満足感がある2. 有意義性(Significance):自己認識と理解が深まり、しばしば人生の転機となる3. 精神性(Spiritual):体験のさなか、世界と一体化した感覚を持ち、時間の感覚を失うピーク体験には他にも、畏怖・崇敬・謙虚さ・自己の明け渡しといった感覚が伴うことが多く、マズローはこうした体験を定期的に得る人はより遊び心があり、自立していて、生き生きしていると考えた。●19の詳細な特性(『宗教・価値・ピーク体験』などより)マズローは『存在の心理学に向けて』の中で、ピーク体験を「最高の幸福と充足の瞬間」と定義し、被存在愛の体験、親としての体験、神秘的・大海的・自然体験、美的知覚、創造的瞬間、治療的・知的な洞察、オルガズム体験、ある種の運動的達成感など、実に多様な文脈でこの体験が生じることを示した。実際、調べれば調べるほどマズローは誰もがピーク体験を持ちうると考えるようになり、報告できない人にはむしろ違和感を覚えるようになった。特性リストの半分近くは、体験が統一的・非二元的で、カテゴリー化されない性質に関するものである。残り半分には、その体験が本質的に価値があり、善く、望ましく、リアルで真実であるという性質、自我・時間・空間を超越する性質、受動的で受容的な性質、そして感情的に高揚した性質(畏怖・崇敬・明け渡しが存在し、恐怖・不安・抑制が不在である)が含まれる。精神分析的な言い回しでは、マズローはピーク体験を「自我、イド、超自我、自我理想の融合、意識・前意識・無意識の融合、一次過程と二次過程の融合、快感原則と現実原則の統合、恐れのない健全な退行、あらゆるレベルにおける人格の真の統合」だと表現した。マズロー的な言い方では、ピーク体験者は「これらのエピソードの中で最も真に自分自身となり、自分の可能性をより完全に発揮し、存在の核心により近づき、より完全に人間らしくなる」とされる。●16の側面(『存在の心理学に向けて』)『存在の心理学に向けて』の中でマズローは、ピーク体験を実現した人々に観察された16の性質を挙げている。ピーク体験にある人は、より統合され、全体的で、断片化・解離が少なく、内的な分裂や緊張が少ないため、より自律的で内面的に平穏を感じる。マズローはピーク体験において人間は自分の本当の自己に最も近づき、最も個性的になると論じ、これを「最もクリーンで汚染のないデータ源」——つまり発明が最小限に抑えられ、発見が最大化される状態——だと述べた。マズローはこの章の結びで、16のアイデンティティの側面の中で、誇りと謙虚さという二律背反的な関係を、ひとつの上位の統一へと融合させることで解消できると示唆している。これは東洋仏教哲学に見られる陰陽の原理にも似て、生とは何ものも単独では存在しえない、二元的でありながら協働的な実体であるという考え方である。■ B価値(存在価値)― ピーク体験の中で知覚される世界マズローが「最も重要な発見」と呼んだのが、B価値、すなわち「存在の内在的価値」である。これはピーク体験の最中に世界がどう知覚されるかを記述したものであり、代表的なものに以下がある。1. 真実(誠実さ、現実性:裸性、単純さ、豊かさ、本質性、当為性、美——純粋で混じりけのない完全性)2. 善(軽やかさ、望ましさ、当為性、正義、慈悲、誠実さ。我々はそれを愛し、惹かれ、是認する)3. 美(軽やかさ、形式、生命感、単純さ、豊かさ、全体性、完全性、独自性、誠実さ)このB価値のリストは他にも一体性、生き生きとした感覚、独自性、完全性、必然性、無矛盾性、遊戯性、自己充足性など複数項目に及ぶ。マズローは科学と宗教が互いに切り離されてしまい、その結果どちらも劣化した形になっていると考え、両者の有用な側面を統合する新しい科学の必要性を説いた。■ 自己実現から自己超越へ ― 階層説の後期改訂とピーク体験の位置づけマズローの自己超越論は近年になってようやく光が当てられるようになった。1943年に階層説を発表した後もマズローは自己実現にこだわり続けたが、5段階の階層モデルでは自己実現した人々の動機づけを十分に説明できず、また自己実現した人々でもしばしば問題行動をとるという矛盾する観察を説明できないと感じるようになった。この矛盾を解く方法を探し続けた末、マズローは自己実現の欲求のさらに上に「自己超越」という第6の動機づけ欲求を置く、改訂版の階層説を講演で説明するようになった。しかし、この自己超越論を広く発表する前にマズローはジョギング中に急死し、彼の最終的な完全版の階層説は歴史の中で一部失われてしまった。2006年にコルトコ=リベラがこれを再発見し、一般向けに詳細な論文を発表するまで、心理学界は自己実現を頂点とする不完全版の階層説のまま何十年も動いていた。自己実現が自分自身の潜在能力を実現することを指すのに対し、自己超越は文字通り自己を超越することを指す。そしてもし成功すれば、自己を超越する人はしばしばマズローが「ピーク体験」と呼んだもの、すなわち個としての自我を超越する体験を得る。ここに超個人心理学と、多くの世界宗教における神秘主義・瞑想的伝統とのつながりがある。■ プラトー体験(plateau experience)との違いピーク体験を補完する概念として、マズローがキャリアの終盤に発展させたのが「プラトー体験」である。ピーク体験がしばしば感覚の恍惚とした噴出であるのに対し、プラトー体験は静穏で内省的な、当人が自分の状況を感じると同時に考えることもできる落ち着いた瞬間である。ピーク体験と異なり、プラトー体験は意図的に育むことができる。プラトー体験は、ピークの「白熱した」恍惚の瞬間とは違い、穏やかな喜びが持続する期間として現れる。マズローは、新生児を何時間も驚異の眼差しで見つめる母親や、互いの目を見つめ合う恋人たちの例を挙げている。個人的な例として、太平洋の輝く海岸に立ち尽くし、寄せては返す波を眺めながら次第に高揚した精神状態に入っていく自分自身の様子を描写した。マズローは、身体が年齢を重ねるにつれてピークの瞬間の強度は、より穏やかで持続的な安らぎの状態、すなわちプラトー体験へと移行していくと示唆した。ピーク体験と違い、こうしたプラトーは意識的で地道な努力によって育むことができるとした。マズローがこの概念を人生の非常に遅い時期に定式化したため、ピーク体験ほど広く普及させることができず、多くの人がプラトー体験について聞いたことがないのはそのためである。ピーク体験と比較すると、プラトーはより認知的で、穏やかで、感情の強度が低く、日常的であり(稀ではない)、思いがけない恩寵というより何年もの意図的な取り組みによって到達するものである。この概念は、彼が1970年にRVPEに追加した序文に要約が示されているほか、マズロー自身、死の直前までこの体験が実際に何であったのかを解明しようとしていた。■ フロー理論(チクセントミハイ)との比較20世紀後半、ミハイ・チクセントミハイはこれに近い概念を「フロー」と名づけて研究した。ピーク体験と同様、フローも自分の技能を最大限使うよう課題づけられた活動に従事しているときに生じる没入状態である。チクセントミハイと同様に、マズローもすべての人がピーク体験をしうると考えていたが、自己実現を達成した人々の方がより頻繁にそれを経験しやすいとした。両者とも没入・時間感覚の喪失など共通する特徴を挙げつつ、その解釈は異なり、マズローはアインシュタインやリンカーンなどを例に、自己実現を果たせる人はごく少数だと主張した。チクセントミハイは、完全にある活動——特に創造的能力を要する活動——に没入している「フロー」という意識状態の中で、人は本物の満足を見出すと発見した。この「最適な体験」の中で人は「強く、油断なく、努力せずに制御でき、自意識を忘れ、自分の能力の頂点にある」と感じる。マズローの後を継ぐ形で、チクセントミハイも幸福は単純に起こるものではなく、各自が準備し育まなければならないものだと主張し、自分の能力に対して要求が高すぎず低すぎもしない挑戦を設定することを重視した。明確な相違点も指摘されている。フローは、チクセントミハイの1991年の著書『フロー体験 喜びの現象学』で述べられている通り、課題志向的であるのに対し、ピーク体験はより受動的で受容的な性質を持つとされる。フロー体験はピーク体験とは対照的に、楽しくはあるが持続時間が短い。心理学者ゲイル・プリベットによる画期的な研究では、ピーク体験・ピークパフォーマンス・フローに共通する没入感・自発性・喜びといった特徴が示された一方で、この3つの中で「フロー」が最も学習可能で反復可能な超越的状態であることも示された(Privette, G. (1983). Peak experience, peak performance, and flow: A comparative analysis of positive human experiences. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 45(6), 1361–1368)。●ピークパフォーマンスとの違い心理学者プリベットは、ピークパフォーマンスを「人間の潜在能力の卓越した発揮の典型であり、習慣的な行動よりも効率的・創造的・生産的、あるいは何らかの点で優れている」ものと定義し、これは長期的な状態や活動の種類というより「卓越した機能発揮のエピソード」であり、稀な出来事、時には一生に一度の出来事だとした。マズローがピーク体験を動機づけを持たない、あるいはメタ動機的なものとして描写したのに対し、プリベットはピークパフォーマンスにおいては強い動機づけと(少なくとも努力に関する)意図が重要であることを見出した。チクセントミハイはフローの主要な特徴のひとつとして内発的動機づけ、すなわち活動そのものに内在する楽しさを挙げている。ピーク体験とフローはともに「遊戯的」と表現されるが、ピークパフォーマンス研究の回答者たちは自分たちの最高の瞬間において遊戯性を感じたとは答えなかった。この3つの体験に共通して最も重なりが大きいのは、没入感・全き注意・明晰な集中である。■ 誘発要因(トリガー)マズローの研究は、ピーク体験の一般的なトリガーとして、芸術・自然・性・創造的な仕事・音楽・幻覚剤・宗教的な祝祭・科学的発見を示唆している。別の研究者ラスキ(Laski, 1962)は「芸術、自然、性愛、宗教、運動と身体活動、創造的な仕事、"美"、出産、科学的知識、回想と内省、詩的な知識」などを共通する"恍惚のトリガー"として挙げた。マズロー(1971)もまた、音楽と性がピーク体験の最も典型的なトリガーであると指摘している。ピーク体験を誘発する状況は人によって、また文化によっても異なると考えられる。一般的には、自然の中にいること、音楽を聴く・演奏すること、大切な人と一緒にいることなどが挙げられることが多い。これらの状況は、ピーク体験の前提条件となりうる感情的な開放性を促すと考えられている。一部の人にとっては幻覚性物質の摂取もピーク体験を誘発しうる。なお、マズロー自身は文化差を研究していないが、心理学者プリベットがこれを研究し、文化によって最も重要な体験の記述の仕方が異なりうることを見出した。マズローは、出産や早期の母子の絆形成の瞬間が、それまで一度もピーク体験をしたことがない人においてさえ確実にピーク体験を誘発すると指摘した。より新しい研究として、デマレス(DeMares, 2000)はクジラやイルカとの遭遇など、動物との自発的な接触がピーク体験のトリガーとなりうる未検討の現象を探究し、6人へのインタビューを現象学的還元によって分析し、相互性、意図、つながり、生命感、調和という5つのテーマを見出した。■ 測定と実証研究ピーク体験はその性質上、実験室での統制された実験による再現が難しく、これまでの研究の大半はインタビュー・質問紙・ナラティブ分析によって構成されてきた。マズローは自己実現していると考えた人物の歴史的・伝記的記録を調査し、アクセスできる人にはインタビューを行い、また大学生を対象にもピーク体験についてインタビューした。こうした調査手法は、あまりに開放的で体系性を欠くと批判されており、豊かな記述が得られる一方で一般化可能性に欠ける可能性がある。こうした限界に対処するため、後続の研究者たちはより広い母集団間でピーク体験を定量化・比較できる標準化された心理測定尺度を開発した。プリベットは「Experience Questionnaire(EQ)」を開発し、ピーク体験の性質を研究した。また1982年にはE・W・メイシスによって「Peak Experiences Scale」が開発された。近年の応用研究として、職場でのピーク体験(Employees' Peak Experience)を扱ったFrontiers誌の研究がある。この研究は、ピーク体験を高度に肯定的な感情として捉え、従業員の職務経験における最高の幸福と充足の瞬間と定義し、感情の次元モデルに基づき、それが高覚醒の肯定的気分であると位置づけている。こうした研究の蓄積の中で、対象者はスポーツ選手(Hollander & Acevedo, 2000)、芸術家(Yeagle et al., 1989)、バックパッカー(Ryan et al., 2003)、大学生(Hoffman et al., 2021)など特定の集団に焦点を当てるものへと広がっている。野外活動領域でも、2021年の研究では、荒野(ウィルダネス)体験が意識に与える影響を検討し、挑戦・没入・美・時間という4つの媒介要因が最大化されたときに、気づきの増大・自信・視点の変化・つながりという4つのテーマが生じ、それが十分に強度を持つとマズローの言う「ピーク体験」を引き起こすことを見出した(British Journal of Psychiatry Open掲載)。■ 批判・限界方法論に対する批判が最も大きい。マズロー理論に対する最も重要な批判は、非科学的なアプローチ、信頼性の低いサンプル、そして個人的な観察と伝記的分析という具体的な研究手法にある。すなわち、マズローの人間動機づけ理論は信頼できる実証研究に基づいたものではなかった。科学界においてマズローの階層説の妥当性を裏づける証拠は部分的にしか、あるいはほとんど存在しない。もうひとつの重要な批判は方法論における自民族中心的偏り、すなわちほぼアメリカ人(その多くが高学歴・知的・男性)にほぼ限定して調査していることであり、これは高度に個人主義的な文化を前提にしている。階層の上位に位置する欲求の多くは達成・自尊心・個人的成長といった自己に焦点を当てたものであり、東洋文化などに必ずしも一般化・移転できるものではない。自己実現という概念自体が定義・測定が非常に難しいという批判もある。何をもって潜在能力の実現とするのか。マズローは主観的な基準を用い、自身の判断で自己実現した人物を特定したため、確証バイアスの余地がある。追試の試みは一貫しない結果を生んでおり、これは構成概念が操作的定義に馴染みにくいことも一因である。ピーク体験論は心理学者・研究者の間で今なお議論のある(controversial)トピックであり、マズローの階層説の多くの部分は研究によって検証されておらず、場合によっては不正確であるとされる。ある批評家は次のように指摘している。基本的な欲求が満たされている西洋社会の(しかも低い社会階層に属さない)多くの人々が、依然として退屈し、権利意識を持ち、フラストレーションを抱え、絶望しており、必ずしも超越を求めているわけではないとすれば、そこには別の説明が必要ではないかという趣旨である。それでも、プリンストン大学のウリエル・アブロフ研究員は「21世紀にこそマズローが必要な理由」の中で、マズロー理論が大衆の想像力の中で持ち続けている共鳴こそが、たとえ非科学的に見えようとも、その理論の重要性を物語る最も雄弁な証拠だと述べている。それは人間の本性を、ほとんどの人が自分自身や他者の中に即座に認識できる形で説明しているからだとしている。ワバとブリッドウェル(Wahba & Bridwell, 1976)による有名なレビュー研究は、マズローの主張を検証しようとした複数の研究を精査し、当初示された形の階層説を支持する証拠はごくわずかで一貫性を欠くことを見出した。どの欲求がどこで終わりどこから次が始まるかを操作的に定義し測定すること、まして下位欲求の「優越性(prepotency)」を実証することは方法論的に困難である。「普遍的な」順序を再現しようとする試みはしばしば失敗し、文化的・状況的な変数が結果を大きく左右する。■ 現代的な意義・応用批判はあるものの、ピーク体験論はポジティブ心理学の源流として位置づけられている。こうした創造性豊かな人々のマインドセット・習慣・パーソナリティ・精神状態についての科学的研究が、後にマズロー自身が「ポジティブ心理学」と呼ぶことになる分野の礎となった。フロイト心理学が人間の本性を無意識的・破壊的な衝動に突き動かされ、制御されるべきものとみなしていたのに対し、マズローは適切な環境と、健全な自己同一性やパーソナリティの発達に焦点を当てたより包括的な教育があれば、若者は強い人格を発達させ、意味のある問題解決や地域社会への貢献へと自らを方向づけると論じた。彼の研究によれば、文化的な刷り込みや学校教育の制約を超えて自信を持って考え行動できる、最も創造的で強い人格を持つ人々の多くは、彼が「ピーク体験」と呼ぶものによって根本的に形づくられていた。職場応用の研究も進んでおり、従業員のピーク体験を研究するFrontiers誌の論文は、ピーク体験を「高度に肯定的な感情」として位置づけ、それが職務経験における最高の幸福と充足の瞬間であるとしている。これに伴い、対象領域はスポーツ、芸術、アウトドアレジャー、大学生など多岐にわたって広がっている。3-highest-human-experiencesの記事でも整理されている通り、ピーク体験・ピークパフォーマンス・フローのいずれにも共通するのは人間の力と可能性への気づきであり、体験の後により統合され、より完全な個人としての感覚を得るという「統合と人格的アイデンティティ」の要素である。これは意味の感覚、責任と力の感覚、あるいは活動の構造を通じた明晰さといった形で現れる。■ まとめマズローのピーク体験論は、1943年の欲求階層説から出発し、自己実現研究の副産物として発見され、『存在の心理学に向けて』(1962)や『宗教・価値・ピーク体験』(1964)で理論化され、晩年には「自己超越」というさらに上位の段階、そして「プラトー体験」という補完概念へと展開していった、マズロー心理学の中核をなすテーマです。チクセントミハイのフロー理論やプリベットのピークパフォーマンス研究など、後続の実証的な positive psychology 研究の出発点にもなった一方で、方法論の非体系性・サンプルの偏り・自己実現概念の測定困難性といった批判にもさらされ続けています。それでも、芸術・自然・音楽・出産・宗教・スポーツなど多様な文脈で人が体験する「至高の瞬間」を語る語彙として、現在も心理学・スポーツ科学・組織行動論・野外教育など幅広い領域で参照され続けています。■ 参考文献・出典リンク一覧DIY
